commission. - (es) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, first of all i would like to thank the four rapporteurs sincerely for the excellent work they have done, which has allowed us to reach the plenary today with reports which are generally positive, which go in the same direction as the commission's proposal and which support the commission's approach. i would also like to thank parliament for agreeing to treat these reports as a package, avoiding the temptation to fragment them, which would undoubtedly have been detrimental to our common objective of finally creating a genuine european railway area. ladies and gentlemen, this is the second stage in a lengthy process. following the entry into force on 15 march 2001 of three directives of the infrastructure package, which will have to be transposed into the national law of the member states as from 15 march 2003, it is now necessary to complete the legislative framework in order to accelerate the establishment of a genuine european railway area. this process is the basis for the four proposals we are going to discuss today. first, i would refer to the proposal to amend directive 91/440/eec to extend the rights of access to infrastructure and freight transport services provided within the member states and to speed up the opening up of the market. the rapporteur was mr jarzembowski, who has done a magnificent job. the white paper on european transport policy, ladies and gentlemen, gives a startling account of the development of rail freight transport. over the last 20 years, the share of this segment - within the overall distribution of freight transport in the union - has been halved from 15% in 1980 to 8% in 1999. in this period the quality of services provided to customers has not improved and in some states has even worsened. this is therefore a matter of the utmost urgency. in my view, it is not possible to wait until 2008 to open up the entire european network to competition in international freight transport. domestic transport must also be considered. the amendments proposed therefore replace the timetable and the opening procedures provided for in directive 2001/12/ec, and bring about the immediate opening of the national and international freight transport to the entire network. in practice, this full opening of access rights in the area of goods would be effective by 2006, which would bring the opening to the whole network two years ahead of schedule. the second proposal for a directive, ladies and gentlemen, is of course about railway safety. i think that the question of transport safety is something that concerns and concerns us all, especially at this time. i also want to thank mr sterckx for his work. we must ensure that the integration of the european rail network does not lead to a lowering of the maximum safety standards in the various member states of the union. but at the same time we must ensure that the establishment of common standards prevents market disruption and discrimination in access to networks through security. the creation of an internal market for rail services would not be possible without the establishment of common safety standards. the opening up of markets and the end of monopolies also significantly change the system of responsibilities in an area such as safety, and therefore a coherent, transparent and clear framework is needed to avoid any doubt in this area. the safety directive focuses on four areas: designation of national safety authorities, distinct from operators, with clearly defined responsibilities; determination of the essential elements of safety systems in relation to the infrastructure manager and railway undertakings and establishment of a mechanism for the determination and adoption of common safety objectives and methods - role to be played by the railway agency; establishment of a common system for the granting, content and validity of safety certificates; and finally, introduction, as in other sectors, of the principle of independence of technical investigations in the event of accidents or incidents. we come to the third proposal for a directive. if we establish the network, if we guarantee a common level of security and clearly defined responsibilities, then we must also establish an interoperable system. the amendment of directives 96/48/ec and 2001/16/ec on interoperability, for which mrs ainardi is the rapporteur, is therefore a necessary step. in addition to the adaptations which experience suggests, the main aim is to ensure consistency in the fields of application of the network in which open access is carried out and the network in which interoperability rules must be applied. it is also a very clear signal that equipment must be standardised in order to reduce costs. we cannot simply abolish administrative frontiers, but we must also abolish technological frontiers in order to create a european railway network. i would like to thank you for the work you have done on a very technical and difficult dossier, but on which the work of parliament, once again, and of the rapporteur, is of the highest standard. finally, i would refer to the fourth proposal, which is to create a european railway agency, on which mr savary has done a very remarkable job. the agency is the key to the vault, the end of the circle, the instrument which will make progress possible in the field of railway safety interoperability and thus guarantee the integration of the european rail network. it is a technical decision-making support agency with no autonomous powers, which will provide the commission with opinions and recommendations. the texts in question will be adopted by the commission in accordance with a comitology procedure, as is already the case with interoperability. its main areas of activity will be: technical preparation of texts for the safety directive - common safety objectives and common safety methods - and for the interoperability directives; establishment of a network of national safety and interoperability authorities; technical advice to the commission and national authorities on specific cases in the field of safety standards. the agency, which will have a staff of about 100, will be responsible for promoting the technical approximation of rail systems and will be independent but will work in close collaboration with experts in the sector. in conclusion, mr president, the texts proposed here are intended, on the one hand, to make 15 incompatible national systems technically evolve towards an integrated and competitive european railway area and, on the other hand, to accelerate the opening up of the freight transport market, so as to enable operators to provide efficient services wherever they are. let us once and for all make a commitment to a modern railway worthy of the 21st century, capable of competing positively with other modes of transport.

commission. – mr president, the commission is committed to addressing the dramatic humanitarian crisis in angola effectively and without delay and to supporting the peace process. the commission is constantly monitoring the situation in angola, as we have done for many years, in order to get a clear picture of humanitarian needs. i will be going to angola – and also to zambia – to assess the situation myself later this month, so i shall gain an overview of the humanitarian situation and the development of the peace process in angola. on that occasion i will be signing the ec-angola cooperation strategy for 2002-2007, including the plan of action. the commission's action in angola is twofold: emergency humanitarian aid and a longer-term strategy based on cooperation. this is funded by echo and by edf funds. as far as the humanitarian aid is concerned, the commission, through echo, has already generated a considerable amount of funding to address the needs and will maintain its presence and commitment in the country throughout this year. last year angola was among the top ten recipients of echo funding, receiving a total of eur 14 million. this year, an initial decision has been taken to provide eur 8 million funding, due to be adopted soon. malnutrition is one of the main targets for our support in the humanitarian area, particularly in forgotten regions where no other donors are present in the country. as far as the longer-term strategy is concerned, in may 2002, a month after the signature of the peace agreement, a plan of action to support the peace process was presented by the commission and approved by the general affairs council on 13 may. the plan of action identified a financial package, originally eur 124 million, from unspent edf funds and budget lines aimed at addressing the most pressing concerns at this stage, including emergency relief, food aid and food security, reintegration and resettlement of refugees and displaced persons and de-mining operations. the implementation of this is now under way and to our great satisfaction we can start doing things in a country where for many years we have, owing to the circumstances, only been able to do humanitarian work. on that basis, and as part of this plan of action, the commission has made eur 30 million available for emergency support for the peace process by reallocating funds from earlier european development funds to support short-term work on the peace process. these funds are targeted at medical assistance, the distribution of seeds and tools, food aid and the resettlement of former unita soldiers and their families. de-mining is also important. we tried to do all this as quickly as possible last year. the decision on all this will be implemented through different un agencies, euronaid and fao for the food security component and different ngos for the de-mining operations. proposals for eur 16 million have been signed and the remaining proposals are awaiting approval by the angolan national authorities. they are expected to be finalised within the next few weeks. although humanitarian support will continue to be provided, the commission considers that pressure must be kept up on the angolan government to urge it to assume more direct responsibility for its own vulnerable populations. we are therefore calling upon the government of angola to make more efforts in addressing the critical humanitarian needs of the population. we welcome the angolan government’s intention to organise an international conference for the reconstruction of the country, and trust that the views of all groups in society will be reflected in the reconstruction plan to be presented. the commission has offered to assist in the organisation of the conference, which is tentatively scheduled to take place in march or april 2003 in brussels, kindly hosted by the belgian government. these are times of great change and challenge for angola after many years of conflict. the emphasis now will be on progress, economic growth, stability and governance. that will change the whole mood of politics in the country and i am looking forward to the dialogue we shall be participating in next week.
the commission has already done so. i would like to continue with what has just been said. angola was one of africa's largest agricultural exporters a few decades ago. it is therefore shocking that food aid has to be delivered to this country today because of war and also because of socialist mismanagement. i want to ask you three questions. firstly, what specific agricultural programmes is the commission implementing? i think the most important thing is that the country becomes self-sufficient and agricultural exporter again. secondly, what is the infrastructure to distribute the food? and thirdly, what about programmes in the fields of education and training? i think these are the three most important points to be made.
commission. – kosovo's status is currently defined under un security council resolution 1244 of 10 june 1999. any decision on its final status will therefore have to be taken by the security council. the international community has not set a clear point in time at which this issue will be debated. consequently it is not up to the commission to draw up scenarios for kosovo's future status. the european union fully supports the policy of standards before status pursued by the un interim administration mission in kosovo to which i have just referred, endorsed by the un security council at its meeting of 24 april last year. unmic has set clear benchmarks concerning democratic and market economic reforms, human and minority rights, which are all necessary to prepare kosovo for future challenges. these basic standards must be met before a discussion on status can begin. kosovo is an integral part of the region for which we have devised the stabilisation and association process to bring it closer to european union structures. we have made sure that kosovo's unresolved status does not prevent it from benefiting from the stabilisation and association process.
i too know that the present status is defined by the un resolution, but we must also look to the future, and i see the following problem: no major investor will invest in kosovo unless he knows what the future of the area is in the long term. people will continue to try to emigrate and not to bring their strength to the country itself if they do not see what kosovo's prospects are. the european union is not prepared to accept the fact that the kosovo crisis has been a catastrophe for the whole of europe. we cannot simply go into a future that is coming very soon without any concept, because the present situation cannot last for decades.

the rapporteur. - mr president, you have rightly pointed out that today is the third reading of the report on cosmetic products. most of us know that this is a subject which this parliament has been dealing with time and again for ten years now. the vast majority of the proposals, both in the previous legislation and in this one, concern the areas of 'prohibition of animal testing and prohibition european union was the question 'can animal testing of toothpaste and shampoo be allowed in the future? other there was a lot of controversy: can a product that has been tested on animals still be sold? we have repeatedly said in parliament that the only way to prevent the export of tests is to link a ban on testing with a ban on marketing, that is to say, a ban on selling. this was also the key issue in the first and second readings of this seventh amendment to the cosmetics directive. but we have also pointed out in the committee responsible and here in parliament that cosmetics and cosmetic products are a direct consumer protection. we have pointed out that, for example, consumers are interested in information on the durability of a product. consumers should know how long they can use a cosmetic product once it has been opened. this parliament has also made proposals on this subject at first and second readings. finally, parliament has also called - and i have been happy to support it as rapporteur - for hazardous substances known to be carcinogenic, reproductive or mutagenic not to be used in cosmetics. these were the essential elements of our second reading. everything was controversial. the second reading was a very large majority, but the commission did not exactly welcome us with open arms. but today, in the third reading, we are actually going to praise ourselves. that is why i say that the conciliation process was difficult. i have witnessed many mediation procedures, directly or indirectly, in recent years. in this conciliation procedure, i was not sure at the beginning that we would reach a compromise. we reached a compromise. the result is that there will be a ban on animal testing for cosmetics six years after the legislation is passed. there will be a ban on the sale of most products containing ingredients tested on animals six years after this legislation is passed. we also said that there will be an exception for three tests where it is not yet clear when alternatives will be developed. the cosmetics industry is not necessarily innocent of this. the reason these tests are so underdeveloped is that the cosmetics industry has been, well, let's say, sleepy in the last few years. but we're giving them an incentive to develop alternatives now, given some time. i want to make it clear that this is a compromise we have reached. this compromise, like all compromises, is not the ideal world. i know the cosmetics industry feels that it's not the ideal world. i also know that the animal welfare organizations believe that more could have been done. i have repeatedly told my colleagues in the animal welfare organisations that if you find someone who can do more, bring him here and let him do it. i have tried with my colleagues to commission. – mr president, i will try to live up to that request. we turn now from one end of europe, as it were, to another. the northern dimension continues to occupy an extremely important place on the commission's external relations agenda. the commission has been working hard to implement the northern dimension action plan that was endorsed by the european council at feira in june 2000, and to prepare for a new action plan. we are determined to continue to take a leading role in carrying forward this important initiative. last year saw significant progress in all nine sectors encompassed by the action plan. the commission's 2002 annual progress report on the implementation of the northern dimension action plan presents a complete overview of these results. i would like to pick out a few concrete examples. the commission has actively contributed to launching the northern dimension environmental partnership, with its support fund for environmental and nuclear projects in northwest russia. the commission is by far the largest contributor to the fund, with eur 50 million over three years, mainly for nuclear-related projects. the northern dimension environmental partnership is a clear example of how cooperation in the northern dimension region can achieve tangible results in very sensitive areas, calling for urgent action. in this context much attention is also being devoted to resolving the remaining details of the multilateral nuclear environmental programme for the russian federation, the so-called mnepr. i hope that we are now very close to a solution and that this key agreement can be signed very soon. much attention has also been devoted to the northern dimension, energy issues, transport, infrastructure, business and trade cooperation and to cooperation in the fight against organised crime. we have continued to support cross-border cooperation through the tacis programme, with a total assistance to northwest russia between 1996 and 2003 of about eur 122 million, about half of this being for border crossings. the commission has also attached great importance to enhancing the coordination and interoperability between its principal programmes operating in the region (mainly tacis, phare and interreg) in order to facilitate the implementation of joint projects in the northern dimension area. this has already helped bring about a considerable increase in the number of joint projects being presented for tacis/interreg or tacis/phare funding in 2001-2002. the past year has also seen continued dialogue with the most important actors involved in the northern dimension. the final agreement with russia and lithuania on the issue of transit to and from the kaliningrad region is a good example of a concrete success in the eu-russia relationship that should bring benefits for the wider northern dimension region. we have already provided more than eur 40 million to the development of kaliningrad and an additional eur 25 million is planned for the coming years. we are determined to assist the russian authorities in improving living standards and addressing the challenges it poses to the wider region. the commission has also been closely following the work of the intergovernmental organisations of the northern dimension region, including the council of the baltic sea states (cbss), the barents euro-arctic council (beac) and the arctic council itself. building on the positive results already achieved, the northern dimension will be further strengthened in the near future. in the coming years, the northern dimension will have to address the impact of european union enlargement, and focus on enhancing links with the russian federation as a neighbour. two ministerial meetings were organised by denmark in the last six months, both focussing on the next action plan. on the basis of guidelines adopted by the council in october last year, the commission is preparing the next northern dimension action plan for the period 2004-2006. we are carrying out an extensive consultation process involving member states, partner countries, and regional bodies, as well as the business world, academia and civil society. our objective is to have a consolidated draft of the action plan (which will replace the current one on 1 january next year) tabled by the middle of this year at the latest. there is still a lot of work to be done. the commission is willingly taking the lead in preparing this new action plan. but i want to make it clear that success will require an active contribution of all partners concerned with the region and i am sure that the european parliament will want to play its part in this process. i am certainly looking forward to hearing the contributions which members have to make in ensuring that the northern dimension, which has begun so well, can go on from strength to strength, particularly after the enlargement of the union.

council the council decided in the first half of 2002 that the european police college would be temporarily located in denmark until a decision on its permanent seat was taken. pending a permanent solution, the current interim arrangement is considered to be functioning satisfactorily. the plan for the management of the external borders of the member states of the european union, adopted by the council at its meeting on 12 and 13 june 2002, provides in its last paragraph for the possibility of setting up a european border guard. however, the plan mentions the creation of a european border guard corps as one of the possible future institutional measures which could be considered appropriate for the development of integrated management of the external borders, after a thorough legal study of the issue of the legal basis and after identifying the means which will become necessary. the european council also noted in seville the commission's intention to continue its examination of the feasibility and practicability of such a police force. the commission has already, as far as we know, started this study. the seville european council also called for the establishment without delay of a common body of those responsible for the surveillance of the external borders, composed of the heads of the border control services of the member states, to coordinate the various measures provided for in the management plan with a view to the progressive establishment of integrated management of the external borders. this joint body was established within the council's strategic committee on migration, borders and asylum on 22-23 july 2002. the joint body, also called scifa +, immediately took over the implementation of the management plan and met five times during the danish presidency. the commission has also held one of these meetings with the participation of the applicant countries.

any cause, however legitimate it may appear. this is of course entirely true for chechnya, but it is also true for our conviction that the fight against terrorism cannot be carried out at the expense commission. – mr president, since at the last session of the parliament in strasbourg i was able to spend an hour with the foreign affairs committee discussing north korea under the benign stewardship i think it is fair to say that, on the whole, since the second world war, we have managed to create global institutions and international agreements which have helped make the world a much more prosperous and peaceful place. i recall that, at the time of president clinton's second inaugural address, he was able to boast that there are today more people living under democracies than under tyrannies; we ended the last century with a world which produced as much in two or three years as we had produced in the whole of the 19th century, with incalculable consequences for the living standards of most people. this is not a bad record after a century which began so badly. plainly, not everything has gone so well. perhaps the greatest failure in trying to create a global rule-book has been our collective failure to establish an adequate regime for controlling and preventing the spread of nuclear, chemical and biological weapons – that terrible arsenal of unimaginable horror. council mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i am pleased to have the opportunity today to present to the european parliament the results of the work of the justice and home affairs council for 2002. the greek presidency attaches particular importance to the role of parliament, to dialogue with it and to the need to formulate a common policy on the issues of concern to us. i would like to thank mrs baroness ludford, whose oral question sets the tone for our debate today. during 2002, the council systematically worked towards the creation of an area of freedom, security and justice, in accordance with the guidelines laid down in particular by the tampere european council. in this context, the council adopted a set of acts on police and judicial cooperation in criminal and civil matters. in particular, more than 100 acts were adopted, including regulations, framework decisions, decisions and common positions, resolutions, recommendations and other acts. the european parliament itself has made a major contribution to this work through the consultation procedure, but it has also helped with its truly exceptional resolutions. among the acts adopted, i would like to make special mention of the establishment of eurojust as a union body to strengthen the fight against the most serious forms of crime, as well as the adoption of the framework decisions on the european arrest warrant, the surrender procedures between member states, and the fight against terrorism. the creation of the european refugee fund, the establishment of eurodac for fingerprint comparison, the establishment of minimum standards for the provision of temporary protection in cases of mass influx of refugees, an integrated plan to combat illegal immigration and trafficking in persons within the european union, the plan for the protection of the external borders, the common list of third countries whose nationals must be in possession of a visa, and the corresponding short list of third countries whose nationals are exempt from the above-mentioned obligation to present a non-formal residence permit for third-country nationals, should also be mentioned. finally, in civil and commercial matters, political agreement was reached on a system of legal aid for parental responsibility to protect the best interests of the child. after this entirely indicative list, i now turn to the questions and would point out that the creation of an area of freedom, security and justice must be based on the principles of transparency and democratic control, and i would assure you that the council will continue its work with a view to cooperating as much as possible with the other institutions of the european union and to a constructive dialogue with civil society. in this context, the council shall cooperate with the european parliament by seeking its opinion at an early stage of the work and by fully applying the rules on consultation laid down in the treaties. the presidency also meets with the european parliament at the beginning of each six-month period to present its work programme and the results of the justice and home affairs council. i would also remind you that the council answers all written and oral questions from the honourable members. at the same time, informal contacts are constantly being strengthened, especially at the meetings of the committee on civil liberties or even on the occasion of informal ministerial meetings. finally, this cooperation will be further strengthened by the new treaty of nice, which places certain matters within our competence in the co-decision procedure. as regards the second question, the council does not believe that for matters as sensitive as those relating to justice and home affairs the time required for the adoption of community acts was excessive. the number and content of the instruments adopted is a reflection of the important work we have done to achieve an area of freedom, security and justice. however, it is equally essential that the requirement of speed be accompanied by a careful examination of each question and by respect for all procedures, in particular the consultation procedure, and henceforth the codecision procedure, so that the council can take due account of the opinion of the european parliament. for this reason, opinions are sometimes requested within fairly short time limits, with the aim of speeding up the adoption of acts at council level as much as possible. as regards the third question, the council notes that its action is carried out within the framework of the rules laid down in the treaties. for example, migration issues are dealt with under title iv of the treaty establishing the european community, while criminal offences against those who are the moral perpetrators of illegal immigration are dealt with under the rules of title vi of the treaty on european union. the complexity of the matter requires a certain pace of procedure, but this is a result of the treaty itself and certainly not of the council's intention. as is well known, the power to amend the treaty does not belong to the council. we are of course following the work being done on this subject in the context of the convention on the future of europe, which will probably lead, and we hope so, to the opening up of new prospects. in the meantime, i can assure you of the efforts of all of us in the council to pursue a coherent and rational policy, showing the necessary political will. as regards the fourth question, the council stresses that the creation of an area of freedom, security and justice is a progressive process leading to ever closer and more progressive cooperation between the member states in the exercise of their powers and the institutions of the union. in this context, the initiatives taken by the member states, either alone or jointly, have demonstrated the exceptional usefulness of their right. for example, it is sufficient to mention the initiative put forward by five member states which led to the creation of eurojust, a union body with an important role in the fight against serious crime. the council framework decision on the status of victims in criminal proceedings was also taken at the initiative of a member state. the regulation on insolvency proceedings, which was the result of an initiative by two member states, was finally put into effect after thirty years of debate in the community. the regulation on the taking of evidence is another such success. the initiatives of the member states, which were adopted by a large majority, contributed to the particular dynamism of the justice and home affairs sector and served as a useful complement to the commission's always worthwhile initiatives. as regards the fifth question, according to the treaty of amsterdam, after a period of five years from its entry into force, that is to say in 2004, the council, acting unanimously after consulting the european parliament, will be called upon to adopt a decision on the co-decision procedure in the fields of visas, asylum and immigration and judicial cooperation in civil matters. the council has not yet been asked to give a ruling on the specific question raised. it is therefore a question on which the council will have the opportunity to take a decision in the future, having taken into account the views of the european parliament. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the european parliament is able to exercise its right of initiative in the matter of the internal market. the council will adhere to these new rules. as regards the sixth question, as i have already said, considerable progress has been made within the council on asylum and immigration with a view to implementing the programme adopted in tampere. the european council in seville on 21 and 22 june 2002 was an important step in the implementation of the tampere programme. as regards time, the council intends to respect the deadlines as far as possible, given the complexity of the matter and the events which have undoubtedly altered the general perception of the political and legislative environment. as regards the last question, the council, as it has repeatedly stressed, respects and applies the principles laid down in the treaty, in particular the principles of liberty, democracy, respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms and the rule of law. the question of whether the charter of fundamental rights should be incorporated into the new treaty is, however, a matter which does not fall within the powers conferred on the council by the treaties. as regards the second part of the question, concerning the work on the common principles on procedural guarantees for defendants, the council is aware that the commission has adopted a working document and is preparing a new one. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos is a very good one. we are convinced, and our initiatives are guided by the principle, that respect for human rights and the rule of law is the foundation of the union and the ultimate justification for all its policies. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. these two principles are inextricably linked. i believe that if the role of fundamental freedoms is ignored, then there is a clear danger that our policy will be fragmented, one-sided and irrational. this is particularly important in the sphere of action of our council, where the question of relations of freedom on the one hand and security on the other is raised on a daily basis. it would be wrong to consider these two goods as competing with each other. i have said many times, and i say it again, that more security does not mean and must not mean less freedom. the greek presidency has therefore proposed a new draft framework decision on the recognition of criminal convictions between member states. our path towards judicial cooperation cannot be one-sided. it should also ensure that the prisoner is not prosecuted multiple times for the same offence for which he has already been tried in a member state. the same principle also governs the question of the protection of minimum guarantees for suspects and accused persons. we have introduced the european arrest warrant, we are taking steps to harmonize substantive criminal law, and we cannot, i believe, ignore the question of guarantees for all those who will be affected by these measures, particularly as suspects or accused persons. the commission has already taken the initiative in the matter of the minimum procedural guarantees for suspects and accused persons, which is why we have already included it on the agenda of the informal council meeting to be held in greece at the end of march. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to conclude by thanking you again for the opportunity you have given me to inform parliament of the progress made in the area of justice and security and to assure you that i look forward to your help and cooperation in meeting the expectations of european society and its citizens. i would like to thank the commissioner for his reply.
commission. - mr president, mr minister, ladies and gentlemen, the annual debate on the area of freedom, security and justice must be seen in the wider context of the progress actually made during the past year, thanks to the commitment of the successive spanish and danish presidencies, but also in the light of the forthcoming enlargement and the work of the convention on the future of europe. first of all, i would like to congratulate baroness ludford on the quality of the questions she has put to the commission and to reply to the first of them at once that the commission still considers that in the future treaty, in the area of the area of freedom, security and justice, we should enshrine the principle of the exclusive right of legislative initiative by the commission. we believe that the transition of most legislative aspects to the codecision procedure will only be consistent if we maintain the framework of the commission's right of legislative initiative. the retention of the right of legislative initiative by one or more member states will always give rise to difficulties and confusion in the application of the common codecision rules. the commission's right of initiative is already the most relevant, precisely because it is exercised within the framework of an interinstitutional programme agreed with the european parliament and the european council itself. as regards the second question, concerning the priorities for combating terrorism and illegal immigration, the commission considers that these were not only priorities in 2002 but will continue to be priorities in 2003. the european union has demonstrated its ability to respond to the terrorist threat by adopting two important instruments: the european arrest warrant and the framework decision on the fight against terrorism. in the commission's view, the final text of these two legislative initiatives strikes a good balance between the objectives of facilitating investigations and prosecutions against terrorists on the one hand and protecting the rights of the accused on the other, but i will return to this question a little later. the seville european council gave new impetus to accelerate all aspects of the implementation of the programme adopted in tampere with a view to creating an area of freedom, security and justice. a new priority was given to measures to combat illegal immigration and to establish a common management of the external borders. but at the same time the seville council also set objectives and timetables for adopting the other decisions on asylum and immigration policy which are envisaged in the framework of the tampere council conclusions. the commission has responded promptly to this new priority by presenting its proposals for an integrated system of external border management, which was generally welcomed by the council and incorporated in the action plan which was not only approved by the council in june last year but also supported by the european parliament in a resolution voted last month. this progress must of course be assessed in the light of the timetable and programmes of measures agreed at tampere. and they must respect a balanced approach between the three components: freedom, security and justice. the commission once again stressed in its latest scoreboard of 16 december 2002 that there are still delays in adopting asylum and immigration matters. we hope that the greek presidency, as the minister has just said, will make efforts to speed up the work on adopting this legislation within the framework envisaged by the european council in seville. with regard to mrs ludford's fourth question, i would like to say that the greek presidency has put the debate on family reunification and the status of longterm residents in the european union as priorities on the agenda, together with the directive on the entry of thirdcountry nationals for the purpose of paid employment which was discussed in this parliament yesterday and the directive on the conditions of entry and residence for the purpose of study of thirdcountry nationals. we will thus have the essential legislative framework on immigration policy under discussion in the council. the commission will also take the initiative of presenting a communication next month on the integration of third-country nationals into european host societies. as regards the future of decision-making procedures, the commission welcomes the conclusions of the convention's working party on justice and home affairs to recognise that in matters of asylum, immigration and other policies relating to free movement, the general rule of decision-making should be the adoption of legislative acts under a codecision procedure where the council acts by qualified majority. and i welcome the fact that this conclusion of the convention's working party was largely a majority. as regards treaty amendments, the commission encourages the convention to adopt the rule of a more explicit legal basis for the development of a common european asylum system going beyond the mere common minimum standards currently under discussion in the council. as regards the question the honourable member raises about the usefulness and effectiveness of networks, the commission would like to make it clear to parliament that it has a positive assessment of the work carried out by networks which have an effective operational purpose, whether europol, eurojust, bodies such as the task force of police chiefs, the european judicial network in civil matters or the judicial network in criminal matters. however, we must stress that not all networks have the same added value and that the council should be more selective in the choice of priorities for the creation of such networks. as regards the relationship between the commission and the european parliament, the commission intends to comply scrupulously with the framework agreement signed by the two institutions on 5 july 2000. in this context, i intend to inform the european parliament's committee on civil liberties and justice in brussels next week on the progress of the negotiations on readmission agreements with third countries. as regards the question of assessing the way in which framework decisions are transposed into the domestic legal order of each member state, the commission draws parliament's attention to the fact that the way in which framework decisions are assessed varies from one framework decision to another. we believe that the priority at this stage is the framework decision on the fight against terrorism, which should have been transposed by all the member states by the end of 2002. we are gathering information from the member states on this transposition and hope to submit a report on it by the end of 2003. as always, the commission pays particular attention to the balance between respect for the law and the protection of the fundamental rights of individuals and the fight against organised crime and terrorism. in this context, following a recommendation from the european parliament, the commission has set up a network of experts on fundamental rights. this year's report by the network of experts will focus on the compatibility of measures taken by the member states and the european union to combat terrorism and respect for fundamental rights. finally, as regards the last question raised by the honourable member concerning the framework decision on procedural guarantees for persons accused in criminal proceedings, the commission welcomes the intention of the greek presidency to include this matter in the discussion of the informal veria council at the end of march. for our part, before that council we will adopt a green paper on common rules on procedural guarantees for accused persons in criminal proceedings throughout the union. this green paper will give civil society and legal professionals, both in the current member states and in the future member states, the opportunity to contribute to the debate with a view to the presentation of a proposal for a framework decision which we believe should be scheduled by the end of this year. the commission is therefore committed to establishing common minimum standards in this area, as was underlined in the presentation of the annual work programme for 2003. i would like to conclude by announcing that work is also under way, albeit at a later stage, on the guarantees of equal treatment in the taking and handling of evidence and the right to remain silent in criminal proceedings, matters which we consider particularly important in order to create a common basis, a common platform, in the field of criminal proceedings in order to make mutual trust and cooperation between judicial authorities more effective in the fight against organised crime. in summary, progress is unequivocal and undeniable. they are not balanced in all areas of the area of freedom, security and justice, but in the light of this experience we can help to overcome the major institutional and procedural difficulties in the convention on the future of europe so that the union can be an area of peace, prosperity, freedom, cohesion, security and solidarity.

commission. – mr president, i would like to start by congratulating mrs stihler and the members of the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy for their excellent work. the same applies to the members of the committees on petitions and women's rights and equal opportunities who also played a part in the process. the report reflects the policy consensus between the european parliament and the commission. i am pleased to inform parliament that, last week, the commission adopted a directive reclassifying breast implants in the context of the legislation on medical devices. breast implants are now subject to the most stringent assessment procedures. more precisely, breast implants have been reclassified from class iib to class iii. it requires, in addition, clinical data and design attributes, namely on biocompatibility, physical and mechanical properties. this will increase the level of safety of breast implants. furthermore, at the request of the commission and the member states, cen, the european standardisation body, is proceeding to an in-depth review of the european standards on breast implants. the commission received encouraging information from member states regarding national measures taken, or further developed, under the recommendations set out in our communication of november 2001. this information will be made available to parliament in a commission staff working document on national measures adopted or planned to be adopted by member states in relation to breast implants. this paper will be finalised in the coming weeks. the commission believes that its communication and the production of the forthcoming working document have produced a significant effect. all member states have acted by verifying existing national policies and by starting to introduce measures as recommended by the communication. both documents will continue to be a useful element that interest groups and national authorities may use, at national level, to promote best practice and inspire further actions. the excellent cooperation between parliament and the commission on this subject should be highlighted, since the overall result has been extremely positive.

with the arab and muslim world, and this has been particularly appreciated by the arab world. thirdly, our aim was to mobilise the arab world, which i think we have done. in the coming days, there will be a delegation from the arab league to the region to convey to saddam hussein a specific and clear message. a second important area is us-eu relations. i think it would be a mistake not to recognize that there's been a lot of tension around our relationship lately, particularly over iraq. perhaps there were other issues before, such as kyoto, the international criminal court and perhaps other issues, but greater tensions were created with the iraq issue. i believe that we all want to maintain a cooperative relationship based on many decades of our common security effort and, of course, on the basis of the common values that europe expresses and that the united states expresses, the principles of freedom, democracy and peace. we therefore want to stress the need for a meaningful dialogue on the future of international security and how we deal with such problems. we have already met not only mr powell but also mrs rice and other actors in american political life with the aim of having a substantive debate between the european union and president bush on these issues at the summit in june. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. as regards the countries of the region, we have close cooperation with turkey, which has taken the initiative of discussing the problems that the crisis in iraq may create, and also its efforts with the neighbouring countries to prevent war and to bring saddam hussein into line. we continue this close cooperation. turkey is also a candidate country, and we are of course concerned about the possible consequences of developments in the region, such as the kurdish question, the refugee question and the wider economic and political implications. so we're working with them, too. the european union has a duty to help the countries of the region to develop their economic and social cohesion. the european union, i would say all 15 if not all 28 countries, have stressed the importance of the role of the un, and i think this is emerging as a key issue for whatever further decisions we take as an international community. the european union has a duty to ensure that the european union is able to take action in the fight against terrorism, and that it is able to take action in the fight against terrorism. we are trying, of course, because we have many of our own members in the security council, to contribute to the extent of our possibilities to a common approach to the problem. as i said, iraq raises new issues, or rather it raises the problems of our time: i would like to thank the commissioner for his report, which is a very good report, and i would like to thank him for his work in this area. europe is a community of values. europe has the experience of integrating countries that have gone through dictatorships and authoritarian regimes, it has shown how it can integrate countries into a new reality of democracy and freedom and contribute to peace in a very wide area of the european continent. i think that this invaluable experience is a guide and an important basis for us to be able to deal with new problems in other parts of the world. i believe that this experience does not show weakness, as is often the case with criticism of europe, but a very important strength, and this very important strength i think we must harness for a united and strong voice internationally. the european union is not only a political union, but also a political union, and it is a political union, and it is a commission. – mr president, i wish to express my gratitude for the professionalism and courtesy of the foreign minister of greece, with whom it is a real pleasure to work. i say that, having worked now with eight presidencies. the minister said that he had spent a good deal of time in the last few weeks at about 30 000 feet. i can honestly say that i have spent a lot of my time in the last three and a half years at that altitude. on the whole, when i have not been at that altitude, i have been in this chamber. because of the range of my responsibilities i have probably spent – and enjoyed spending – more time in this chamber than any other commissioner. i think the house will know that i have tried to be pretty brief in my remarks so as not to take up too much debating time. i hope today that the house will allow me to speak at slightly greater length, because i would like to talk about one or two things about which i feel very strongly. i hope that i have never knowingly oversold to this house the achievements of the common foreign and security policy – or even its potential under the existing treaty. i have always been acutely conscious of its limitations. let me quote briefly from a speech i made almost three years ago, in june 2000: 'in the important advances achieved in cfsp in the last decade, the member states have not given the commission a sole right of initiative; nor, in general, have they agreed to abide by majority votes; nor do they accept that europe has ‘occupied the space’, reducing national freedom of action… foreign policy remains primarily a matter for democratically elected member state governments.' despite the brave and extremely professional efforts of the greek presidency, that has never been more evident than over the last few miserable weeks, which have also amply illustrated what i went on to say in that speech, namely that: 'all member states should acknowledge what those actually doing the work of cfsp have long understood – that mere inter-governmentalism is a recipe for weakness and mediocrity,(applause)for a european foreign policy of the lowest common denominator. that will become more obvious as the union takes in new members.' the sorry figure cut by the european union in recent weeks should not blind us to the real and remarkable achievements of the common foreign and security policy over the last decade, in the balkans, afghanistan and many other parts of the world. but it should also remind us how far we still have to go. of course, it is possible, as some have suggested, for a small group of member states to act as a driving force to give europe a coherent, high-profile foreign policy. but without better machinery to harness common political will, they are just as likely to drive an incoherent high-profile policy. this has not been a good time for those who believe that the way forward for european foreign policy is to leave things to the big member states. one lesson we can already draw from the unfolding events – a point made by the minister – is the importance of developing the role and authority of the united nations. it is in the interests of the whole world that power should be constrained by global rules, and used only with international agreement. what other source of international legitimacy except the un exists for military intervention? on what other basis is it possible, indeed, to address the problem of weapons of mass destruction? i am here thinking not just of the particular case of iraq, but of the wider issue. america’s refusal to press forward with ratification of the comprehensive test ban treaty hardly strengthens the hand of the international atomic energy agency and others seeking to prevent the proliferation of nuclear technology in iran, north korea and beyond. i regretted, too, america’s decision to resile so lightly from the anti-ballistic missile treaty. for such decisions – and there have been many – send a dangerous signal about the value that the united states places on international commitments. that, surely, is a critical battle lost in what some call the ‘war against terrorism’. for i find it hard to conceive how the terrorist threat can be confronted effectively except through international cooperation and disciplines. (applause) impressive work has already been done within the european union and through the un counter-terrorism committee. we should continue to help countries which find it hard to meet their counter-terrorism obligations under un security council resolution 1373. and we should continue to work for a less unequal world – for example in the wto doha development agenda, by carrying forward the monterrey decisions on development financing and by implementing the johannesburg decisions on sustainable development. as a general rule, are wars not more likely to recruit terrorists than to deter them? it is hard to build democracy at the barrel of a gun, when history suggests that it is more usually the product of long internal development within a society. because of the un’s unique role as a source of legitimacy, it is of the greatest importance that if a war is waged in iraq, the un should authorise the decision to attack. if, tragically, the position of the united nations remains ambiguous – for example, if authority for an attack rested solely on resolution 1441, but without explicit security council confirmation that iraq’s failure fully to comply constituted a casus belli – then it is still likely to be desirable that the un should provide the framework as soon as possible for humanitarian assistance that may be necessary thereafter, that it should oversee the emergence of the new iraqi polity, driven by the people of iraq themselves and that it should help to coordinate the international reconstruction effort that will certainly be required. no-one can seriously dispute, however, that it would be preferable if – a huge 'if' – we were able to disarm saddam hussein by inspections. the european union is a massive donor in the balkans and in afghanistan, and we are already the largest humanitarian donor in iraq. if it comes to war, we shall certainly have to step up that help, not just to the victims of the conflict, but to those who may seek refuge from it. the commission has been engaged in intensive contacts with un organisations and with the countries around iraq about how we might best contribute on the humanitarian front. eur 15 million has already been set aside, but we may well need to go much further – drawing, if necessary, on the budget’s emergency reserve. it will be essential that, with other international assistance agencies, the european union should be free to give independent and impartial help. a strict separation will need to be maintained between military action and assistance in order to preserve the so-called ‘humanitarian space’. that objective will be much easier to achieve if the un is recognised, at an early stage, as the lead assistance coordinator. immediate humanitarian help is one thing, but the demands upon us will certainly extend much beyond that. as the house is all too well aware, europe’s external relations budget is already heavily committed. it will be very difficult in any circumstances to launch massive new programmes in iraq and in the neighbourhood of iraq. but it will be that much more difficult for the european union to cooperate fully and on a large scale – also in the longer-term reconstruction process – if events unfold without proper un cover and if the member states remain divided. when i have made this point in the past i have sometimes been accused of, as it were, issuing a threat of european union non–cooperation if the united states chooses to proceed without un backing, on the principle suggested by the new york times columnist, tom friedman, from the sign in a china shop: 'if you broke it, you own it'. but that is not my point. i am simply making an observation of fact: if it comes to war, it will be very much easier to persuade you – the european union's budgetary authority – to be generous if there is no dispute about the legitimacy of the military action that has taken place; about the new political order that emerges thereafter; or about who is in charge of the reconstruction process. i am not making a quasi-legal point. i am simply offering a political judgement of no great novelty or sagacity. it seems pretty obvious to me. i am gravely concerned – and i know that many in this house share my concerns – about the potential collateral damage of recent events and of a war, if it comes to that. our joint efforts should be directed to trying to minimise those potential effects. i am thinking not just of the death and destruction that might be wrought by war itself, or of the destabilising consequences for iraq’s immediate neighbours, but of potential damage, for example to the authority of the united nations, to nato and to transatlantic relations, which are going through – to put it mildly – a very difficult passage. in all these contexts we must look beyond the immediate arguments and remind ourselves of our long-term interests to cooperate and to strengthen the flawed but necessary apparatus of international governance. but there are three other areas, finally, where we should also work to reduce collateral damage from recent events. the first is the common foreign and security policy itself, which has suffered a severe setback because member states on both sides of the debate have chosen to take firm national policy positions as if they spoke for the european union as a whole. we must not be disheartened by this setback. there have been similar divisions within the united states, and even within the us administration, but these do not pull the country apart because in the end the president is empowered to speak for the nation as a whole. as a union of independent nations we do not enjoy that luxury. but that is a reason to redouble our efforts to build an effective cfsp, not to abandon them. as we return to the work we shall find, perhaps, a little more humility even among the large member states, which can surely see how much they have damaged their common enterprise and how much they have reduced their common influence as a result of public squabbling. (applause)a second european project that risks being hurt by recent events if we do not work actively to sustain it is the cause of enlargement. it is particularly damaging that disagreements over iraq have been allowed to overshadow the debate about enlargement. we should not call into question the european vocation of countries simply because of their views on the iraq crisis. (applause)let us assure the acceding countries that we continue to look forward eagerly to their imminent membership.but, on the other side of the argument, let us also acknowledge that those who join our union are making an existential choice. they are not declaring themselves for europe and against the united states – emphatically not. but, in the words of the treaty on european union, they are accepting a responsibility to 'refrain from action … likely to impair [the effectiveness of the union] as a cohesive force in international relations.' the present members may have set a very bad example,(applause)but that does not reduce the responsibility on all members, including the acceding states, to meet that treaty obligation. finally, i want to say a word about israel and palestine. what happens if there is a war in iraq? let us suppose, let us pray, that it is brief. let us further suppose that all the worries expressed about the consequences in terms of the stability of the country prove unfounded. let us, in short, put all or most anxieties to one side. i want to ask two questions. first, will the peace that breaks out drive palestinians and israelis into an historic reconciliation? the state of the palestinians was described last week by peter hansen, commissioner general of the un relief and works agency, and one of the finest international public servants in the world. 'the stark fact is', he wrote, 'that almost a quarter of palestinian children are suffering from acute or chronic malnutrition for purely man-made reasons. no drought has hit gaza and the west bank, no crops have failed and the shops are often full of food. but the failure of the peace process and the destruction of the economy by israel’s closure policy have had the effect of a terrible natural disaster'. second, in the aftermath of a war, will america - the leader of a un-backed operation or of a more limited coalition - take a much more proactive role in forging an israeli-palestinian peace? we have been told that will happen. european leaders have been told that will happen. we have been told that the road map will see the light of day before we all run out of road. i sincerely hope that is so. i genuinely fear the outcome if war in iraq is followed by another year or more of violence in palestine and israel. that would further inflame opinion in the islamic world. some say that to defeat terrorism it is necessary to defeat saddam hussein. that may or may not be true – some of us are at the very least agnostic on that point. but what i am absolutely sure about is that to invade iraq, while failing to bring peace to the middle east, would create exactly the sort of conditions in which terrorism would be likely to thrive. (applause from the centre and the left) and the truth is – and we should face this fact – that none of us would be immune from the consequences of that. (applause)

commission. – mr president, i wish to begin by associating myself wholeheartedly with all that the foreign minister has just said about the murder of prime minister djindjic. i should like to extend my sympathy and, i am sure, the sympathy of the house to his family and friends and to all democrats in serbia. clearly we must not allow this assassination to set back the remarkable progress which has been made by serbia in rejoining the european family, not least thanks to the bravery of men and women like mr djindjic. in about one and a half hours i am supposed to be flying to croatia. this means i shall miss the end of the next debate, which will be left in the capable hands of commissioner bolkestein. tomorrow evening i had planned to fly to belgrade. obviously, if it is still convenient for the authorities, i would like to do that and to express the solidarity of parliament, the commission and the union as a whole with the government and people of serbia in what is an extremely worrying time for them. the first european union military operation is, as the foreign minister has said, about to start operations in the balkans. it is an historic step for the european security and defence policy. after the copenhagen decisions we are now moving towards a wide-ranging set of arrangements with nato – described by the foreign minister – which will enable our strategic partnership with them to go hand in hand with the entry into operation of the esdp. the decision taken by the council in january to embark on a joint action opened a new chapter in the history of our integration, and it is not surprising that this chapter will have its first lines written in the balkans. this historic dimension justifies fully the debate we are having today on the basis of the motion for a resolution by the committee on foreign affairs, human rights, common security and defence policy. all of us remember the tragic events which took place in south-east europe at the beginning of the nineties. faced with a situation no one would have thought possible in our continent, the european union had to develop new tools to strengthen its capacity to prevent and, if necessary, deal with any similar crises which could potentially endanger our security and which certainly offend our deepest values. it is therefore not by chance that the former yugoslav republic of macedonia is to be the setting for this new step forward by the european union. the context of this operation is no longer the imperative to put an end to the civil conflict and to separate the fighters. it is rather the continuation of the build-up of a closer relationship between the union and a country which is moving towards the european union and which needs our support to consolidate the stability without which it will not be able to progress along this path. i would like here to remind the house that only two years ago the former yugoslav republic of macedonia was on the edge of a civil conflict, but thankfully turned its back on war when an agreement was reached between the conflicting parties. during my first two years or so as a commissioner i visited fyrom much more than any other place. in one period of just over a year i was in macedonia almost ten times. a substantial and sustained commitment by the european union – political as well as financial – supported the process. thus we offered both a european perspective to the country through the stabilisation and association process and through increased financial support. a few figures can illustrate how substantial our financial assistance package has been. more than eur 30 million was allocated in 2001 through the cards programme and the rapid reaction mechanism, while nearly eur 7 million was delivered in humanitarian assistance. these funds have been focused on de-mining, housing reconstruction, local infrastructure rehabilitation, confidence-building measures and institutional reforms required under the framework agreement. this effort was quickly followed up by the adoption of a multiannual programme which, under cards, earmarked eur 130.5 million for democracy, the rule of law, justice and home affairs, and economic and social development. these efforts have been paying off. the last few months have shown that political life is returning to normal, based on the implementation of the framework agreement and on the stabilisation and association process. it is true that the security situation is still fragile. last week’s incident, which tragically cost the lives of two polish nato officers, has been a further illustration that a continued international security presence is needed for the coming months in order to consolidate peace and security in the country and to underpin the implementation of the lake ohrid agreement. this assessment is shared by the government, the president, the main political parties and international players. here i would like to address some of the concerns which may have emerged regarding the scope and the objective of the european union military mission. even if the european union operation will only be of limited size, let me state clearly that i do not consider that this has ever been a useful criterion against which to evaluate its worth. it will be a visible sign of our commitment to safeguarding stability in this country. secondly, we do not need to have second thoughts. our objectives are clear. as rightly pointed out in the motion for a resolution, the planned european union takeover of the nato military mission will be a further demonstration of the european union's commitment to peace and stability in the country and in the region. it is fully consistent with our policy to contribute to the long-term security of the former yugoslav republic of macedonia. let me just remind the house of the comprehensive package of financial assistance given by the community in the security sector, under the justice and home affairs heading. between 2002 and 2004 eur 31.2 million have been earmarked for this purpose. this encompasses two crucial elements in particular. the first is support for the country to manage its borders through a comprehensive integrated border management programme, which includes creating an effective border police corps. the process of improving border security and management has a strong component of regional cooperation, and so the european union is currently working closely with nato and the osce to support the efforts which the countries in the region have started to make themselves. the second element is support for the former yugoslav republic of macedonia in developing a comprehensive strategy for the reform of its police service, to make it a well-trained, multi-ethnic and community-based public service. in the view of the commission, the european union operation in the former yugoslav republic of macedonia will contribute to consolidating a stable environment conducive to the implementation of reforms that will facilitate its future integration with the european union. in this perspective, i have no doubt that a limited and focused eu military intervention can only reinforce progress towards full civilian and democratic control of the reforms under way. this morning, we spent some time dwelling on an area of foreign and security policy where – i shall be diplomatic – we have not made as much progress as we would have liked. however, we have to recognise that in some parts of the world – most notably in the balkans – europe has in the last few years got its act together. you only have to compare the humiliations and bloody mayhem of the early 1990s, when europe was unable to deal with awful problems on its own doorstep, with our success in the last few years in shaping policy and in helping to lead the countries of the balkans towards the european family. we know the journey is not an easy one and today's tragedy reminds us how much work there still is for us to do. as i have said in this house before, it would be a terrible mistake if we were to think that the problems in the balkans, or in afghanistan for that matter, were done and dusted. we still have to focus, concentrate and be generous with our time, assistance and experience in helping those countries down the road towards eventual membership of the european union. whatever the tragic setbacks, i am sure that they will attain that objective in the years ahead. the rapporteur. - mr president, i have to go. we are still waiting impatiently for the commissioner, who has also announced her presence. i hope she'll show up soon. in my own-initiative report from the committee on women's rights and equal opportunities, i deal with gender mainstreaming in the european parliament at both the political and administrative levels. we have discussed this with the stakeholders in our committee, we have had a series of talks with both the president and the secretary-general, a public hearing followed, and we have also had talks with the staff representatives and the advisory committee. the european union's commitment to equality between women and men is enshrined in articles 2, 3 and 13 of the ec treaty and in article 23 of the charter of fundamental rights of the european union. gender mainstreaming as a policy strategy is intended to help achieve this ambitious goal. this follows the definition of the beijing platform for action, whereby gender mainstreaming will drive the development, organisation and evaluation of policy-making processes and policies in a way that takes into account the starting conditions and impacts on women and men in all policy areas and at all levels, in order to contribute to the goal of effective equality between women and men. the european parliament must prove itself to be a driver of equal opportunities and has done so many times in the past, and gender mainstreaming must now be integrated in a coherent and comprehensive way into our political activities and our structures. this report therefore proposes a series of measures to ensure the long-term implementation of the principle of gender mainstreaming. the empowerment of women is therefore an essential but not the only aspect, and the dual strategy should be given priority as a principle. the report proposes the following measures: the european union must take the lead and show its active commitment. the external sign of this is the establishment in the european parliament, similar to the commission, of a high-level working group on gender mainstreaming chaired by the president of the parliament, as was already done in the commission under president santer. we're a little behind on that. the conference of committee chairs shall be involved and shall, together with the heads of delegation, develop proposals and make recommendations to the conference of presidents on how to achieve gender mainstreaming in their respective policy areas. our proposal is to appoint a member - preferably the chair or a vice-chair - as responsible for gender mainstreaming, and then each committee should select projects in its work programme on how gender mainstreaming is implemented in its area of activity and systematically review the impact of the measures on women and men. the planning and implementation should be guided by established quality standards and allow for internal benchmarking, as should the evaluation. each committee then undertakes an annual evaluation of its gender mainstreaming activities and results against pre-defined objectives and reviews these actions. our proposal is that the committee on women's rights and equal opportunities should then compile the individual reports into an annual report on gender mainstreaming and make recommendations for further work. a further package of measures must also be taken in the field of the arrangement of professional and family activities for employees. the use of gender-neutral language, for example, is an important goal. we must also aim to include the candidate countries, especially in view of enlargement, and to ensure that there is a balance between men and women in the run-up to the 2004 parliamentary elections. the situation is that, although the european parliament has always been a leader, the proportion of women in the european parliament in 1979 was 17.5%; we're now at 31%. the convention, however, has taken a step backwards. i think it is very important that we set a political signal by implementing benchmarking and gender mainstreaming so that there is progress and not a setback in the 2004 elections.
