commission. – mr president, let me commence by thanking and complimenting the rapporteurs mr whitehead, mrs patrie and mrs thyssen for their dedicated hard work of such high quality. first of all i would like to say a few words about the new consumer policy strategy, which was adopted by the commission last may and the purpose of which is to give a clear sense of political direction covering the next five years. it has three key objectives. the first is to achieve a high common level of consumer protection. the second objective is to make sure that there is effective enforcement of consumer protection rules. the third objective is to provide for the involvement of consumer organisations in eu policies. i would like to stress that these three objectives have been designed with the three following cross-cutting ideas in mind: to help achieve integration of consumer concerns into all eu policies, such as competition policy, transport and justice; to maximise the benefits of the single market for consumers – this is a result which should benefit business and consumers alike; and, last but not least, to prepare for enlargement. all three objectives of the strategy – a high common level of consumer protection, effective enforcement of consumer protection rules and proper involvement of consumer organisations – were very much designed with the perspective of new and future countries joining the eu shortly and in the future. the action plan on consumer protection and the green paper on consumer protection put forward a number of options and raised a number of questions on the future of eu consumer protection policy. they suggested, in particular, the idea of a framework directive on unfair commercial practices. the commission also suggested the development of a legal instrument for cooperation between enforcement authorities. the favourable response to the consultation exercise encouraged us to continue working on this idea of a framework directive. however there was a general feeling that more information, clarification and consultation on the content of any such framework directive was needed. the follow-up communication of june 2002 responded to this need. we also recognised the need to complete the evidence of existing problems and opportunities. both mrs patrie’s and mrs thyssen’s reports recognise this need. we therefore commissioned three major studies. first, a survey of 16 000 consumers looking at consumer experience of, and attitudes towards, cross-border shopping. second, a parallel survey asking similar questions to nearly 3 000 businesses, mainly smes, that advertise and sell to consumers. this gives us a clear sense of what the impact of a framework directive will be on small and medium-sized companies. third, we commissioned an independent consultant to carry out an impact assessment of the legislative options set out in the green paper. the conclusions of this impact assessment and surveys can be summarised as follows. eighty million europeans would shop more across borders if they felt as secure as they do when shopping at home. forty-six percent of companies expect the proportion of their cross-border sales to increase with harmonisation. only 1% of companies expects a decrease. sixty-eight percent of european businesses said that harmonisation in this area is an efficient way of facilitating cross-border sales. the impact assessment concluded that a framework directive based on full harmonisation would be the most effective way to remove barriers to cross-border retail trade. in addition, my services have been working on the nature of the legal barriers faced by business and consumers. first, we have been working with a group of national governmental experts to examine and compare national laws on unfair commercial practices. second, we set up a team of academics who are currently completing a comprehensive comparative legal study. and third, we have organised a two-day workshop on several key issues, with all stakeholders. this very thorough consultation and research process has enabled the commission to gain a comprehensive understanding of the various nuances of national rules on unfair trading and the concerns of all stakeholders. i hope it has also enabled us to build a broad consensus on a workable framework directive. the view of the european parliament plays a very important part in the commission’s deliberations. i therefore very much appreciate the constructive reports by the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy and the committee on legal affairs and the internal market confirming a growing consensus on the way forward. i hope today’s debate will enable us to reconcile the remaining points of divergence between the two reports. i look forward to hearing your views in this debate.

commission. – mr president, i wish to begin by saying how much i welcome this constructive and lively debate and how pleased i am at the extent to which the views of the commission have been supported consistently across the house. not only i, but also my staff and collaborators who have worked so hard on this proposal, take satisfaction from that. i will start with the points relating to the framework directive and then i will address some points on the action plan. a number of members mentioned full harmonisation. as you know the commission is determined to complete the internal market, and making the single market work for business and producers is just one side of the story. internal market rules should also promote the confidence of consumers to buy goods and services without being put off by national borders that may lie between buyer and seller. i reject the idea that you can have one without the other. the treaty requirements on consumer protection and the internal market are entirely compatible. the history of eu consumer protection is largely one of minimum harmonisation that leaves the member states free to go beyond the basic level of harmonisation if they so wish. this has led to legal fragmentation. it has also created obstacles to the smooth functioning of the internal market. recent surveys reveal that only 13% of eu consumers made a cross-border purchase in the last 12 months. and, as i indicated before, harmonisation of consumer protection regulations was cited by 68% of businesses as one of the most efficient of a number of options in facilitating cross-border sales. we need, therefore, to strive for simpler and more common rules and practices to promote consumer confidence in cross-border transactions. the importance of this is further heightened by enlargement. if neglected, fragmentation of consumer protection rules would significantly increase. we have, more specifically, to overcome the real barriers arising from national laws and national case law on unfair commercial practices. for example, take the benchmark consumer – against whom misleading advertising is assessed. this, according to the ecj case law – for instance the clinique case – is the average consumer, reasonably well informed and circumspect. but this test is not applied consistently across the eu. for instance, in the saint-brice case of 2000, the belgian cour de cassation ruled that the benchmark consumer against whom misleading advertising should be assessed is the vulnerable consumer. in the scanner advertising case, the german highest court ruled that the benchmark consumer is the casual observer instead of the reasonably circumspect consumer. therefore it is our intention to provide for full harmonisation of rules on unfair commercial practices and codification of the average consumer test, thus removing significant barriers. i turn, briefly, to mutual recognition. the framework directive will provide full harmonisation of the laws on unfair commercial practices. this convergence and the effective level of consumer protection achieved should set the political conditions to make the principles of mutual recognition and country of origin acceptable. the overall level of protection will be increased within the eu since a number of member states do not at present have a comprehensive regulation on unfair commercial practices. naturally, we recognise that the framework directive must deliver an effective high level of consumer protection. this does not mean the lowest common denominator of existing national regimes. nor does it mean a compilation of all the stringent existing national provisions. we need to strike the right balance between the interests of consumers to receive protection from rogue traders when they shop across borders and the interests of businesses to reduce their marketing and legal compliance costs. a number of members raised the issue of simplification. the commission will try to incorporate as much as possible of the acquis in a framework directive. those elements of the acquis that were included in a framework directive would be repealed. of course, this will not include contract law provisions, which will be addressed in the context of the action plan recently adopted by the commission. the framework directive will simplify the regulatory environment on unfair commercial practices by repealing the predominant business-to-consumer provisions of the misleading advertising directive and by repealing, for example, the inertia-selling provisions in the distance-selling directive. these matters, which are currently subject to minimum harmonisation rules, will be fully harmonised by the framework directive. in addition, the general clause in the directive will replace all the divergent general clauses in the member states and so create a more uniform regulatory environment. i know people are calling for it. it is an important aspect of this proposal and will make it generally more acceptable to business and consumers alike. on the question of 'fair and unfair', the framework directive would hinge on a general clause prohibiting unfair commercial practices. the central question is, of course: 'what is unfair?' this was one of the main issues for consultation. the results of the consultation, our work with national governmental experts and the legal study we commissioned made it clear that it would be easier to define what was unfair rather than what was fair. the definition of what constitutes an unfair commercial practice should lead to more legal certainty. businesses trading fairly will not have to change the way they do business. to help achieve this legal certainty, a non-exhaustive list of unfairness categories and a list of examples of banned commercial practices will supplement the general clause. a number of members mentioned codes of conduct. different positions have emerged in the light of the eu consultation on the idea of endorsement of codes at eu level. some have argued in favour, others have argued against. mrs patrie’s and mrs thyssen’s reports reflect these differing positions. i want to encourage responsible businesses to treat their customers fairly and recognise that voluntary codes of conduct may play a key role towards this aim in their particular sectors. any endorsement process should be voluntary. a code owner would choose whether to apply for endorsement, and a firm would, therefore, choose whether or not to join this code. on the question of vulnerable consumers, this is an issue of some complexity. we are looking at this. there are a number of different aspects. we will make our minds up before we draft the legislation which i hope will be brought forward in the very near future. i turn to mr whitehead's question on funding. i want to stress that it is as important to improve the quality of expenditure as its quantity. this is an issue we are also taking into account. finally, i thank members again for their constructive comments and the rapporteurs for their reports. i look forward to taking into account the views expressed here this morning in the final drafting of the legislation, which i look forward to presenting to parliament in the very near future.

the commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank the rapporteur for his report. firstly, i would like to say that the commission is also very much in favour of the initiative to tackle this very difficult issue. we can also accept most of the points and join those contained in the motion for a resolution. i would like to divide my answers to the questions raised in the various speeches into three groups, and i would like to thank them for having led to a very well-rounded debate. firstly, i believe that despite structural and support policies, we must not ignore the fact that we are in a market economy system and that the first task must be to ensure that the market economy system works. this has nothing to do with manchester liberalism, but it has to do with, for example, the respect of our european competition rules, because if we do not make sure that competition works, then our whole promotion policy and our whole cohesion and structural policy will be completely countered. i think we must not allow that to happen. so statements that point to the importance of having a functioning market economy system are very important and should not be ignored. the second is: what can we do to ensure that the funds we give are used for the purpose they are intended and that there is no abuse? is therefore time to have a frank discussion about what the real problems of our time are, what the real challenges are, how we are going to deal with the big issues, from weapons of mass destruction (applause) so the future of transatlantic relations is a matter of real concern to all of us and it was of course entirely appropriate that the foreign minister referred so eloquently to that issue during his remarks. the greek presidency made heroic efforts to maintain a common position. the european council’s declaration of 17 february was, in my view, extremely well judged. member states pull things together again? how can we emerge not just healed but strengthened from the trials of the last few weeks? we should remind ourselves how closely and effectively we are cooperating - not despicable murder of zoran djindjic. i hope that at the european council later today and tomorrow, heads of government will renew their pledge to maintain the momentum of development and of association between these countries and the european union. we must also maintain unrelenting concentration on afghanistan, on which we had a donors' meeting here in brussels at the beginning of the week: a recognition of how prominent a part we are playing under un auspices in the reconstruction in that country, which still faces appalling problems. after the fighting of 2001, the european union pledged that it was there for the long haul, to help deliver stability and sound government. this house helped to ensure that we put resources behind that pledge. we must remain true to it. i repeat what i said to this house last week, that we must also maintain the momentum of our own enlargement. the decision to bring in ten new member states is not some whim, which might be called into question by unrelated events. it is a strategic choice for our continent. and it is a choice of historic proportions. we must press forward undaunted, just as we must press forward with the work we announced in our paper last week on wider europe. that communication set out a vision about how our neighbours, not just to the east but to the south, too, can expect to share in our prosperity and stability if they are ready to align themselves on our values and on our legislation. our proposals for ‘wider europe’ mean the creation of a common economic and social space where all countries enjoy full membership of the internal market and, potentially, share in the four freedoms. we must press forward, too, with the middle east peace process. it is encouraging that the president of the united states is now ready to proceed with the road map towards a two-state solution that was prepared, i have to say, several months ago within the international quartet. but we must ensure that this means the urgent implementation of these ideas, not a long discussion with the parties about their validity. such discussions have proved to be endlessly frustrating in the past, as the parties have sought to impose incompatible conditions upon their cooperation. we really cannot allow this peace process, once again, to be subject to conditional sequencing so that in practice there is no peace but more bloodshed. (applause) more immediately, the whole european union must strive to build on what we share in our approach to the conflict now beginning in iraq. the commission has been working hard behind the scenes, in cooperation with international agencies, to contribute to the humanitarian assistance that may be needed. i have discussed these issues myself in jordan, turkey and iran in recent weeks. echo, the commission’s humanitarian aid office, has reinforced its presence in the region. there are now five permanent expatriate technical assistants in the amman regional office covering iraq and the whole of the middle east, an additional expert based in jerusalem and a seventh one on standby in amman. echo has also kept regular contact with the main humanitarian organisations such as the international committee of the red cross and the un high commissioner for refugees. since january this year, echo has carried out three missions to iraq itself to assess the situation and prepare for possible operations. it has also conducted several missions to neighbouring countries. besides the eur 15 million that had been earmarked for humanitarian operations in iraq in 2003, the commission has, of course, delegated authority to approve fast track aid for a further eur 3 million in less than 72 hours. if there were a crisis in a neighbouring country, it would be possible to agree another eur 3 million for that purpose, too. depending on the scale of the needs, we may need to apply for additional funds for humanitarian purposes from the emergency reserve. on the basis of previous experience – echo has been providing humanitarian aid to iraq since 1992 – we expect that the commission’s contribution is likely to be focused on health, on water and on sanitation. some international organisations and ngos are also predicting food shortages, with disruption of the oil for food programme. that is something we may need to look at in due course, if the problem emerges. in all this effort, echo will work closely with un agencies, and will participate in on-the-spot information exchanges. i should like to add one point here. nobody in this house, i am sure, under-estimates the courage and commitment of our humanitarian aid teams in the field. i think all of us have good reason to be proud of them, proud of the work they have already done in that region and proud of the work which, alas, they have to do in all too many parts of the world. (applause) we must also do all that we can to help turkey cope with the political pressures generated by recent events, and to help iraq’s other neighbours, too – from jordan and syria to iran. as i said earlier, during my recent trips to the region i had a chance to gain a better understanding of the impact that war on iraq could have on these countries. the commission will continue monitoring and assessing the situation closely and would look, with the council, at possible eu responses. in the present circumstances, i am bound to say that i am extremely pleased that we have taken the initiative to develop our relationship with iran, not in an ill-informed way, not overlooking the disagreements we have with that country. i think trying to develop our relationship with iran makes considerable sense. in an article earlier this week a respected newspaper columnist reminded us that after the plagues and misfortunes had streamed from pandora’s box, hope remained behind to assuage the afflicted. so perhaps we should hold onto hope that the war will be over quickly, and with minimum casualties – a point felt especially strongly, whatever your views on the conflict, by all those with fellow countrymen and women engaged in the fight. (applause) we should hope as well that it will be possible to deliver humanitarian aid quickly and effectively, under international auspices, where it is most needed. we should hope that the political and economic reconstruction of iraq can begin soon, again under international auspices. a point i made explicitly last week – perhaps the house will excuse me for repeating it – was that if post-war iraq is managed under a un mandate like east timor, kosovo and afghanistan, i hope that it will be recognised in those circumstances and that part of the credit for that should go to those who have insisted on it from the outset. we should hope, then, that reconstruction under international auspices can begin, guaranteeing iraq's territorial integrity and providing for iraqi ownership of the process. we should also hope that those who believe that the real choice in the arab world lies between pro-western despotism and anti-western democracy are wrong; hope that the regional repercussions will be benign – or, if they are damaging, that they will be contained; hope that the current crisis will serve to galvanise the middle east peace process after a desperately bleak period in which things have drifted backwards; hope that those who believe that this war will strike a blow against international terrorism - rather than stoking the flames of it - are right; and hope, finally, that those many institutions and relationships which have been tested in the fire in recent weeks, including the european union and the common foreign and security policy, will emerge strengthened by a renewed recognition of how badly we need the apparatus of international governance. i should like to leave the house with this last thought: the challenge that we face today, the challenge that we will face in the coming weeks and months, goes far beyond what winston churchill once called 'the thankless deserts of mesopotamia'. we face a very clear choice in the coming months. are we to go back to the way the world was run, or not run, in the nineteenth century - a world of rival national sovereignties and balances of power? or do we try to rebuild the institutions and habits of global governance which have been so painfully constructed in the last half-century? that is the clear choice which is going to face us. i know which side of the argument i come down on. president of the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the debate we are having today concerns the recent european council: the council has been held at a time of serious international crisis and has therefore required a great deal of effort from the greek presidency. it is therefore with particular warmth that i would like to thank prime minister simitis and foreign minister papandreou for the skill and wisdom with which they have conducted the summit. the spring european councils are the traditional meeting on the union's work calendar devoted to economic issues. however, the council meeting in brussels in recent days took place entirely in the shadow of the iraqi crisis. and that's where i'm going to start my speech today. as i speak to you, a war is underway and no one can say how much longer it is destined to last: a war in which some member states have their own troops engaged on the ground; a war that has created great divisions within us; a war opposed by the vast majority of european citizens and by many others around the world; a war that, even if it will eventually lead to the fall of a dictator, brings with it, like all wars, death and pain. on behalf of the commission and my staff, i would first of all like to express my sympathy with the families of the victims and the sufferings of all those affected by the war. and i want to stress the need for respect for human dignity even between belligerents. we also have to consider another fact: the additional funds required for this operation, $74.7 billion, are far greater than the total amount of aid the world gives to the poorest countries each year, which is just over €50 billion a year. (applause) i would like to thank the statement on the iraq crisis, which we adopted at the end of the council's work, lists in detail the many important points on which there is unanimous agreement within the union, points which we must emphasize here too, and among which the following stand out: the central role of the un during and after the crisis; the fight against terrorism and the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction; respect for the territorial integrity of iraq; the need for urgent action in the field of humanitarian aid; the commitment to multilateral management of world politics; the strategic priority, today as always, of the atlantic alliance. the points on which we all agree are therefore many and fundamental and it is good to remember this after all that has been said and written in recent days and weeks about our divisions. but we must not hide the fact that these divisions exist. we must not lie to ourselves or to our citizens. the european union is facing a very delicate moment in its existence. i am referring to the role that europe is not playing and should play. international events have in fact raised the question of the enlarged union's foreign and defence policy with extreme severity. we must ask ourselves what role we want to play on the international scene. i said 'we want to' because i am convinced that the union has the means to become, over time, an active and influential international political actor, not only from the economic point of view but also from the security point of view, starting from the values on which europe itself is founded. let's start with the security issue. the european citizens have already made their choice. the will for peace, multilateralism and europe - a europe that brings peace but also security - that has emerged in recent times is impressive. it is not just a shudder related to the emotion of the moment, to the anxiety and concern that, anyway and naturally, war evokes; it is something much deeper, which it would be unforgivable to ignore and on which we must find unity of purpose. the treaties already require member states to 'actively and unreservedly support the union's foreign and security policy in a spirit of loyalty and mutual solidarity'. they are required to act jointly quote to strengthen and develop their mutual political solidarity, and must refrain from any action which is contrary to the interests of the union or which would impair its effectiveness as a cohesive element in international relations. it is before our eyes that the letter and spirit of these parts of the treaty have been so little respected in the recent past. this is happening at a time when the representatives of all the governments, institutions and parliaments of europe, gathered in the convention, are working to bring the new constitutional charter of the union to life, and when the forthcoming enlargement of the union offers us and imposes on us new opportunities and new responsibilities. in this connection, i would like to welcome, after malta, the positive outcome of the referendum on accession in slovenia. the path we have travelled over the last 60 years to build a united europe has not been easy. there have been many difficult moments, but it was precisely from the deepest crises that europe has been able to draw the impetus and courage to make the most important progress: it was after the failure of the ecsc of the project to create a europe of defence that the impetus was found which led to the treaties of rome; it was the decision to end the convertibility of the dollar and, with it, the whole system created by the bretton woods agreements that led europe to plant the seeds of its own monetary union. it was the oil crisis of the 1970s and the currency crisis of the summer of 1992 which gave us the strength to create the european monetary system and to write the rules for economic and monetary union in the maastricht treaty. today, history repeats itself: europe is facing a crisis on which its future depends. we could aim at a system of international relations based on the balance of power and rely on the sovereignty and national interests of individual european states, but that would be like choosing, as commissioner patten said in this very chamber, to respond to the challenges of the 21st century with the tools and policies of the 19th century. it would also be contrary to the very nature of our union, which is based on dialogue, solidarity, multilateralism and an enriching mixture of ethics and politics. we must decide to complete the unification of europe and give it the institutions, instruments and decision-making mechanisms to transform it into a genuine political union. this is the path the citizens are asking us to take: a union capable of expressing a unified policy in the fields of economics, international relations and defence. in the field of defence, an initiative has been launched in recent days which could also go a long way: belgium, france and germany have agreed to start talks to examine possible ways of proceeding towards closer integration. this initiative, which has been duly declared open to all other member states - because it is not to divide but to unite - does not come out of nowhere. i am not just referring to the long-established experience of integrating european armed forces into multinational bodies such as eurocorps, eurofor and euromarfor. let's go back to december 1998 in saint-malo for a moment. it was then that a process began which, in the course of six months, led to the european security and defence policy and which today allows us to rely on instruments such as the political and security committee, the military committee and the general staff of the union. the countries that initiated this action and this remembrance were france and great britain, and it is thanks to this agreement that we can now consider the goal of a rapid reaction force of 60 000 men within reach. it is the embryo of what the people, for the first time in the history of the european institutions, are asking of us, namely our common defence. the european convention has set up a working group on defence matters. in its conclusions it stressed the need to develop europe's defence capabilities and to strengthen its industrial and technological bases. two weeks ago, the commission adopted a communication addressing defence industrial and market issues, with the aim of facilitating and promoting more effective coordination of european policy on military equipment. on 18 march the council finally decided to launch the first military operation in the union's history to take over nato forces operating in the former yugoslav republic of macedonia at the end of this month. we europeans, ladies and gentlemen, are not from venus, as some people would have us believe. we, the old and wise europeans, have had a long and painful history: it is a history which has led us to base our union on law and which has taught us to work for an international order, itself based on law and not on force. (applause) i would like to thank we know very well, however, that humanitarian policies alone are not enough, just as it is not enough to be the main protagonists of development aid policies. we are aware that the world will not take us into account as long as we continue to present ourselves as divided; as long as we continue to rely on the union to promote economic development and on the united states to guarantee our security. and there is no anti-american sentiment in this remark of mine, not least because cooperation between the united states and europe has increased in recent times, even here, too, we must be honest with ourselves. progress in implementing the reform strategy adopted in lisbon three years ago is too slow. i am not simply pointing out the widespread dissatisfaction through our mountains. investment in trans-european networks currently amounts to less than eur 20 billion per year; at this rate, it will take more than 20 years to complete all of them. the situation of major research and development programmes is equally depressing, to the extent that, despite the sums made available in the union budget and despite the loans granted by the european preventing us from implementing these major projects quickly, and i know just as well that these are works which take many years to complete. that is why, ladies and gentlemen, we have no time to mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your work. i want to argue realistically, not emotionally, certainly not ideologically. plant protection products contain substances which protect crops and eliminate pests or diseases and can be used and used in a wide variety of ways. in the cereal, fruit and wine-growing sectors, they are often indispensable, since a good harvest is the essential condition for a producer's economic performance. the income and thus the survival of a farm depend on it. we must not therefore deprive users of the opportunity to use plant protection products when necessary. we all know that plant protection products have more than their merits. they may also pose risks to human health and the environment. ten years ago we adopted our own eu plant protection product directive. it regulates precisely which active substance may be used for which purpose on which plant. the commission's communication is a complement to this, aims at better risk management and is therefore going in the absolutely right direction. the epp-ed group supports the following points: training measures for farmers in the sense of a professional and targeted application, the promotion of alternative concepts such as the so-called integrated crop management, the approximation of vat rates on plant protection products in order to reduce existing distortions of competition in the internal market, careful disposal of packaging and tüv-certified agricultural equipment, because the cleanliness of our drinking water is particularly important to us. the epp-ed group is in principle in favour of the sensible and professional use of plant protection products. the risk reduction is only possible if producers, users and authorities work together in the best possible way. the report by mrs van brempt goes beyond the commission's communication. in particular, a mandatory 50% reduction in the use of plant protection products would create additional risks. experts warn that such a reduction promotes the development of resistance. a higher incidence of weeds then requires the use of higher quantities of plant protection products. the use of an active substance is rather a matter of location, local weather and the general conditions of growth and disease of a plant. a mandatory levy on plant protection products certainly does not minimise risks, let alone the introduction of a pesticide pass and a total ban on aerial spraying. the latter would impose major restrictions, particularly in the wine sector. the epp-ed group cannot support mrs van brempt's report on the points already mentioned. i therefore ask my colleagues to support a feasible and workable approach which reduces the risks without restricting the work of the users, because europe's fruit, vegetable and cereal farmers produce food for us all. (applause from the centre)
i would like to thank the commissioner for his reply. this commission report focuses on sustainability in the whole economy. this means, above all, reducing resource consumption and, through progressive standards, putting an end to economic activities that pollute the environment as quickly as possible. the commission has already taken a number of initiatives in this field, including the establishment of a european environment agency. the core business of agriculture remains to produce healthy, safe and high-quality food. nevertheless, or precisely for this reason, it must be said that many farmers are in favour of using plant protection products to prevent crop yield and quality losses due to disease, pests and weeds in the interests of low-cost food production. in public discourse, the word 'pesticide' is associated with the poisoning of soil, plants and food. for some, it has become a rallying cry against the peasants. the reality is different. the cultivation of fruit, vegetables and wine is unmanageable without pesticides. the only way to protect plants from pathogens, pests and weeds is to use the least possible amount of chemicals, while using more potent biological and mechanical alternatives. for me, the fundamental element of a sustainable plant protection strategy is that integrated farming becomes a socially normal way of production. this will minimise the adverse effects of plant protection products across the whole of agriculture. this objective, however, cannot be achieved by organic farming on the necessary scale. this finding is a factual finding. it is not in contradiction with the necessary support for organic farming. in particular, i believe that the following are necessary and desirable: to protect consumers in the eu internal market, harmonisation of mrls in plant-based foods across the eu is essential. the same is true of the harmonization of the authorization of plant protection products. as long as this is not done, the principle of mutual recognition must be allowed in each member state. this is a requirement of equal opportunities in competition. in view of the current problems in the horticulture sector, i would urge that before the introduction of the substitution principle, the effects of reducing the number of active substances authorised in the eu from more than 800 to about 300 by the end of 2000 be analysed. the time-limits for the notification procedures are far too short. the result is that restrictions, or temporary regulations, or debt, are seen as the worst alternative, rather than a solution at all! under the current approach, plant protection product manufacturers are obliged to ensure that their products meet the required safety standards. the public scandals show that these procedures are not thoroughly regulated. i am convinced that serious and serious solutions will only be achieved if the manufacturers of precursors are obliged by means of a labelling obligation to mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your report. we often talk about food scandals in this house. but we are not talking about the daily scandal that unfortunately our food contains far too many pesticides. some of the speakers have already pointed out that we know that pesticides have been shown to cause cancer. there are studies that show that in norway, for example, children of agricultural workers have a significantly higher risk of cancer. other similar studies make it clear that there is a clear link. we must therefore make every effort, and the commission must also give a very clear signal and make pesticide reduction programmes compulsory. we have seen in countries like denmark and sweden that pesticide reduction programmes can achieve a reduction of up to 70% in pesticide use within a few years without any loss of agricultural yields! there's a study by the u.s. environmental protection agency that made it clear years ago that 90 percent of all pesticides are unnecessary. and you have to imagine, 90% of all pesticides are unnecessary! the problem is that the commission has not yet taken a decision on the matter. i would therefore like to make it clear once again that our group - as we have already made clear in the paul lannoye report - is committed to reducing the use of pesticides and wants to ensure that prices also tell the environmental truth by means of a levy, because ultimately consumers have to pay higher groundwater prices because pesticides are still so cheap and used on such a large scale. the essential point is that we want more transparency through labelling. we have the problem that the control authorities in the member states are blind to the pesticide controls because, for example, the german authorities do not know which pesticides are used in spain or greece. we therefore need a kind of identification, a kind of passport, so that effective controls are possible. i think we really need to make a big effort here, because overuse of pesticides ultimately means that we have to take into account the health costs. my great appeal to you, commissioner, is that your strategy should actually reduce the use of pesticides and allow more labelling for the consumer.
the commission has already made a number of proposals. the commission has already achieved one thing, madam commissioner, namely a broad-based process of discussion and consultation with all the groups concerned. that's a good thing. over the years, we in the european union have developed and introduced a whole series of directives and regulations, first on the placing on the market, then on the prohibition of placing on the market, but also on the use of plant protection products. i therefore believe that the first thing that is needed is the full implementation and review of the effectiveness of these existing rules. we need to improve the licensing system. i believe that community marketing authorization procedures are an essential part of the principles of the common internal market. substances which are permitted in italy, luxembourg and belgium, for example, cannot be prohibited in austria or germany. a pure reduction strategy - 50% is what mrs van brempt's report proposes - is not, in my view, the way to go. a reduction in the quantities used is always limited by the sufficient effectiveness of the means. integrated farming is now a natural part of everyday farming. the commission has therefore decided to extend the scope of the existing aid to the following areas: we must reduce risks while ensuring the necessary protection of agricultural crops. it is therefore counterproductive to prevent the professional, targeted application of plant protection products by helicopter. aerial pest control means that a panel of experts, in the sense of integrated pest management, decides whether, when and how much to treat. i think that is safer than having every small individual vine-garden and winegrower decide for himself and then end up on the slope of the cliff, in the mist of the pesticide, when he is planting. i am firmly opposed to the introduction of taxes and duties on plant protection products. the increase in prices means a reduction in competitiveness rather than a reduction in the use of pesticides. finally, i would like to say that it is unacceptable for european agriculture to allow food and feed to be imported from third countries if it has been treated with active substances not authorised in the eu.

creation of a european financial prosecutor to deal with the growing number of cases of crossborder crime against the eu budget. the time has come. the eu is set to expand by ten new member states next year. the community budget will continue to grow, and the management of european funds will become even more complex. at the same time, crossborder crime will increase, becoming more professional thanks to modern technology. the territorial fragmentation of criminal justice systems and the difficulties in judicial cooperation between member states mean that offenders are rarely caught, and even less often convicted. statistics show that international and organised crime causes up to €1 billion in damage to the eu budget every year. this money may be used to finance other criminal structures. the best example is cigarette smuggling. the money of european taxpayers is wasted on the eu's own objectives. i repeat: lost, because we still do not have in europe effective structures for prosecuting eu financial crimes. the council recognized this danger when it enshrined the protection of financial interests in the first pillar of the maastricht treaty and established cooperation with the commission in the amsterdam treaty. with today's report from the committee on budgetary control, parliament is joining the 72 opinions which the commission has received and examined from various quarters on the green paper. i would like to point out that our report is an owninitiative report, not a legislative one. we in the committee took the time to analyse the issue of 'creating a european public prosecutor' in depth, commissioned experts to carry out external studies, and held a hearing with national parliaments and civil society representatives. we are now proposing options in this report, we are calling for improvements by the commission, particularly with regard to the respect of fundamental rights and the rights of the defence, the control of the european public prosecutor and his link with the existing structures. we want to link up with the existing structures of olaf, eurojust and europol. we want to avoid duplication of effort, but at the same time, with the fiscal prosecutor, we want to create an efficient instrument for protecting eu finances at european level. there are clear proposals for how the future european financial prosecutor could work with the national authorities in the member states. the principle of subsidiarity is a maxim here. all questions of the functioning of the public prosecutor's office can then be regulated by secondary law. i would like to thank my colleagues on my committee and also those on the constitutional, legal, internal affairs and petitions committees for their positive and constructive cooperation. their european parliament, should appoint this new body. the revision of the treaties is therefore an indispensable prerequisite, since only a treaty reform can legitimize the proposal. we call on the european convention to provide now for this legal basis for the establishment of a european public prosecutor to protect the financial interests of the eu, so that it can be put on the agenda of the refused. i think that is a reasonable course of action. so for us, when we go into a discharge procedure, there are always both options. in the language of the rules of procedure, both the option to postpone discharge and the option to grant discharge are mentioned. i think it should also be made clear that after four years we have now had the experience that parts of the house - and i mean the self-appointed eurosceptics - have been constantly trying to reduce the discharge procedure to an option of gathering as many votes as possible to shoot at the commission - perhaps it will eventually fall. i don't think that's what we mean by taking into account. there are always two options, not just one. to put this into the context of the accounting system, we have always assumed that, on the the commission is aware of the fact that the european parliament has been involved in the negotiations on the new agreement with the united states, and that the united states has been involved in the negotiations with the united states. the new amended proposal for a directive on the right to family reunification, on which the european parliament is due to vote today, was adopted by the commission in response to the mandate given by the heads of state or government meeting in laeken on 15 december 2001. the european council confirmed that a common policy on asylum and immigration would require the establishment of common rules on family reunification. the european council recognised, however, that progress was slower and less substantial than expected and that new impetus and new guidelines were therefore needed to make up the backlog. to this end, the european council invited the council of ministers to speed up its work and to adopt the provisions on family reunification by july 2003. the commission considers family reunification to be an essential element in the successful integration of thirdcountry nationals into european societies. this instrument is therefore for us an essential part of the common immigration policy proposed by the commission and was precisely the first of all the proposals which the commission submitted to the council in the implementation of the tampere mandate. the commission has adopted a new approach to the points on which there have been major differences between the member states for two years. this new approach recognises that achieving harmonisation of national legislation will require several steps. this proposal is therefore only the first step towards such a rapprochement. to this end, we have introduced a certain amount of flexibility into a number of instruments, particularly in relation to those areas where member states have diverged. this flexibility is, however, framed in two ways: first, on the substance, by the use of a standstill clause, which is intended to prevent member states from abusing derogations introduced subsequently from the legislation in force at the time of the adoption of this directive; the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the member states are able to apply the principle of equal treatment in all areas of family law. secondly, the commission introduces a rendezvous clause, which sets a deadline of two years after the transposition of the directive and expressly defines which provisions should be reviewed as a matter of priority in order to open the second stage of the process of harmonization of national legislation. this is obviously the case with the provisions considered to be more sensitive, such as the definition of family members and the possibility of also covering family members of community citizens who have not exercised their right to free movement. the main changes introduced in relation to the commission's initial proposal relate firstly to the definition of family members: the right to family reunification is guaranteed for the spouse and minor children. in the interests of flexibility, it has been specified that a member state may, only if its legislation already provides for this today or at the date of adoption of the directive, examine whether a child over the age of 12 meets an integration criterion. the admission of cohabiting couples, ascendants and older children is now optional for the member states, which will have to decide on this matter by law or regulation. as regards the arrangements for family reunification, the conditions relating to accommodation, material resources and sickness insurance are maintained on an optional basis. however, it is envisaged that it may be exercised after reunification, at the time of renewal of the residence permit of the family members. a derogation also allows national legislation to be maintained which takes into account the reception capacity of the member state when examining applications for family reunification. in such cases, depending on the capacity to receive, the applications may be staggered in time, provided that the waiting period for family members is no longer than three years. finally, the provisions on family reunification of refugees have been brought together in the same chapter to take better account of the specificity of their situation. in short, the proposal falls short of our initial intentions. however, it does not create any obligation to level the conditions for family reunification from below, and we see it as a first step on a path we wish to speed up, but which we will continue to follow with conviction and persistence. i am grateful to the rapporteur and to parliament for their support of this debate over these three long years of our journey together.

council mr president, commissioner, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, as president of the council of the union, i have the honour and pleasure today of speaking to the european parliament on the topical and urgent subject of enlargement, and i consider it a privilege to be here today to discuss this. this is a historic day for the european union and for the european parliament. in a week's time, on 16 april, greece as the presidency will have the pleasure of hosting the historic signing ceremony of the enlargement treaty in a historic place, the ancient agora, under the acropolis. despite the modern meaning of the word "market", the ancient market of athens has gone down in history for something else: it was there, in fact, that the concept of democracy was born and developed 2500 years ago, and the symbolism of this ceremony, which we have chosen to hold in this particular place, is that democracy and many other values associated with democracy are the common denominator that permeates every corner of the european union. we are a community of values and the success of the union and enlargement is determined entirely by the strengthening and continuation of these values. the states which are about to join the union are part of our common history, heritage and culture. their accession marks the end of the artificial division of our continent. we are today putting into practice our goal of building a europe based on the ideals of democracy, pluralism, the rule of law, respect for human rights and a free market economy. the union has always been committed to this objective. this is why, immediately after the fall of the berlin wall, the union responded to the challenge and reacted decisively and dynamically to the changing european political landscape. it offered a framework and a perspective for a united europe. it has offered a europe based on the free choice and solidarity of its citizens. the union's relations with the candidate countries have been gradually strengthened through various procedures, association agreements, structured dialogue on a range of issues, accession criteria and negotiations, pre-accession mechanisms and procedures. through all these steps the position of the european union has been very clear: to ensure the comprehensive, progressive, inclusive character of the accession process with all candidates participating on an equal footing and joining the european union with equal opportunities. at the start of the accession negotiations, the union made it clear that such accession entails full acceptance of the actual and potential rights and obligations associated with the union and its institutional framework, including in the field of external relations, and that accession entails the effective and substantial implementation of the acquis, including the establishment of a functioning and reliable public administration. the road to the conclusion of the negotiations was not an easy one. the commission has also been active in the field of the environment, and has been involved in the development of the european union's policy on the environment. but thanks to the persistence and determination of all parties, these negotiations were conducted in a thorough, efficient and transparent manner and i believe i can say on behalf of all those involved that we are proud of the process and its outcome. i would like to take this opportunity to thank in particular the commissioner here, mr verheugen, who was in charge of the negotiations, for his enormous contribution to the success of this whole process. the negotiations with the 10 acceding countries, as you know, were concluded in copenhagen last year on 13 december. the conditions for this are well known and are contained in the draft treaty and the act of accession submitted to the european parliament. the results of the negotiations we believe represent the best possible outcome and a fair deal. as we stressed in 1993, the union must have the capacity to absorb new members while preserving the momentum of european integration. the results of the negotiations will bring about this institutional balance. a balance is struck between the desire to ensure that the acceding states benefit fully from the various union policies and the need to ensure that the union is effective and competitive in the context of globalisation. in addition to the enormous and unprecedented work done by the council and the commission in this process, i would like to highlight the consistent and significant efforts made by the acceding states. i would also like to express my sincere thanks to the european parliament for the political support it has given us throughout the process. we particularly appreciate the open and constructive political dialogue with your democratically elected partners in each of the acceding states. this work, carried out by the joint parliamentary committees, has been invaluable, as has the work of so many of the parliamentary committees. it has made a significant contribution to clarifying for the acceding states what accession to the union entails. today the eyes of all the citizens of the acceding states are on us. some have already expressed their will. the positive results of the referendums in malta and slovenia are a clear and decisive sign of their confidence in the europe of tomorrow. the enlargement, ladies and gentlemen, gives us every reason to be optimistic about europe, even at a time when the international economy or the war in iraq are giving a negative sign of developments. there are, however, many reasons for this optimism. the european union as a whole has a healthier economic and fiscal base than a very large part of the rest of the world. it has succeeded in establishing a pole of relative stability; it has created a single and credible currency and a common policy framework that ensure the credibility of the emu as an international monetary pole. the union has developed a social model which, despite its diversity, acts as a shield against uncertainties and a loss of confidence. the union has a unique development model which combines the economic element with a wider range of social elements covering the fields of employment, social inclusion and a number of other issues. the union is launching a renewal of its policies through fine-tuning in a number of critical areas, such as structural policy or rural policy, to ensure its growth potential, social cohesion and capacity to meet international challenges. the union is addressing its internal concerns by renewing its institutional framework, particularly in the light of the deepening of the process of european integration. finally, in a number of areas such as trade, investment flows, technology transfer and the mobility of workers, enlargement creates new conditions for the union's functioning and thus opens up new possibilities for the european approach and the european model in the global context. i would like to conclude with two points. the first sign is that we are in a state of tension. the member states must show that we can achieve convergence of views through self-restraint, mutual concessions, political will to support the union's dynamic, strengthening the values of democracy, human rights and solidarity. the concept of solidarity is not limited to the negotiations on financing from the structural funds or the protection of the common agricultural policy or other specific issues. it is a horizontal approach to a wide range of union policies. the second point is that we must succeed as an enlarged union in the near future on multiple fronts. we must re-assemble the consequences of the differences that have existed in the field of foreign policy and sealed the issue of iraq. we must convince the citizens of the union and of other countries outside the union that we are a pole of values of peace, stability, trust and development support and we must rebuild our relations with all our key partners through a systematic and sincere effort. the european parliament has been a very active participant in the process of european integration. everyone deserves a share in that future. enlargement brings that vision much closer. the european union welcomes the future member states with the certainty that a new shape and a new dynamism are being achieved, a kind of dynamism that has also been manifested in these states during their transition period, in terms of economic, political and social issues and reforms. it is up to all of us to make enlargement a catalyst for faster european integration, a force which will ensure that europe is able to meet the challenges of a new era in global relations.
the commission is not prepared to accept the amendments tabled by the committee on budgets. today you are deciding one of the most important issues for the future of our continent. only you, only the european parliament, has the right to say yes or no to the accession of ten new member states. no other parliament in europe will have the opportunity to say yes or no to individual countries, but all the others will have to ratify the whole treaty. that is why this is certainly one of the most important decisions the house has had to make in its entire history. we are thus at the provisional end of a long, long road marked by the strong will to overcome the european division once and for all. i am infinitely grateful that the european parliament has always been absolutely clear in its support. i think it should also be noted that, like hardly any other european parliament, it has repeatedly, even during the cold war, raised the open wound of europe's division and called for a european future in which the peoples freely determine their own destiny in democracy and freedom. we are talking today primarily about the fate of nations and the fate of men. we are talking about 70 million people in europe who have looked forward to this day with infinite hope and expectation, but who have also paved the way with courage and determination for a free and united europe. they are peoples who are taking back their rightful and natural place in our midst. it's about the millions of people who have for many years been undertaking difficult and radical reforms and changes to create modern societies. if i may make a comment here, with a little side view of the reform policy or the reform debate in one or other member state: i wish that in one or another member state at least a little of the strength, courage and determination to reform that we have found in the future member states. (de) the the reunification of europe is a historic opportunity. however, there are doubts as to whether the czech republic is founded on the european legal order. czech prime ministers have described the expulsions after world war ii as "justified" and "necessary", and even recommended them in cases of modern conflict. the charter of fundamental rights of the european union, on the other hand, states that mass deportations are not allowed. therefore, the european parliament, in its resolution of 20 november 2002, states in point o that measures concerning ethnic groups which result in mass persecution and destruction of cultural values constitute a flagrant violation of european fundamental rights and the common legal philosophy of europeans. this verdict is clear. it does not seek any remedies but clarifies that various czech positions such as those mentioned above infringe the fundamental principles of law which the eu wants to preserve. we are of course pleased to note that president klaus has said that the events of violence and human tragedy which also affected the germans in bohemia are 'acts which are unacceptable from today's point of view'. however, no such statements were made by the government, the parliament of the czech republic, or any groups or parties. the czech republic has not yet been able to establish a legal framework for the implementation of the acquis. the czech republic has therefore not fulfilled all the conditions for accession to the eu and we cannot therefore approve its accession.

in writing. - i abstained from the vote on the czech republic's accession to the european union. the decisive factor for me was that the government in prague did not consider it necessary to renounce the decrees of former president benes. these decrees declared legal the most serious crimes, including murder, committed in connection with the expulsion of germans, austrians and hungarians. it is unacceptable that in april 2002 the czech parliament confirmed this form of expulsion as 'indisputable, unassailable and unchangeable'. a major part of my work in the european parliament is to ensure respect for human rights, the rule of law and the protection of minorities. these principles are part of the copenhagen criteria which all states wishing to join the eu must meet. it is the respect of these conditions - not merely of the acquis communautaire - that accession depends on. since these conditions have not been met on the czech side, a 'no' from me to action by the political authorities there would be absolutely reasonable. but as it is not a vote on governments but on states and their peoples, i did not vote today. i hope that the czech citizens will have a better understanding of the european union, a society of values and law, after accession.

- mr president, mr commissioner, mr president of the council! it's always been my dream to speak like a de gaulle, but not like a man who gives speeches like that. today, as we debate the future of european security and defence policy, we are witnessing the war in iraq. we thought we could prevent this war by diplomatic means. but we failed because we were politically divided and militarily non-existent. when it came to war and peace, we were once again unprepared. we were late, like in bosnia, like in kosovo, like in afghanistan. in none of these conflicts did the european union, as an international actor, play a role in determining the course of events. that is why one of the key tenets of the morillon report is that only a union with clearly defined foreign policy objectives and interests, equipped with effective military capabilities, counts. only such a union can become an independent actor in world politics and a confident partner in transatlantic relations. there are now some heads of government who, in view of their impotence in the face of the iraq war, feel that they must now publicly announce the aim of a european defence union. i wonder: have these heads of government not been involved in the decisions since helsinki in 1999? why have they not done more to ensure that the eu rapid response force is operational by 2003, as planned, with the necessary command structures and transport capabilities and with the latest technology? why has the reform of the adaptation of their national armed forces lagged behind the new security challenges? why have the military budgets been cut in this way? why did you have to go to the aircraft leasing company ukraine for the transport of your own soldiers in your own country? since 1999, the european parliament has consistently advocated the addition of military capabilities to the union's external policy instruments. this is what the convent is all about. this report is also intended to be the european parliament's contribution to the question of the future: how can the european union protect the security of its citizens in the face of new threats from terrorism and how can the union contribute to peace and stability in the world? preventive wars without legitimacy must never happen again! that is why we support in this report all those in the convention who are in favour of updating the petersberg tasks, who are in favour of a vanguard of member states being able to take over military emergency missions, who are in favour of a kind of european arms agency, who are in favour of a european assistance and solidarity clause and who want to introduce in particular the crucial point of majority decision-making in foreign policy and increased cooperation in defence policy. we do, however, think that governments should be aware of the following: millions of people also demonstrated in the streets of european cities in the run-up to the iraq war to demand that parliaments, not cabinets, decide on war and peace. the decision-making process on the crisis deployment of a european task force requires a very high degree of democratic legitimacy. let me make one final point: all the crisis operations envisaged under the esdp will have a civilian and a military component. that is precisely what distinguishes us from nato. we are now represented in bosnia by a police mission. next year, we may be replacing nato's sfor mission. we can best ensure cohesion between civil and military operations if they are governed by the same rules and the common costs of each are financed by the budget of the european union. this is a matter of parliamentary control, but it also gives governments democratic support and approval for their actions. the citizens of the european union are already saying yes to the concept of a european defence policy as set out in the morillon report. 71% of europeans are in favour. only the cabinet hasn't figured it out yet.
the commission has already made a number of proposals. i would like to begin by congratulating mr philippe morillon on his excellent report. this debate and the fact that there are relatively few amendments has shown that he has been able to achieve a very broad consensus in this house on this very important issue. if we compare this with the situation five years ago in similar debates, we can see that there is now a very broad consensus in this house on the need for a european defence contribution. i would like to congratulate philippe morillon. the report is an important building block in the development of a european union security strategy. why is it necessary? we took note of the new security strategy of the united states last september. we are now seeing week by week the systematic implementation of this united states security strategy. what we need as europeans is a response to this, a european security strategy. it is necessary that we europeans, as the building blocks of a common foreign policy, first of all define our security interests together. i think that's entirely possible. firstly, there is a broad consensus that we as the european union are capable of defending ourselves, within the framework of nato, together with our allies, but also, if necessary, autonomously, against any conceivable aggressor. i would very much welcome it if the convention decided to propose a mutual assistance clause for the new constitution of the european union. second, we should develop the skills. we need some time to make the necessary contributions to the management of crises in the geographical environment of the european union, both civil and military. we haven't done that yet, we haven't been able to do that autonomously yet, but it's a skill that we have to develop. thirdly, we as the european union should be able to carry out rescue operations anywhere in the world and at any time when the safety of european citizens is at stake. these are three further building blocks for a security strategy for the european union. in developing this, we must take account of the experience we have gained in similar large projects, such as the internal market or the european currency. the only reason these were successful was because we had clearly defined the content and timing of what we wanted to be able to do and when. some answers to this question can be found in the report by mr philippe morillon. what the citizens expect from the european union is peace, security and stability. we, as the european parliament, must do our part to ensure that the european union as a whole actually meets this requirement.
