the rapporteur. the commission has already made a number of proposals. let me start by saying that i am very pleased to announce that 15 national presidents of 'europa donna', the european breast cancer coalition, are attending this debate in the visitors' gallery today. breast cancer affects all of us. in the european union, a new breast cancer diagnosis is made every two and a half minutes. 216,000 women are affected every year. 79 000 women still die of this disease, even though 90% of breast cancers are curable - but only if they are detected early and treated properly. these women usually die at an age of high social responsibility. breast cancer is still the number one cause of death for women between 35 and 55. but 25 000 women could be saved every year if all member states offered reasonable precautions, i.e. mammography screening according to eu guidelines. this is to ensure that radiologists perform only chest x-rays and read about 5 000 x-rays a year to have a trained eye. it is totally unacceptable that, eleven years after the eu guidelines were presented, only eight member states offer national mammography screening programmes. in sweden, finland, the netherlands and the united kingdom, for example, 90% of all women aged 50 to 69 are already screened, whereas in my country, germany, only just under 2% of women in this age group are offered this screening. and this is despite the fact that mammography screening has been shown to reduce mortality by as much as 35 percent, according to the world health organization. but even the best early detection is useless if subsequent treatments are inadequate or even wrong. the report therefore calls on the member states to establish an eu-wide network of interdisciplinary breast centres, i.e. one interdisciplinary breast centre per 330 000 inhabitants, certified by an independent body and, of course, regularly recertified. in these wards, the entire medical and nursing team must be specialised in benign and malignant diseases of the breast only, and each case must be consulted in a joint case conference. it is particularly important that the surgeon performs only breast surgery and that the center itself performs at least 150 operations for first-time patients each year, since only experience makes a master. the reason these breast centers are so important is that women who are treated there have been shown to have better chances of recovery. for example, the survival rates of patients in sweden, where there is nationwide screening and breast centers, are 16% higher than in austria, where there is no such thing. by the way, breast centres are only found in sweden, denmark, portugal and the united kingdom. it is precisely because the mortality rates and the survival rates are so different that we must come to a common european strategy in the fight against breast cancer. we need to inform ourselves faster, exchange information more effectively, introduce benchmarking and learn from best practice. this is the only way to save more women's lives and at the same time help reduce health care costs. i am convinced that this is the only way to put positive pressure on the countries which are still lagging behind. this is also true of national cancer registers, which are the basic prerequisite for reliable data and which are only available in half of the first vice-president of the european parliament delegation to the convention. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your work. the fact that we reached a consensus in the convention on friday on the proposal for a european constitution has been called historic, and in fact: what has happened? we have drafted a constitution for 25 or more sovereign states and peoples who have been plundering, warring and destroying each other for centuries. this is unprecedented in history. we have drawn up a constitution for so many peoples and states, each with its own long history, each speaking different languages, each preserving its own identity and yet all wanting to take their destiny into their own hands. this has never happened in the history of europe and the world! what's new? i would like to mention only six points which i consider particularly important. first, the constitution sets out the rights and duties of citizens. we have made the charter of fundamental rights an integral and legally binding part of the european constitution. secondly, the famous four freedoms of the treaties of rome were also promises for the future. those promises have been fulfilled today. the new constitution puts a new promise in articles 2 and 3, namely sustainability, justice, security and solidarity for european citizens. thirdly, the most important contribution to democracy and to the acceptance of european policies is clarity. the citizens must be able to see what the european union can and cannot regulate. the citizens must be able to see who is responsible for political decisions and who is not. the constitution makes great progress on this point. we have created a system of competences which for the first time defines competences between member states and the european union more clearly than has been the case until now, and i would remind the senior members of the european parliament that our parliament has twice failed to achieve this in the past. we have drastically simplified and cut back on decision-making. fourthly, our european parliament. the co-decision procedure in the legislative process will become the rule. today it is the exception, tomorrow it will be the rule, and this is a quantum leap from the situation today. finally, the president of the commission will be elected by this parliament. this will increase his political legitimacy and will enhance the importance of the european elections. fifthly, we have tried to strike a balance between the institutions. we have strengthened all three, the european its security strategy. i think this is the first time that this has been done, and i would like to stress that it seems to me an important step in the construction of a europe that is moving along the path of politics. i shall start with a fundamental premise from which the entire content of the document itself is deduced. i believe that a europe of this size, with 25 democratic countries, which will soon have a population twice that of the united states of america, which will have four times the population of japan (and i take as an example two large countries with a strong currency like ours), which contributes approximately a quarter of the gross world product, cannot but be, i repeat, an international actor. whether we like it or not, we're gonna have to be an international player. the whole theory of how the security process in europe should be conducted must be based on this principle, which i deeply believe in - and i hope that you believe in too. the document is about to be finalised and will be presented to the heads of government on thursday and friday in thessaloniki. i would like to briefly introduce its structure. it starts with an analysis of the security environment in which we live, obviously regional conflicts, the causes of those conflicts, which affect us: poverty, exclusion, or lack of natural resources, to move on to also analyze the more recent threats such as international terrorism, the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction and failed states. the second chapter, which is based on this analysis, deals with the major strategic objectives which, in our view, european security should have. the first strategic objective must of course be to extend and stabilise the security zone around our european union, that is to say around our continent, namely to the east and to the south. i believe that the document which the commission has recently presented on the new europe and its borders has a lot to do with where and how the european union should start to maintain its security environment. the second important point about the strategic security objectives must, in our view, be to strengthen the international order. i think that if europe has a sense of international order, it could probably be described in two words: we are effective multilateralists and on effective multilateralism we must build our theory of world order. we are working from that point of view and we want to continue to work to defend european security through all the organizations and, above all, through the united nations. of course, we have more specific actors, such as the united states, the russian federation or other large countries or large international actors. but i would like to say - and we are trying to make this profound reflection reflect in this document - the following: for an effective multilateral system to exist and, more specifically, for the un system to be credible, we must in principle be prepared to enforce all the principles of the un and for the un to have the credibility it deserves. when some of the principles on which the charter is based and some of the resolutions of the security council are not respected, the european union cannot remain passive and must act; and it must act with all the means at its disposal, which are many. the european union, fortunately, has a whole range of means of action which could range from diplomatic action to peacekeeping action, with the deployment of forces. mr hughes, who is not here at the moment, has made a very useful and beautiful reflection on how the european union can also play an important role in effective dialogue in the event of conflict. but we must have the courage to tell ourselves that when the rules, the principles that we have all decided to defend in the framework of this effective multilateralism are not respected, the european union must also be prepared to deal with that breakdown of international agreements or contracts, commission. mr president, over the last three or four years the high representative and i have made speeches on this subject which i guess you could measure by the metre, and if you were to look at them, you would find that they were all remarkably similar and reflected the arguments which the high representative has put again so forcefully and ably today. in many respects it is remarkable that the european union has proceeded so far and so fast towards a common foreign and security policy, and towards a security and defence policy without the benefit – until now – of a formal security strategy. the commission very much welcomes the decision to rectify that omission and looks forward to the debates that will take place on the strategy document which is going to come forward shortly. on the defence and military side there has been impressive progress in creating european capacities that the union is already beginning to put to use. as the high representative has said, we need to be explicit about our strategic purposes, and the circumstances in which the european union might deploy force. as i have said before and as he has said, we also have to challenge our colleagues in government and our electorates about the gap which exists between ambition and what people are prepared to pay, and what people are prepared to cooperate over. the commission, as i have said before, is not a silent and disinterested onlooker in this debate. we have no direct role in defence and military matters, and even in the absence of my honourable friend mr van orden, i repeat that we do not aspire to a direct role in defence and military matters. but whatever the eu does militarily – whether in conflict prevention, crisis management or post-conflict reconstruction – is inevitably part of a wider european strategy including many elements for which the commission does indeed have the lead responsibility. the european union needs a seamless approach, which is why the high representative and i – with our respective services – have worked so closely together, and why i am pleased that the european convention has proposed even closer integration in future. the real point i want to make, however, is that defence and military issues are only one dimension – and for the european union still a relatively small dimension – of any 'security strategy' which is worthy of the name. in a sense, the eu itself – its creation, its development and its enlargement – can be seen as a european security strategy, and it has been a brilliantly effective one. the union has provided the central economic and political organising principle for our continent over the last half century, helping to secure democracy and stability for countries emerging from dictatorship and oppression. through the wider europe agenda, too, we seek to extend stability to our neighbours and the circle of friends around us. perhaps the central element in any security strategy for europe must be to ensure that the eu itself continues to prosper and to develop. beyond that, the eu is a major contributor to international security in a host of different contexts: through, for example, our contribution to global trade. the eu has played a central role in the creation and development of the world trade organisation, and we are now engaged in the doha development round. it would be hard to exaggerate the importance of that work for global security, because security and prosperity are so closely intertwined. we also contribute to global security through external development assistance. i have pointed out to the house before that we are responsible – the eu, the commission and member states – for about 55% of all such assistance worldwide, and for about two-thirds of all grant assistance. that is a vital contribution to security because poverty and inequality are not just moral issues but also security issues. through our assistance, too, we work for human rights and for better governance. again, these are security issues linked, for example, to the fight against terrorism, because inequality and oppression are the breeding ground of hatred, intolerance and violence. above all, however, the eu can contribute to international security through its work in – and support for – multinational frameworks and disciplines that are increasingly necessary and important for managing the affairs of an interdependent world. i am thinking here of un disarmament and non-proliferation conventions; environmental treaties such as the kyoto protocol on climate change; and, of course, the international criminal court. i could go on – but the point is clear. we cannot simply divide between our security interests on the one hand and our development and trade interests on the other. in order to prevent future violent conflicts we have to have policies on environmental degradation, poverty and global governance, aids, justice and home affairs, nuclear safety, and so on. i think the point is clear. so the underlying conclusion is that effective multilateralism should be the motto on the european union’s banner. that is the essence of our security strategy. i shall say a brief word about small arms and light weapons, because that too underlines the importance of practical and effective multilateralism. we are committed to combating the spread of small arms around the world. a code of conduct on arms exports was adopted five years ago, under which member states set high common standards for the management of conventional arms transfers. the code has since established itself as a comprehensive international arms export regime. in a joint action covering small arms later in 1998 the eu pledged to promote a number of principles including commitments by all countries to supply small arms only to governments, and to import and hold arms exclusively for their legitimate security needs. the eu has set aside funds for the provision of financial and technical assistance to small arms programmes and projects around the world. i look forward to the publication of the document on security. as the high representative said, this will be the beginning of a very important debate, and of course much of that debate will take place in these hallowed chambers. we look forward to hearing the contributions of honourable members who have already made a significant contribution to the broader comprehension of security which is now shared throughout the eu. the commission (es) mr president, this proposal is intended to put into practice definitively the objectives already set out in amsterdam in article 191 of the treaty. this article was supplemented by the treaty of nice by adding a legal basis for the adoption of the necessary legislative measures by the co-decision procedure and by qualified majority. political parties are an important part of the democratic architecture in the european union, they are factors of integration and contribute to promoting european awareness, expressing the wishes of the citizens of the union and fostering political debate at european level. to do so they need to have the resources, it is therefore appropriate and necessary to help them to carry out the tasks assigned to them by the treaty and for this they should receive funding, at least partial, from the community budgets. the regulation aims to establish a sound and transparent legislative framework for the recognition and funding of european political parties. we are not starting from scratch, ladies and gentlemen; this new proposal builds on the constructive work that parliament and the council did in 2001, especially during the belgian presidency. let me congratulate mrs schleicher on her report. we have taken advantage of the new possibilities offered by majority voting against the commitment reached in 2001 to propose higher thresholds for obtaining funding. our fundamental approach has been to avoid too restrictive political requirements for european political parties for two reasons: firstly, we want an open and pluralist system in which all opinion trends can be represented in the european debate; secondly, otherwise the debate in the council and parliament would be unnecessarily prolonged, perhaps even beyond the 2004 european elections. the three institutions agree that a european political party wishing to be recognised as such and to receive funding from the community budget must meet a minimum of conditions. we have tried to establish conditions which are not restrictive but which are coherent and essential. parties must have a certain degree of representativeness, a statute and objectives, a clear intention to stand in european elections, clear responsibilities for their financial management and, above all, respect for the democratic principles laid down in article 6 (1) and (2) of the charter of fundamental rights of the european union. at the same time we need a reliable system of verification. parliament should be able to check whether all these conditions are met before registering a party. there is also a special verification procedure in the event that a minority in parliament rejects this first decision. in order to receive funding, we propose that parties should have elected representatives at european, national and regional level in one third of the states of the union, because these are european parties and we are in the european arena and therefore it is precisely this arena that we are trying to promote. in line with declaration no 11 annexed to the treaty of nice, the commission proposal prohibits cross-financing of national political parties. the financing by political groups of the provision of services is also prohibited, unless it is paid for in a verifiable and documented manner, i.e. through invoices. article 8 provides for strict control and audit measures to support the transparency and legitimacy of the system; we believe that parties should not be completely dependent on public funding and therefore propose that at least 25% of their budget should come from their own resources. we have taken a balanced approach to the controversial issue of donations in line with the 2001 commitment, so we propose that donations be allowed, but only under strict conditions of transparency. in conclusion, mr president, i should like to congratulate the greek presidency on the results, on the compromise reached between the council and parliament, to which the commission has contributed and which should hopefully allow this dossier to be concluded at first reading. i congratulate mr leinen and the presidency and i want to express on behalf of the commission our full acceptance and support for this compromise which we consider appropriate and which will allow us to meet the needs of the various stakeholders in this complex matter.

re-evaluation process in order to take new scientific information into account. companies must demonstrate the positive effect on the animal or in the feed and the absence of any risk to human health, animal health or the environment when applying for authorisation or re-authorisation of a feed additive. at present, four antibiotics are authorised for use in animal feed as growth promoters. the eu otherwise under the immunity law in force in germany. the commission must not even begin to draw up a file and to investigate without a specific decision on the waiver of immunity. but in view of the circumstances of this particular case, it seems to us appropriate, particularly in view of the relatively close proximity to the european elections, not to waive immunity in the present case. i ask the house to follow the committee's proposal.

commission. mr president, i am happy that these two issues have now entered their second reading, as a quick but thorough examination is necessary to avoid the dangers of the proposals not being adopted before the end of this legislature. our common task and aim is to modernise and simplify public procurement rules and in this respect i believe that the texts agreed upon in council already strike a fair balance among the different interests at stake. indeed, although there are a few issues that the commission considers less than ideal, overall these common positions clearly represent an advance compared to the current legislation. when i look at the substance of most of the amendments tabled to date by parliament i feel even more convinced of what i said just now. i am therefore fairly optimistic that the vote due to take place later this week will preserve our chances of closing this file in a way that is satisfactory to all three institutions, indeed, in my view quite a number of amendments are already incorporated in one form or another in the common positions. i refer for example to the social aspects – other than social award criteria – where i understand that the main concern of this parliament is to clarify that both contracting authorities and bidders respect the obligations laid down in social legislation. that concern was also explicitly debated with council. it is therefore in my view appropriately reflected in the recitals of the current text. i am ready to accept that it should be mandatory for contracting authorities and entities to indicate where information on the applicable social, fiscal and environmental obligations may be obtained. equally, with some redrafting, the commission could accept amendment no 29 to the public sector – or classic – directive and amendment no 26 to the utilities directive, which emphasise certain possibilities which already exist in the social field. as for the environmental aspects and in general on the issue of award criteria, the amendments which parliament has tabled clearly show some differing views. i am ready, as always, to debate further this interesting issue with parliament through answers to questions, though in respect of the real aim of public procurement rules, as interpreted and confirmed by the european court of justice. indeed, i have no doubt that we all agree that our priority is to make public procurement rules a simplified tool for public bodies to spend taxpayers' money as well as possible. these differences of views have often meant that conflicting amendments have been adopted in the committee on legal affairs and the internal market which, if accepted, would make legislation incoherent. we should perhaps all keep in mind our common stated goal of 'better regulation'. this inconsistency is well illustrated by the amendments to the utilities directive concerning award criteria. let us start by looking at how the common positions deal with this issue. in full accordance with the current state of jurisprudence, the common positions already clarify that environmental characteristics may be used as award criteria and that it is not necessary to show that each and every award criterion taking individually provides an economic benefit for the contracting authorities or entities. it is sufficient that, taken as a whole, the award criteria meet their proper function: to allow an objective evaluation and comparison of the intrinsic qualities of the product or service and the award of the contract to the most economically advantageous tender. it is, therefore, with some concern that i see amendments to the utilities directive that would go well beyond this. the effect of such amendments would be to allow vague, immeasurable elements, for the benefit of civil society in the broadest sense, to be used as award criteria. that would not only prevent award criteria from playing their proper role, but also introduce an unacceptable degree of arbitrary choice, or perhaps even discrimination to the detriment of potential contractors. in respect of social award criteria, we should also keep in mind that the common positions already clarify that such criteria may be used where they meet the same conditions as environmental award criteria. however, these amendments to the utilities directive would permit social award criteria to be used to meet social policy objectives concerning the behaviour or the social responsibility of the tenderer, rather than the intrinsic qualities of the product or service in question. this could lead to the award of contracts on the basis of considerations which have nothing to do with the principal of better value for money. on the amendments aimed at favouring small and medium enterprises, i should like to stress that information available to us does not show that smes currently encounter any major difficulty in gaining access to public tenders. their european federation even told us that they would not support any positive discrimination in favour of smes vis-à-vis big enterprises. in general, we should all be careful not to introduce changes which might de facto lead to national preferences which are incompatible with community law and which might end up protecting economic interests. let me draw the attention of parliament to the sensitive issue of thresholds, which may be the one where our divergence of views may be very hard to reconcile. my aim is to ensure effective competition at european level. if we increase the thresholds, not only would we breach our international obligations, but we would also reduce efficiencies. if we raise the thresholds we do not necessarily simplify life for local authorities, which are in any case subject to an obligation of adequate publicity under the current case-law of the european court of justice. that is why the commission cannot accept those amendments. in line with the interinstitutional agreement on better regulation we have recently reached, we all share the three objectives on modernising, simplifying and increasing the flexibility of the current rules. it is in this spirit that i have some reluctance in accepting some further amendments relating to different subjects such as e-auctions, framework agreements, dynamic purchasing systems, the competitive dialogue and the choice between separate or joint awarding of contracts for design and execution of works contracts. in fact, i fear that these amendments would multiply or complicate procedures unnecessarily or impose certain choices at community level where the necessary flexibility could be better assured by making such choices possible at the national level. i should now like to say something on some central issues specific to the utilities directive. concerning the amendments to the mechanism for exempting contracting entities from the directive – article 30 of the common position – let me stress that the common position is based on two principles, legal certainty and real, effective liberalisation. the commission is therefore of the opinion that the presence of genuine competition should be established by a known procedure. otherwise, neither contracting entities nor interested suppliers would be sure of their legal position. the commission is also opposed to other initiatives regarding specific sectors, which would permit exclusion on the basis of free access alone, irrespective of whether or not this results in effective and real competition. for essentially the same reasons, the commission cannot accept the proposed changes concerning postal services. finally, concerning the 'intra-group' exception of article 23, the commission already made it clear that it has major difficulties in accepting the extension of this exclusion to works and supply contracts. it does not however, want to make the directive less flexible than it already is. for that reason, the commission can accept the fact that the extension to works and supplies contracts should be eliminated, but not that contracting entities should be deprived of the existing flexibility for services. in concluding i repeat that i am confident that by focusing on our main common goals to modernise, simplify and ensure an effective use of public money, we can provide a happy ending to the long saga of this reform to public procurement rules. this result is impatiently awaited by european enterprises, public authorities and contracting entities. it will be of great benefit to the european economy as a whole. finally, may i point out that the commission's opinion on the individual amendments has been provided in writingcommission's position on amendments: see annex..

powers between the various institutions. our democratic legitimacy is enhanced by extending the codecision procedure to almost all cases, which is extremely important for parliament. the european union is facing a new challenge: the creation of a single foreign minister for the whole of the union, with a single legal personality, with new rules on foreign policy, common security and defence. finally, the constitutional text now includes the charter of fundamental rights, which guarantees the rights of all european citizens. these are the lights, and these are really important lights. however, there are still some areas where the compromise reached does not have the ambition it should have. the draft constitution does extend qualified majority voting, but it is certainly not enough, because the proposed solution risks paralysing a union with 25 or 30 members in many respects. at the institutional level, it will also be difficult to convince the public that only half of the commissioners will have voting rights in the college, at least at this very complicated stage in our institutional life. it will also be difficult to understand the relationship between the new president of the council and the president of the commission, which is likely to overlap. although some progress has been made in economic governance, we must also establish the external representation of the euro: without this, the euro is certainly more fragile and our economy more exposed. these are not technical issues but problems which require us to take the courage to overcome the fears and cautions of the present and to look beyond. we must realise that if we do not make a leap forward today, in 30 or 40 years europe will no longer have any influence on the international chessboard. but overall, the draft prepared by the convention is a good basis and a common definition which i share for the intergovernmental conference which is responsible for adopting it definitively. the commission will do its part in this respect to improve it, starting with the opinion we will publish in september, before the igc opens. i now turn to the second point: the reform of the commission and the staff regulations. we are approaching the last year of the commission's mandate. when i took up my post, i had made the reform of the commission itself one of my priorities, and i remember that the white paper was already out in march 2000. a key element of this process was the revision of the staff regulations of european officials. i should like to thank the greek presidency once again for the impetus it has given to the negotiations, which have been objectively very difficult. thanks to this valuable work of mediation and impulse, consensus was reached on the best possible compromise, a compromise - i would like to stress this - which respects the broad lines of the commission's initial proposals. following this agreement, the commission will present a second proposal in the autumn, which will of course take account of the opinion adopted by this house on 19 june and of the negotiations between the representatives of the staff, the institutions and the member states taking place within the conciliation committee. the aim is to apply the new statute on 1 may 2004, the same day as the new member states join the union. beyond this objective, however, i look at the overall policy objective of the exercise, which is to ensure continuity, independence and excellence in our services. i must say that i have worked with many administrations in my life, but i have rarely found such a high level of work capacity and quality as in the european institutions. i therefore believe that the new statute will enable our civil service to work with more strength, with more pride, especially as colleagues from ten new countries arrive. this effort to absorb new cultures will not be easy, precisely because ten countries are coming together, not just one. the third point i would like to touch on is immigration and asylum policy and the management of the union's external borders. the commission welcomes the greek presidency's consistent and balanced position on these issues. i am also pleased to note that the conclusions of the european council were based on the communications presented by the commission on 4 june. to get down to the specifics and to start with the problems still on the table, i would point out that community funding must gradually be brought up to the level of our political ambitions and objectives; i would like to ask the commissioner whether he is aware that the commission has not yet taken a decision on the matter. of course we have estimated the resources which do not exceed the budgetary limits - that is, we have remained strictly within the budgetary limits - but we have estimated the necessary resources at eur 140 million for the period 2004-2006 and eur 250 million for a multiannual programme of cooperation with third countries for the period 2004-2008. this is pending the new openings in the framework of the financial perspective applicable after 2006, which, as stated in the thessaloniki conclusions, will have to reflect this political priority of the union; otherwise, it is clear, the very identity of the union is at risk if we fail to provide security for our citizens. as regards relations with third countries, the new cooperation programme proposed by the commission on 11 june will be an important support for readmission policy, which is another basic chapter, and it will be crucial for parliament and the council to approve this instrument before the end of the legislature. the negotiation of community agreements with the support of the council and the member states must also be intensified. in my view, this concerns russia, ukraine and morocco, three key countries in these agreements, as a matter of priority. the european council has called on the commission to move towards integrated management of the external borders, and we believe that the best solution is to create an agency to improve the implementation of the council's strategic guidelines, in conjunction with the relevant national services, in order to form a coordination network. we are also laying the foundations for the so-called vis, the ambitious european system for identifying visas, which is also a common tool for implementing a policy that gives our citizens peace of mind and freedom of movement, while respecting their rights to freedom. the commission has already taken a number of initiatives to ensure that the european union's citizens are able to enjoy the same rights as citizens. the fight against illegal immigration must therefore go hand in hand with measures to facilitate the entry of legal immigrants into the union. in this connection, i would like to remind you that some proposals are already on the table, particularly those relating to entry and residence for work and study purposes, as well as to the vocational training of immigrants and to voluntary work to help them integrate. parliament has already expressed its views on these proposals, which are still being discussed in the council, and the commission welcomes the european council's invitation to draw up a comprehensive policy for the integration of legal immigrants. the national approaches also need to be better coordinated at community level, and i believe that an annual report on progress would certainly be a step in this direction. we've talked a lot about benchmarking and comparison and all that stuff. i think that, on this subject which is so complex and so full of different aspects, a report which tells us what is going on at european level could be useful, and to you and to us. the same political will must be applied in the field of asylum. i am very sorry to say that it has not been possible to reach agreement in the council on the directive defining the concept of refugee and harmonizing forms of subsidiary protection. this is what we have to do, again in the context of the rights debate, which we have just highlighted. this instrument, together with the procedural directive, is the heart of the common system. i take this opportunity to assure the italian presidency of the commission's full cooperation in order to achieve the adoption of these two texts by december at the latest, which is the deadline set by the thessaloniki council. i now come to the last point: the statute of political parties. we welcome the recent adoption by this parliament of the statute for european political parties: it is the fourth success of the greek presidency that i want to talk about today. i join the many who have recognized its contribution to solving a problem that was now a year old and that absolutely needed to be defined. a number of factors contributed to this result: the commission's proposal for a regulation on the common organisation of the market in wine positive conclusion was reached only by majority voting and the codecision procedure. i think it's a lesson for the future as well. finally, european political parties can operate on a clear, transparent basis and rely on a source of funding that is at least partly borne by the community budget. this is a basic prerequisite for the management of democratic life and a measure which is part of the wider constitutionalisation of the european integration process. the proposal which has been adopted, while imposing some simple and coherent conditions, avoids overly restrictive and formally bureaucratic criteria and therefore seems to me to be a decision of good sense and capable of producing positive political consequences. we all know that political parties are an essential part of the democratic architecture of the union: without them there can be no integration, without them there can be no european consciousness. i have to say that i am not in favour of the amendments. as i said mr president, ladies and gentlemen, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your work. the thessaloniki summit statement on the security policy of the european union was an important step towards a common security and defence policy of the european union. the united states has clearly stated its security policy and it acts on it every day. the european union must respond constructively to this situation. this paper before us is the beginning of such a joint response. and if you look at it, you find that whenever it comes to analyzing the new threats in the world, there are common statements that are made that are extraordinarily profound and extraordinarily true. but when it comes to defining the answers, to saying what needs to be done now, you find that it is extremely difficult to arrive at a coherent statement by way of unanimity. that's why this paper can only be a beginning, a beginning with important statements. but we need a broad debate on this in the european union, including in the european parliament, in order to arrive gradually at a common security strategy. we need clearer statements on our relationship with nato, our relationship with the united nations, the role that russia and turkey will play in this security concept, and we need a clearer mandate - including the one given to the intergovernmental conference - for the defence agency that is now being planned. but above all, we need a phased plan. we have seen that the european union has only been successful in implementing projects if it had a plan with clear content and timetables. the task before us now is to formulate such a european union strategy in greater detail.
commission. madam president, i am very pleased that we have now reached the final stages of the deliberations on the gm food and feed proposal – which i first presented to you almost two years ago. the discussions have been intensive, complex and have often provoked strong emotional reactions and divided opinions. it is now important to draw the discussions to a close. allow me to draw your attention to the three principal elements of the proposal. first, it will ensure a high level of protection of human and animal health on the basis of a streamlined, efficient and more transparent authorisation procedure. animal feed produced from gmos will, in future, be subject to authorisation. the simplified procedure based on substantial equivalence will be abandoned and authorisations will be limited to a period of 10 years. the public will have the opportunity to make comments prior to decisions and to the authorisation of products. second, the proposal provides consumers with what they so overwhelmingly demand – an indication of whether or not food and feed ingredients are produced from gmos. this will provide consumers with the freedom to choose between gm and non-gm products. similarly, feed produced from gmos will have to be labelled to facilitate the freedom of choice for farmers and other operators dealing with animal feed. third, the proposal increases the legal certainty for operators and traders, which they need to carry out their daily business. the common position adopted by the council in march is both balanced and rational. it represents a major step forward in building public confidence in the application of biotechnology to food. i am pleased that a compromise package has been tabled to facilitate the final adoption of the proposal. i would like to thank the rapporteur and also the shadow rapporteurs for their hard work towards arriving at this compromise package and for their willingness to ensure a balanced result as well as a timely resolution of the outstanding issues. the compromise package includes provisions concerning the issue of coexistence between different forms of agriculture. the commission agrees that this is an important issue for which appropriate solutions need to be devised. the commission would have preferred to address coexistence separately in the context of commissioner fischler’s current work. however, the commission is prepared to support the compromise package and – as outlined in the package – to develop guidelines on appropriate measures to be taken at national level. such guidelines are on course to be adopted by the commission later this month. to conclude, let me state the commission's position on the amendments as tabled. the commission can adopt the compromise package, consisting of amendments nos 1, 7, 8, 9, and 44 to 48, provided all the other amendments are rejected.
commission. madam president, we all know that the gmo issue is a political one as well as a technical one. as policy-makers and legislators we have a clear responsibility to provide a high level of safety for european citizens and to enable them to exercise choice. the european union has been building a system that allows us to base decisions on whether or not to authorise the use and release of gm products on the best available scientific and technical advice. once that base is secured it is then a matter of ensuring that the consumer is correctly informed so that he or she is able to choose whether or not to buy gm products. the two proposals now being considered in second reading are important parts of the overall design of our system for dealing responsibly with gm products. they have been fully debated inside all the political groups and different committees. turning to the proposal for which i am responsible, i would like to thank the rapporteur, mr trakatellis, and the presidency for their efforts to finalise the proposal on labelling and traceability. i hope that parliament and the council will be able to agree on the amendments to be adopted later in plenary, so that we can reach agreement on both food and feed and traceability in labelling in this part-session. this proposal will provide an important complement to the existing regulatory framework. you will all be aware of the difficult negotiations leading up to the adoption of the common position. the gap between the different positions has narrowed, as many of the amendments adopted at first reading were introduced in the common position. as was to be expected, the issue of coexistence has surfaced as the key issue at second reading of both proposals. the new article to be introduced into the directive under the political agreement for the proposal on food and feed will provide for a legal base under which to work. this, linked with the forthcoming initiative from the commission on guidelines for coexistence will provide member states with the possibility of implementing appropriate measures to deal with coexistence. in terms of the key issues, the commission can support the amendments that provide clarification of the common position. these include amendment nos 1, 3, 4, 18, 24, 26 and 27, as well as the second part of amendment no 17, and the first parts of amendment nos 8 and 13. conversely, amendment nos 22, 23, 25, and 28 seek to introduce texts on coexistence that are identical to that which would be laid down in directive 2001/18/ec and the regulation on gm food and feed. the commission considers this to be duplication but we could accept it. the remaining amendments, the majority of which are retabled from first reading, cannot be supported. amendment nos 2, 9, 10, 14 and 15 refer to exemptions via thresholds. acceptance of these amendments would undermine the political agreement reached on the proposal on gm food and feed. as i have previously said, consistency and coherence between the two proposals must be ensured. in addition, the first part of amendment no 15 seeks to reinstate national provisions for traceability under directive 2001/18/ec. to accept this would only create legal uncertainty, given that the proposal on the table will provide community rules for traceability as well as labelling. amendment no 7 refers to the 'may contain' clause for food and feed products in the original commission proposal. this was also the subject of a very difficult debate and to reopen it now would have serious consequences for the operability of our system and the forthcoming wto panel. amendment no 6, which refers to the definition of the placing on the market, was also subject to considerable debate in the council, following adoption of the same amendment at first reading. the wording of this amendment was included in the common position via reference to the full definition of placing on the market from directive 2001/18/ec. the commission cannot support further amendment of this definition particularly as the tabled amendment would contradict definitions already laid down in community legislation. amendment nos 5 and 29 refer to the precautionary principle. i would point out that the council addressed this amendment in the common position as supported by the commission. the precautionary principle relates to risk assessment which is why it appears in directive 2001/18/ec and the proposal on gm food and feed. traceability is a facilitating measure, but it is not based on risk assessment. to go further than the current wording of the recital is not appropriate and the commission cannot support these amendments. amendment nos 11 and 12 refer to traceability and labelling requirements for processed products and acceptance would again impinge on the agreement reached under the proposal on gm food and feed which covers such products. the second parts of amendment nos 8 and 13 seek to extend the time-period for the holding of traceability information from five years to ten years. even if traceability were still possible after ten years this information would be of no practical value. amendment no 20 addresses the reporting obligations of the commission, which are duplicated in amendment no 3. reporting obligations are already reflected in article 12 of the common position and further requirements are not necessary. in terms of coexistence, amendment no 16 in a similar manner to an amendment on the proposal gm food and feed, seeks to introduce text to address this issue into a new article 26a of directive 2001/18/ec. however, the text of amendment no 16 is not in line with that proposed for this new article under the political agreement for the proposal on gm food and feed and therefore we cannot accept it. finally, amendment no 21 refers to the date of application of the regulation. it should be noted that the applicability of the regulation was referred to in the council and commission statement, accompanying the common position. in this regard the commission points out that member states have already endorsed a community format for attribution of unique codes to gmos based on the oecd format. of course the commission will make sure that this system is accounted for in terms of new authorisations as required under directive 2001/18/ec. to conclude, it has been a very intensive debate on the whole issue of how the european union should handle gmos. with some difficulty we have put together a system which will offer security and choice to our citizens. i hope that the vote tomorrow will give us a workable compromise and i thank you all for the discussions we have had and for finding a good solution.
the commission has already made a number of proposals. the rapid entry into force of the present proposals for regulations is a prerequisite for the de facto moratorium on green genetic engineering, which has been in place for some years, to be finally lifted. the current ban on the cultivation and import of gmos has been responsible for cutting off europe's science, consumers and farmers from the positive developments in the field of green genetic engineering for years. we are also facing the threat of wto action from countries which want to export genetically modified products to the eu but are not allowed to do so because of the moratorium. the us has already complained. what all those who often want to prevent gmos in our country for purely ideological reasons forget is that genetically modified food and feed have long been a reality worldwide. and in the area of protein feedingstuffs in particular, we are dependent on imports from third countries where the cultivation of genetically modified crops is the order of the day. in 2001, the eu imported over 16 million tonnes of soya from the usa and south america, with gm soya accounting for 68% of total soya production in the usa and 100% in argentina. this is the reality facing europe's uncertain consumers and farmers, and research without planning certainty. consumers and farmers in our country are wary of green genetic engineering because they do not know what it is. this is due to a lack of information policy, which is being pursued with full intention - at least in my home country, germany. we're not doing client politics here. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the consumer is not forced to buy a product that is not in conformity with the rules of the market. but we must also take account of agriculture, the environment, small-scale seed producers, industry, the food retail trade and many other sectors. and we need a labelling obligation to finally be able to assess imports from third countries accurately. the first step was to set reasonable, realistic thresholds - political thresholds anyway - based on what is technically feasible and achievable. it is a great success, especially for our group, that all the other groups now support the council's common position on the thresholds: 0.9% for authorised gmos and 0.5% for authorisation-ready gmos which are in the queue because of the moratorium. the same shall apply to the waiver of a seed regime in this regulation. seeds need their own rules and the question of coexistence, that is, the coexistence of genetically modified and conventional plants in agriculture, must not be used as a vehicle for a general blockade of green genetic engineering. it is only on this basis that my group has agreed to the compromise. the commission now has a duty to ensure that the de facto moratorium is not artificially extended by some member states. mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your work. mrs corbey has tabled a report for the second reading, which i support in principle. for the 58 million tonnes of packaging material produced in the european union every year - and more are being produced every year - we need optimal systems. we are thus improving environmental protection and giving planning certainty to important industries. i am particularly concerned about one amendment in the vote tomorrow. amendment no 4 concerns packaging materials which are available in small quantities and therefore have very little market penetration in the member states. one material that is found in such small quantities is ceramic packaging. ceramic bottles, cups and trays are produced in the netherlands, france and spain, for example, and are used mainly for the packaging of foodstuffs such as schnapps, pralines and pastries. ceramic packaging accounts for only 0.1% of packaging waste generated in the eu. so that's 58,000 out of 58 million tons. ceramics are made of burnt clay and are often kept or reused in many households due to their artistic and creative appearance, so they do not end up in household waste. ceramic cannot be thermally recovered or recycled. it is not an environmental problem. the commission has not yet decided whether to grant aid to the producers of ceramic tiles in the united kingdom. i therefore expressly ask that amendment no 4 be supported. waste management already established or yet to be established in some member states under this directive should concern materials suitable for recovery. it must focus on materials whose collection and processing is economically and environmentally viable.

president of the council. mr president, as a founding country, italy has a long history of fidelity to the letter and spirit of the treaties, which in a few decades have led us to build, in the name of peace, one of the most extraordinary political and institutional experiments in the history of mankind. we therefore feel with a keen moral and intellectual tension the responsibility and honour of presiding over the union at a constituent stage, when we must firmly grasp the lesson of the past in order to build the future, to face new things and opportunities hitherto unthinkable, to overcome differences and resolve them into a new wealth to be invested in the common project. the full membership of new member states and the consequent redefinition of our identity mean that the art of mediation must be revived. contemporary europe, as constructed by its ruling classes, has been born of great efforts of the will and of great insights of the intellect, which have given a soul and a language to common values and feelings, integrating and reviving the different strands into which the history, tradition and culture of the national states are divided. europe is big today: the european union is great for the path it has traveled, for its potential, for its proud contribution to peace and international law, but it is great for the concreteness and technical expertise with which it has managed to overcome every kind of crisis, every difference of interest, every diversity of vision, through a common method, common rules and a common style in adapting this method and these rules to the reality of the world in motion. we all know that the art of mediation sometimes has its costs, and sometimes heavy costs. without the vital and compelling breath of shared objectives, mediation can become something very much like bureaucratic paralysis, a long and exhausting series of problem-avoiding and solution-postponing. the italian parliament, which has never lacked the courage to speak the truth, has warned with great sensitivity and has often denounced with sincere european spirit the phases of fatigue and downward play which have characterized certain periods of our life in the house of commons of europe. that is why italy, with the confidence it derives from its long experience and with the humility it needs in dealing with the great and decisive political questions, will do everything in its power and everything it considers its duty to ensure that this parliament, the commission and the european council government have the most fertile ground for an informed, calm and responsible political decision on our future. the aim of mediation is to decide on the substance of things, and the settlement of our differences will only be successful if it enables us to take a great leap forward and to give our progressively integrated economies, our cultures, our foreign and defence policy a new and efficient institutional shape. a great europe needs great institutions. and if the world is asking for a europe that is authoritative in the face of the great challenges of combating international terrorism, reducing inequalities and imbalances, and restoring the global economy, it is our duty to offer it a union that is able to weigh in because it decides, a subject capable of making decisions with a loud and clear voice based on a clear perception of common interests and convictions, which are superior to any kind of particularism. this union, which we have decided to build together and whose outlines we have also discussed in the splendid work of the convention chaired by president valéry giscard d'estaing, with the active contribution of the greek presidency and the representatives of the commission, the european parliament and national parliamentarians, can only be based on the framework of values and historical experience which has united us for over half a century with the other great subject of modern liberal democracy, the united states of america, co-founder, together with us, of the atlantic alliance. and if this web of different partnerships, at different levels of political integration, is to live up to its ambitions and its achievements as a civilization, in a spirit of world peace and security, then all forms of monologue must be banished from relations between states in favour of the most open, sincere and correct dialogue. europe can cure itself of hamlet's syndrome and decide to be an unreservedly active player on the world stage; the european union must be able to provide itself with the diplomatic, economic and military means to do so in a convincing manner, without questioning its autonomy, its roots or the great foundation of freedom that it has defended for decades in the framework of its western alliances. as we saw recently at the thessaloniki summit, there is a great common awareness of this, which is set out in a document of great interest coordinated by the representative for foreign and security policy, javier solana, and which is already tending to overcome the differences that have emerged in recent months on the dramatic iraqi crisis and the developments in the crucial middle east issue in a new strategic vision. italy knows that it is not alone in taking the gamble once again, the bet on a happy, positive mediation that will get things moving. in the parliament chaired by mr pat cox and in its political groups, which we met with pleasure and profit in rome, we feel we have a patient and attentive interlocutor, but one who would not make concessions in the face of our mistakes. in the executive committee, chaired by romano prodi, we see the essential element of continuity of administration and daily coordination of our institutional system. and the european council, both in the relaunch of the growth plan, based on the investment of large resources in civil infrastructure, and in the great constitutional occasion of the forthcoming intergovernmental conference, will be the parliamentary seat in which this six-monthly presidency of the union, entrusted to italy, will try to define a courageous but not reckless understanding on the great questions of institutional structures, the extension of majority voting, the boundaries of the common foreign and security policy, and the european judicial area. we cannot ignore the fact that there are still differences of opinion between member states on some of these issues. the italian presidency will make every effort to bring these positions together, but it is clear that it will not be possible to proceed to a complete reexamination of the draft constitutional treaty of the convention. the intergovernmental conference will therefore have to concentrate its european citizens to vote in the elections for their parliament without knowing the institutional guidelines of the future union. finally, i can only be pleased that, for an appreciable reason of utmost to give the representatives of the member states a welcome worthy of the occasion and, of course, in keeping with our tradition. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, mr president of the commission, constitutional reform is certainly a priority for the future of european integration, but the union must also be able to respond day by day to the legitimate expectations of its citizens. europe must increasingly become a factor of economic growth and prosperity. we move in this area from solid foundations: the euro is a stabilising factor for the economies of countries that have chosen to share monetary sovereignty, and the lisbon strategy has identified a consensus path for strengthening european competitiveness. but we must not hide the continuing weakness of our economic structures, confirmed by growth rates that are below expectations. the italian presidency has prepared some concrete initiatives, based on the annual operational programme which we presented together with greece at the beginning of the year. the modernisation of agriculture, the protection of the environment, consumer protection and food safety are all essential needs for our citizens, and italy will work on them in pursuit of the objectives already identified by previous presidencies. i shall therefore limit myself to three points which we consider to be crucial for europe's competitiveness. the first is the need for more effective support for the economy through increased public and private investment with the cooperation of the european financial institutions, primarily the eib. in our view, this strategy must be based above all on a revival of the policy of large transeuropean infrastructure networks. in the enlarged union, the effective functioning of the internal market requires increased mobility of goods and services, and therefore a more efficient transport network. the aim is to reconcile the legitimate requirements of monetary stability and financial rigour - which are not in any way called into question - with a greater stimulus to economic growth, through investment not only in infrastructure but also in research and technological innovation, since we are firmly convinced that human capital is the main resource of the european economy. (applause from the right) the second priority is to consider the sustainability of european pension and social security systems. solidarity between generations and the adaptation of existing regimes to the reality of a progressively ageing society are challenges we cannot avoid. taking into account the different situations in each member state, we need to consider policies to increase the employment rate of older workers and to reduce the propensity for early retirement. finally, the third point is the modernisation of labour markets and the promotion of entrepreneurship, especially in small and mediumsized enterprises. here too, only a coordinated approach among the various members of the european union will enable us to seize the opportunities offered by the great common market which is being extended to the new ten members. these lines of action can be implemented through dialogue between the social partners. the european model is based on a market economy which aims to balance free enterprise with the needs of cohesion and solidarity. in this connection, we must not forget the more fragile, silent europe, too often overlooked by the inertia of legislation, but no less rich in civic value and moral significance: i am referring to the 38 million european citizens who are disabled. the european union has proclaimed 2003 the european year of people with disabilities. the italian presidency, together with the events and awareness-raising and information campaigns already organised, will work to lay the foundations for legislative action against discrimination: the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos at work. (applause from the right) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, mr president of the commission, the european union is also a factor of international stability and its responsibility in this respect begins at its immediate borders and depends on its ability to be open to ever more advanced forms of cooperation with its neighbours. here too, the italian presidency intends to continue the work of those who have preceded us in the exercise of the presidency. in the current phase between the signature and the entry into force of the accession treaties, we will seek to ensure the full participation of the 10 new member states in the council's work and facilitate their full integration into the union's institutional mechanisms. at the same time, we will try to define by december a roadmap for bulgaria and romania that opens the door to accession for these two countries by 2007. we will continue the pre-accession strategy towards turkey on the basis of the conditions defined at the copenhagen european council last december. we know that the decision on the date of the start of the negotiations will not be taken until the end of next year, but in this perspective it seems to us most appropriate that the union actively supports the reform process already initiated by the current turkish government. we will continue to stress the european perspective of the western balkan countries, in line with the zagreb process. the agenda we adopted in thessaloniki on this subject is a further step forward. looking back on the role of the european union in the balkans, we can be proud. if we compare the present situation with that of ten years ago, we see that the intervention of europe and the united states has made it possible to bring to an end the bloody conflicts in the former yugoslavia, the last great european civil war, and hopefully the last time european blood has been spilled on european soil. we believe that it is now appropriate to move from the current phase of the association and stabilisation agreements to a more integrated strategy, with the aim of strengthening our relationship with the countries of the region. we are aware of the complexity of this approach, but we also know that the european perspective is the only one capable of providing an effective incentive for the governments of these countries to proceed without delay on the road of reform, modernisation, free markets and the rule of law. the italian presidency views extremely positively the commission's invitation, which is shared by the member states, to foster ever closer relations with the areas closest to us, for the so-called wider europe; we will therefore seek to strengthen our relations with ukraine, belarus and moldova. we will also seek to strengthen relations with the russian federation in particular through an ever closer dialogue and through concrete measures which give tangible sign of russia's desire to belong to the economic, political, social and cultural fabric of europe and the west. we believe that the attention paid to eastern europe after the collapse of communism must now be balanced by an equal interest in the euro-mediterranean dialogue: the european parliament has been a key player in the debate on the middle east, and it is a key player in the debate on the middle east. our perspective is the implementation of a euro-mediterranean free trade area, already opened by the barcelona conference. the economic and social development of the southern mediterranean area is essential for the global balance, given the cultural, political and demographic level of the southern mediterranean. the integration of the european economy with that of the arab countries is a major challenge of our time and the key to peace and security in this area and in europe as a whole. we will therefore promote the euro-mediterranean dialogue, to which we will devote a number of initiatives in the economic, cultural and social fields, including a foundation for dialogue between cultures and civilizations, and we will promote the project of transforming the financial facility currently operating within the eib into an autonomous body, that is, into a genuine mediterranean bank. the italian presidency, on the basis of the decisions adopted by the euro-mediterranean ministerial conferences in valencia and crete, transposed by the thessaloniki european council, confirms the will expressed by the european parliament and the national parliaments to establish within the six-month period of the italian presidency the euro-mediterranean parliamentary assembly, a sign of a permanent desire for dialogue between europe and the countries bordering the mediterranean. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, mr president of the commission, the creation of conditions of international security is today a primary task for countries which share a system of universal values based on freedom, democracy and peace. this is the main ground on which the fundamental transatlantic relations and the partnership between europe and the united states must be revived today. we want to reiterate our conviction that there is no contradiction between a strong european commitment and an equally strong transatlantic solidarity. in this spirit, we intend to work to restore the depth and dynamism to the relationship between the union and the united states of america, which is also an essential condition for europe's greater authority on the international scene. the establishment of a strong and balanced transatlantic relationship also depends on a substantial european defence commitment that is consistent with the nato framework. the fight against terrorism and the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction, support for the promotion of democracy and respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms are concrete grounds on which to test our capacity to build a solid relationship of cooperation between the economic, cultural, civil and, i would say, spiritual interests which link europe to latin america, which is now living through a period of change which europe hopes will be fruitful in terms of freedom and justice. it is the latin american countries that are asking us to open up the frontiers of economic trade. the success of latin america is that of the other america, linked to europe in a strengthening of europol. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, mr president of the commission, the considerations i have made make it clear that the challenges facing the european union are delicate and complex, and our presidency will try to help to solve them, in the limited time available, with a spirit of humility, a spirit of service and the firm and full conviction that the security and prosperity of our future will depend increasingly on the process of european integration which has already guaranteed us, for half a century to date, peace, freedom, security and prosperity. today's europe is no longer that light kite, able to catch the wind of history, of the treaty of rome. our union has become very weak and has therefore become burdened with responsibilities and duties towards president of the commission. mr president of parliament, mr president-in-office of the council, ladies and gentlemen, the italian presidency opens at a crucial time in the life of the union: the european parliament has the challenging but exciting task of bringing to a successful conclusion the process of revising the union's founding treaties and drawing up the first european constitution. the intergovernmental conference will be held during the italian presidency and will work on the basis of the thessaloniki conclusions of the draft constitutional treaty drawn up by the convention. thanks to this convention, europe experienced a constitutional process for the first time. we cannot therefore underestimate the intrusion of the word 'constitution' into our european life. this breakthrough has made it possible to achieve results that seemed totally unrealizable some time ago: the charter of fundamental rights becomes part of the constitutional treaty; the union acquires a single legal personality, which strengthens its international stature. the definition of the union's powers will enable citizens to distinguish more clearly between the union's and the member states' competences. however, i have never made a secret of my dissatisfaction with the fact that some of the indispensable reforms - which many have called for - have either not been undertaken or have been undertaken with excessive timidity. that is why the commission is preparing to put the key issues still outstanding back on the negotiating table of the intergovernmental conference in its opinion on the opening of the intergovernmental conference in september. qualified majority voting has been extended to many areas but not to the extent necessary to meet the needs of an enlarged union: there are other areas where unanimity must be eliminated. it is difficult to think of an efficient europe if it has to take decisions with the unanimous consent of 25 states: it's not possible. the solution identified for the composition of the commission does not reconcile the needs of representativeness and efficiency. the permanent presidency of the european council is liable to give rise to overlaps and conflicts with the commission. the euro, one of the union's greatest political achievements - perhaps its greatest - continues to be underrepresented in an effective and consistent way at international level. it is also necessary to insert clauses for the revision of the constitution by an enlarged majority. i cannot imagine how the constitution can be adapted to the new needs of the union without a revision procedure based on majority rules. nothing is reformed by unanimity. finally, a more democratic and efficient institutional framework will have to emerge from the intergovernmental conference and is also essential for a more effective economic and social policy and a more effective foreign policy. the commission has the political will, the arguments and, let me say, the enthusiasm to push these points hard and to the end. mr president of the parliament, mr president of the council, ladies and gentlemen, the other major challenge of the next six months is to strategies towards the candidate countries. the commission is actively working on this. the aim is to make this process work well, at the service of citizens and at the service of member states, old and new. the thessaloniki summit will also enable us to continue on the path of an ever closer partnership with the balkans, without which this stage of the enlargement process will never be complete.
