particular, as regards the mediterranean area, i expect that the euro-mediterranean bank and the foundation for intercultural dialogue will be established by the end of the year. it will also be essential to play a key role in the implementation of the roadmap, as you said, mr president, to the drawing up of which the european union has made a decisive contribution, together with the united states, russia and the united nations. transatlantic relations will continue to receive our full attention. the recent eu-us summit in washington was a major positive turning point in our relations with the united states. beyond the content of the summit itself - which proved to be one of the most intensive in recent years - the most significant element was the firm will, expressly expressed by both sides, to recreate a climate of cooperation and solidarity. i do not mean by this that there are no differences in the way we see and approach specific issues, but even when that happens, the soundness of our relationship cannot be called into question. as i said at the summit, our objectives are the same, although we sometimes want to achieve them by very different methods. perhaps the most striking example of this is the relationship between the united states and the european union in international trade. we both want fewer barriers, better access to markets, fairer trade, more certain rules but also intelligently tempered to favour the poorer countries. on some of these issues, however, our operational proposals differ. but this does not prevent us from having a close and continuous relationship, through which we manage our differences, nor does it prevent us from working together to ensure a successful outcome to the multilateral negotiations in the world trade organisation. i would like to stress this very strongly, because all this is possible because, in trade matters, the union speaks and negotiates with one voice. it is therefore an authoritative and influential partner, whereas it is not at all so in the fields where competence is divided and fragmented. mr president, mr president-in-office of the council, ladies and gentlemen, the most difficult challenge we face is to re-create the conditions for strong, balanced and lasting economic growth in the union. the situation is difficult: economic growth is very slow, although i think it is inappropriate to talk about deflation. we must also, at the same time, tackle the reform of the european social security system. competition from our trading partners and the ageing of our population make it all the more urgent to implement this reform. at the same time, however, we have a huge, unique opportunity: an integrated internal market of almost half a billion people. i think we don't realize this is a great tool for our future. it is therefore essential to think operatively about the instruments for closer coordination of the union's economic and fiscal policies, in order to face the difficulties together and to enjoy together the enormous advantages that the union offers. conscious of the seriousness of these challenges, the commission has already launched two initiatives in recent months, which have received strong support from the european council: on the one hand, we proposed, and we have succeeded, in using all the flexibility provided for in the stability and growth pact to allow each country's fiscal policy to be adapted to its specific economic situation, without losing sight of the stability objectives and without exceeding the 3% ceiling. as i have said many times, however, this was necessary, but not sufficient. the commission has also proposed that the member states should be able to apply the principle of subsidiarity to all their taxation policies. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of the environment is a very important one, and i would like to thank the rapporteur for the work he has done. i also noted with concern in the same council that research investment in the member states has fallen in absolute terms compared with last year, while large european companies are moving an increasingly large part of their research outside europe: hundreds of thousands of our best talent go to work and stay there for life, unlike asians, who go home to the united states. the commission has therefore decided to react. in cooperation with the european investment bank, we are finalising an initiative to help increase overall investment and private sector participation in the two key areas for achieving the lisbon objectives: trans-european networks and research and development projects. we want to mobilise and coordinate all the union's current sources of funding and explore possible alternatives, without compromising the stability of the budgets of the member states. the commission has noted with satisfaction the strong support recently expressed by the italian government for this strategy. finally, we must speed up the adoption of the proposals which the greek presidency has prepared but which have not yet been adopted. the adoption of these measures during the italian presidency will contribute disaster; security of gas and electricity supply; the second package of liberalisation of rail services; environmental liability rules; implementation of the 10-year action plan for disabled people, finalisation of the european patent directive; the harmonisation of asylum procedures; the refugee status; and, finally, the agreement with esa for the development of the european space policy. i am confident that, with the help of the italian presidency and your personal help, mr president, we will be able to adopt rapidly the operational decisions which are lacking in the achievement of these objectives. economic recovery is not just about reforms; it is also about trusting that proposals will quickly become reality. mr president of parliament, mr president of the council, ladies and gentlemen, these are the main challenges we will have to face in the coming months. we are facing a genuine process of re-founding europe, not only constitutionally but also politically and economically. the commission works to maintain and consolidate a europe that is strong and prosperous, just and united. the greatness of the european project lies precisely in its capacity to strengthen and extend peace, democracy, justice, prosperity and solidarity. finally, the commission has launched a broad internal reflection on the financial perspective for the period after 2006, as it was obliged to do. in the autumn, we will present our political project for an enlarged and reformed european union, which will be discussed under the italian presidency at the european council in december. the next financial perspective is a key step in the european project: by 2007, the union will have a new constitution, probably 27 members and almost 500 million citizens. ladies and opening up entirely new fields. in the aviation sector we are entering fields which until now have remained absolutely outside any kind of regulation or agreement at the level of the european union. i would therefore like to express my gratitude to the two rapporteurs and to all the members who, as far as i know, have been very active in the discussions in committee, and to remind them of something we all know: up to the year 2000, this sector has been developing systematically, at intergovernmental level, through eurocontrol or the international civil aviation organisation. but - as mrs sanders-ten holte said a moment ago - we all know that the citizens' demands go further, that they are asking us to solve pressing problems and that there is a possibility of significantly improving the capacity and safety of our airspace and the efficiency of its management, if we are able, here too, to achieve european integration. the aim is therefore to make the organisation and management of airspace consistent with mobility in the sky, creating a single sky by the end of 2004. and as you know, this is one of the flagship initiatives of this prodi commission. i would also like to say that in the meantime there have been events, to which the honourable members have referred, such as the crisis in the aviation sector in some respects, september 11, the war in iraq, the uberlingen accident, which undoubtedly had an impact on our work, but which in no way diminished the importance of the initiative or the urgency of developing it. i would point out that, unfortunately, it does not seem that your reactions to the council's common position will lead to an agreement at second reading. the questions put by the honourable members seem to me legitimate and deserve discussion with the council, but we must bear in mind, when we are dealing with this initiative, that we are making the first foray into a new area, in which there are several sensitive aspects, in which we must make progress progressively and that it is a very delicate work we are doing, that the council must accept that step forward and that we must be pragmatic and realistic and achieve operational texts that favour the immediate achievement of concrete results. i know that you think that the final proposal in the council's common position is not enough and that you are calling for more action at community level. i would like to say to the honourable members that i share their concern, but there are legal and institutional obstacles which prevent us from accepting some of the amendments they have tabled, such as, for example, in the case of mr fava's report, amendments nos 1, 8, 9, 10, 11, 13 and 14 and, in the case of mrs sanders-ten holte's report, amendments nos 13, 16, 25, 29 and 33. the other amendments, whether substantive or partial or with a wording change, will be incorporated in part or in full in due course. i would point out that we are still opposed to certain amendments which could affect or undermine the operational institutional reality. among the amendments i have cited as unacceptable are, in particular, amendment no 14, concerning the consultation of the media concerned within eurocontrol, as well as amendments nos 13, 16, 25 and 29 to mrs sanders-ten holte's report, the second part of amendment no 15 and amendment no 33, which has been superseded by technological progress. i shall raise two issues which will be central to the forthcoming discussions between the institutions in the framework of conciliation and to which the honourable members have referred: civil/military cooperation and the creation of the functional blocks, the first of which is contained in both reports and the second in amendment no 26 by mrs sanders-ten holte. the civil/military issue is a key element for the success of the single sky, you are right, but you must also remember what the competences are at community level, and that is a forced footing with which we have to play in this whole exercise. the discussions in the council have shown that the management of the trade-offs between the needs of transport policy and the requirements of defence policy requires coordination mechanisms which go beyond the possibilities offered by the first pillar. in order to support the creation of the single sky, despite this obstacle, the union states have committed themselves, in a declaration, to developing military cooperation as a complement to the initiative in the field of the first pillar. i think we must seize this opportunity and proceed pragmatically in this area. amendment no 29 in the sanders-ten holte report establishes the primacy of transport policy in the use of the single sky, which does not sufficiently reflect the legitimate needs and concerns of the union's states from the point of view of defence. as regards the second aspect, the functional blocks, amendment no 26 to the report by mrs sanders-ten holte, the commission shares parliament's view but believes that an acceptable solution would be to strengthen the role of the commission in conjunction with the 'single sky committee' and with the technical support of eurocontrol, in order to assess the two blocks together in a coherent way, leaving the right of initiative and decision to the states of the union. the creation of these blocs has military implications, to which i referred in the first part of my speech. we therefore accept in principle amendment no 26 in mrs sanders-ten holte's report, but we will have to put it differently. in conclusion, mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would remind you that the proposals we are discussing today are the fruit of a year's work by a high-level group, made up of civil and military representatives of the member states of the union, and a social group made up of the various actors in the civil aviation sector and also involving all levels of this field. in september 2002 you delivered your first reading opinion and i thanked you for your support and the effort you put into this initiative. we agree on many points, but - i repeat - what we need is a realistic position that which will make it possible to achieve the famous single european sky before the end of 2004.

mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your work. yes, mr schmitt is right; today is the anniversary of the überlingen disaster, in which two planes collided and many people were killed. the single sky project is widely perceived as the european response to the more than unsatisfactory situation in european skies. what's the situation? we have three times as many control centers as the comparable sizes in the united states, a patchwork of skies that were created in the 1960s. a flight from brussels to rome has to pass through nine different control rooms, a flight from brussels to geneva has to change the radio frequency five times. with the increase in air traffic in the coming years, all this will become an increasing security risk. at the same time, it is highly inefficient, with one in four flights delayed, 350,000 flight hours wasted each year. this costs airlines almost two billion euros a year. the commission's response in its package of regulations and parliament's first reading have met this challenge. the common position of the member states, however, falls far short of expectations and needs. why would you do that? firstly, the functional airspace blocks are at the heart of the single sky; how are they created? what is the added value of a regulation if it is left to the discretion of the member states? member states can already create bilateral airspace blocks. we believe that we need a normative proposal from eurocontrol and the commission, otherwise nothing will change. secondly, the common position makes little real progress on civil-military cooperation compared with the status quo. i know that this is a highly sensitive subject, but we cannot wait another decade for europe to be able to fly directly from a to b. thirdly, it is painful that there is no european response to the dramatic shortage of air traffic controllers. this issue is part of this package of regulations and should be addressed as soon as possible, not least for safety reasons. my group supports the reintroduction of the amendments adopted by parliament at first reading. we shall have to speak clearly to the council in the conciliation committee. i would like to thank the rapporteurs for their good and cooperative cooperation.

commission. - mr president, on behalf of mrs de palacio, who is exceptionally well-chosen outside strasbourg and who asked me to take her place on this report by mr schmitt, i would like to present the commission's view on this proposal for a regulation of the european parliament and of the council on the negotiation and implementation of air services agreements between member states and third countries. in november 2002, the court of justice of the european communities delivered a landmark judgment on international air transport. the present proposal is an essential element in the follow-up to that judgment. in eight cases concerning different member states referred to it by the commission, the court held that the community had legal competence over many matters relating to air navigation. the court found that the member states had acted unlawfully in negotiating and concluding bilateral agreements independently. since the community and the member states currently have shared competence in air transport, it is common practice for the community to take the initiative in international negotiations. however, there is a real problem. the member states have probably concluded nearly 2 000 bilateral agreements between themselves. the commission cannot assume the responsibility of managing all of them. it is therefore necessary to find a way of allowing member states to continue some of their negotiations in an acceptable legal framework. the proposal we have on the table is designed to enable the member states to do this. the idea is very simple: member states will have to inform the commission and the other states of any negotiations envisaged, which will allow the commission to verify the conformity of the planned measures with community law and to identify any common interests. other member states will also be able to identify common difficulties. the commission will then be required to inform the member states of the results of the negotiations once they have been concluded, and the member states will authorize the conclusion of the agreement if it is in accordance with community law and the community's transport policy. apart from this provision, the proposal also imposes an obligation of non-discrimination on member states in order to ensure equal treatment for all community airlines and to prevent member states from favouring their own national airlines. the court of justice has clearly stated that all airlines established in a member state must be treated fairly. two aspects should be taken into account in the examination of this proposal. in accordance with current practice, all international negotiations on air transport must be conducted at community level. this proposal constitutes a special and unusual authorization recognizing the bilateral track record in air transport; it strikes a balance between respect for community law and the establishment of a pragmatic system. in view of the special nature of this authorization, it is essential that the activities of the member states be subject to systematic control before and after the negotiations in order to avoid any abuse. secondly, the council has examined this proposal and, subject to some improvements or modifications, has approved it in principle. in particular, he approved the idea of prior notification of the negotiations and of ex post facto approval of their results. member states request flexibility to continue negotiating with their bilateral partners; the commission, ladies and gentlemen, is satisfied with the council's favourable reception of its proposal and hopes that the steps will now be taken rapidly towards its final adoption. in view of all the above, i would ask you, mr president, ladies and gentlemen, to follow the development of the approach as we have proposed it and as i have had the opportunity to describe it to you on behalf of mrs de palacio.

i suggest. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, it is a great opportunity for me, as president of the council of the european union, to address you, and i am particularly pleased that this is happening in the context of a debate on human rights. before proceeding, i feel it is my duty, and that of the italian presidency, to reiterate our condolences on the death of sérgio vieira de mello, who, in his capacity as united nations high commissioner, had already established himself as a strong advocate of the promotion and defence of human rights at international level. the protection and promotion of human rights is one of the fundamental pillars of the european union's foreign policy and a constant reference point for its international action. in this respect, the union is committed to a basic principle, namely the universality of human rights, which cannot be called into question or conditioned by any cultural understanding. human rights have a strategic weight in addressing the major challenges of our time: i do not think it is necessary to dwell on the close connection between peace, security and stability on the one hand and respect for human rights, fundamental freedoms, democracy and the rule of law on the other. the fight against extreme poverty and underdevelopment is also closely linked to initiatives to promote the fulfilment of the fundamental rights of the human person, starting with the right to life, integrity and dignity of every human being. in this context, we therefore consider it of central importance, during the six-month presidency, to channel the north-south dialogue, which has been considerably fractured in recent years, on a more constructive basis, starting with the human rights component which must remain an essential part of this dialogue. the programme of the italian presidency on human rights was made public; i do not need to go into it, but i will just mention a few essential chapters. they cover the mainstreaming of human rights in the union's wider external projection, as well as a strong global push for a moratorium and abolition of the death penalty; the european union is also committed to the promotion of human rights and the protection of minorities. particular emphasis should be placed on the structured dialogue with iran and china, and a serious reflection should also be initiated on the functioning of the commission on human rights. the italian presidency also attaches great importance to the tragic plight of child soldiers. finally, i would like to mention the initiatives which the union will take in the third committee of the general assembly, as well as the preparation of the annual report of the european union on human rights and the annual meeting with non-governmental organisations, which we would like to give a more operational content this year. i now turn to congratulating mr bob van den bos on the extension of the european parliament's annual report, which is full of insights, analyses, proposals and recommendations. it is a document which deserves a very thorough analysis, which certainly cannot be exhausted in the course of this sitting. it will also be carefully evaluated by the other components and bodies of the european union. i would therefore like to refer to only a few points in the report which, in my view, deserve special attention. i would like to start with a general observation which is contained in the report and which i personally agree with: the situation of human rights and fundamental freedoms in the world today, despite the efforts of the union and other countries, is still marked by serious abuses and violations. the causes of this can be traced to several factors. the report focuses on some of these, such as the prevalence of political and economic interests over human rights and the need to reach compromises in international forums at the expense of positions of principle. if we are convinced today that the promotion and protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms are the very precondition of democracy and civil coexistence, we cannot but consistently believe that the pursuit of legitimate political and economic objectives also requires the consolidation of democratic institutions and the principles of freedom and justice. it is well known that dictatorial regimes, which are based on terror and violence, reject the democratic ideal, deny fundamental rights and freedoms, pursue the objectives of prevarication over other peoples and, in the final analysis, establish themselves as unreliable interlocutors. what strategy should the european union pursue in dealing with these regimes? the report reads: political condemnations by the european union often produce no results. should we therefore consider them to be a fruitless instrument of action and admit that the policy of human rights dialogue with third countries has in many cases not achieved appreciable results and should lead us to abandon them? the report by mr van den bos contains the answers to these questions, which are acceptable to us. the public denunciation of the aberrant practices of certain regimes is a duty, since it puts the latter in a position where they must at least justify themselves, forcing them to face the judgment of the international community. as regards the formula for the structured dialogue on human rights with third countries, i note that the approach suggested in the report is exactly the one which the council intended to give to this instrument of action. in my view, this is not a permissive dialogue as an alternative to political complaints, but it fully involves civil society, with the participation of ngos and academics active in the field of human rights, and is based on the pursuit of precise objectives, the implementation of which is subject to regular and careful verification. i also share the report's observation that condemnation and political dialogue must be accompanied by programmes and action aimed at combating poverty, supporting institution building and education. monitoring, resolutions, dialogue exercises, human rights clauses and technical cooperation and assistance programmes in this field are all instruments aimed at achieving a single objective, namely the unremitting defence of human rights and fundamental freedoms in the world. the ongoing dialogue of the union on human rights with china and iran does not prevent, where it is considered useful, the denunciation of violations and abuses of human rights, including through ad hoc resolutions in the human rights commission or the united nations general assembly, nor does it preclude the possibility of providing them with technical assistance in the field of strengthening respect for human rights. the same applies to the part of the report which strongly criticises the council's failure to publicly denounce the regimes responsible for serious and repeated human rights violations. i do not mean to dismiss such criticisms out of hand; i think it is important to clarify a few things. judging the union's action by the number of resolutions/countries it submits to the human rights commission or the general assembly, or even by the resolutions that obtain sufficient support, is surely reductive. moreover, the role of the european union in human rights in international fora is widely recognised. in fact, as already mentioned, the union's action in this area covers a very wide spectrum, consisting of a whole series of differentiated initiatives, ranging from démarches of the heads of mission reports to public statements. this european activity is aimed at a large number of countries. there is another aspect which is particularly thoroughly dealt with in the report and on which i should like to focus: the european union is a major partner in the process of european integration. the report makes a point of highlighting the central role that this issue has assumed in the wider context of the protection of human rights. i represent a country which, because of its geographical position, culture and traditions, has always been particularly sensitive to this problem and which, as it stands, has taken on implications and significance unknown in the past. what was once seen as an opportunity to be seized has now become an imperative necessity. the ideological opposition and the political exploitation of human rights and fundamental freedoms are unfortunately a fact, however deplorable it may be. the conflict which is increasingly characterizing the debate in the united nations commission on human rights, to which the report also devotes a great deal of space, is a problem on which the greek presidency has already started to reflect, and which we intend to continue and develop. the action taken by the union and by western countries in general in the field of human rights is clearly perceived by a part of the international community, apparently mainly in the global south, as instrumental in pursuing the aims of political and cultural prevarication. the very principle of the universality of human rights, the belief that they cannot be constrained or limited by any social, economic and/or cultural exception, is called into question. integralisms, whatever their origin or nature, are partly the result of an inability to communicate, to seek common values based on mutual respect and tolerance. i do not think it is enough for the union to simply firmly reject the accusations of double standards that are often levelled at it. i think it is appropriate to start a debate on these matters, and the european parliament itself could contribute to it. in this connection, i would also like to remind you that a conference on the universality of human rights and dialogue between cultures will be held in milan in march 2004 on the initiative of italy. in defining the guidelines for our six-month presidency in the field of human rights, one of the key points we thought it appropriate to highlight, as i have already mentioned, is the issue of mainstreaming. it must be our aim to integrate, in a harmonious and coherent way, the issue of respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms into all union policies towards third countries. i am therefore particularly pleased to note that this concept is expressed strongly and clearly by parliament in this report. in this context, i fully share the view that the human rights clause in association and cooperation agreements should be promptly made enforceable when the conditions for its application are met. i also believe that a cooperative relationship with a country at all levels - political, economic, scientific and cultural - cannot be without an open and constructive dialogue on the protection of fundamental rights and freedoms. the report contains interesting operational proposals on which i have already given instructions for studies and technical studies. i would also like to point out that in sharing objectives and objectives, the roads to be followed may be different. experience shows that the setting up of committees or working groups can often be the most immediate and obvious solution, but that it is not always the most effective way of doing things. another important theme in the report is that of transparency. the danish presidency is rightly credited with encouraging and promoting a practice of timely and regular consultation with civil society, which has undoubtedly helped to raise the visibility of european union action. this practice was continued by the greek presidency and will continue to be a strong reference for action by the italian presidency. i believe that it is above all a fitting and useful recognition of the essential and indispensable role played in this field by ngos, which are and remain the necessary and privileged interlocutors of the european union. finally, i would like to make a critical point in the document, namely the institutional relations between the council and the european parliament in the field of human rights. we will look into the rapporteur's view that these relations need improvement, and i urge the italian presidency to continue the work already begun by the greek presidency in this regard. the invitation by the greek presidency to the author of the report to attend a meeting of the human rights committee is indicative of an approach which aims to involve the european parliament more closely in the council's policy-making. the italian presidency is fully in favour of this and i confirm that we intend to continue along the path already traced, identifying appropriate solutions to the problems and inadequacies highlighted in the report. in this connection, i hope to be able to report back to this house at the end of the semester on the council's activities in the field of human rights. the governments of the member states of the union now recognise the imperative need to ensure the european parliament's leading role in the protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms and to encourage closer cooperation. the operational proposals put forward by the rapporteur will therefore have to be seriously considered. i am pleased to conclude by noting, as the most important political fact, that both the council and parliament share the importance and the centrality of the subject of human rights and fundamental freedoms in the union's external policy and relations. this is a significant element reflecting the continuing evolution in the approach to these issues, which are no longer confined to the sphere of ethical and principled statements but are increasingly intended to influence policy choices in relations with third countries. the view that international peace, security and stability are based on full respect for fundamental rights and freedoms is not empty rhetoric but reflects the objective observation of a reality which is destined to influence in an increasingly decisive way the foreign policy choices of governments and the strategies of international organizations at all levels. commission. mr president, i wish to begin by paying tribute to mr van den bos for his excellent report. the engagement of the european parliament on human rights issues serves as a critical stimulus to eu policy, and there is much food for thought in this latest publication. the commission will, as usual, respond in writing to all the recommendations addressed to it in this report. first, some remarks on the principal themes of the report – freedom of thought, conscience and religion. we tried to work on these issues in several different ways. first, through efforts in international fora. with eu support, ireland tabled the resolution on the elimination of all forms of religious intolerance at the un commission on human rights and the third committee of the un general assembly, which urges states to guarantee freedom of thought, conscience, religion and belief, facilitate worship and combat intolerance. the eu’s statement on human rights in the world at the last chr highlighted concerns relating to religious freedom or freedom of expression in 12 countries, including china and iran. second, thorough dialogue with third countries. dedicated human rights dialogues offer a particularly valuable opportunity to address the issue. in evaluating the dialogue with iran, for example, the general affairs and external relations council of 18 march 2003 underscored its concern at discrimination against religious minorities – particularly baha’is – and the need for more progress as regards freedom of opinion and expression. corporal punishment and the abhorrent condemnation to stoning, pronounced in the name of sharia, have also been the cause of in-depth debates with representatives of the iranian government, judiciary and clergy. thus far, the eu has noted with satisfaction that the de facto moratorium on stoning is still a reality. i hope further results will be achieved with our iranian partners. freedom of expression will form the main subject for mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your report. what water means to people and nature, we have experienced for ourselves this year in the hottest and driest summer since weather data was recorded. we europeans, spoiled children, long for rain and rivers and dams. experts have calculated that it would take at least fourteen days of rain to restore normal levels to dams and rivers in our area. fortunately, we still have enough clean water from the taps. water supply in the eu is clearly secure and affordable for every citizen. after this hot summer, we europeans can guess what it means that currently about three billion people, more than a third of the world's population, do not have access to clean drinking water or sanitation. although 189 governments have committed themselves to halving this number by the year 2015 in the united nations millennium declaration, there is no sign that this ambitious goal will ever be reached. since 1990, water use has increased tenfold worldwide. the largest water user is agriculture, followed by industry, and then households. the united states uses the most water, about 296 liters per capita per day. the german households and many european countries, on the other hand, need only half. in the middle east and parts of asia, but also in parts of mexico and africa, large sections of the population have access to less than about 2.5 litres per capita per day. many people in water-scarce regions do not even have that much available. almost 40% of the world's population lives in river basins that span more than two countries. upstream countries often exploit their natural advantages over downstream countries. if there are still wars over oil today, wars over water could break out in the not-too-distant future. the situation in the middle east is explosive. israel, jordan and the palestinians are struggling to divide the jordan. the countries bordering the euphrates and tigris - turkey, syria and iraq - are trying to use the water of these two rivers. since the battle for fresh water is a foregone conclusion, unesco declared 2003 the year of fresh water. the european commission and the european parliament are aware of the scarcity of water and the problems that this raises, including, above all, the need to ensure that water is managed fairly. the important issue of equitable water management has therefore been put on the agenda. the epp-ed group in the european parliament is committed to ensuring that water management cannot be a monopoly of the state or large global corporations. a healthy mix of public and private sector should ensure that the population in the water-scarce areas of our planet can be supplied with affordable fresh water. it must not come to this: if you are rich, you have water, if you are poor, you do not get fresh water! in order to allow for the mix of public and private water supply, the epp-ed group has tabled several amendments to the annual report on the european commission's communication on water management in developing countries, which is being discussed here today, and i would like to ask all my colleagues in the european parliament to accept them. i'd like to thank our assistants and staff.

the commission (es) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the proposal we are now discussing obviously concerns other types of activities and actions, although it also relates to energy. we are talking about the proposals concerning the security of supply of petroleum products and natural gas. the proposal is simply an extension of the green paper and its aim is to try to move from a statement to action. the proposal on oil is intended to give the union the means to act with unity and credibility, without difficulties in the supply of oil, so that certain situations which may disturb the economy, society and the functioning of the market are resolved in the best possible way. the european union must meet three requirements if it is to act effectively in these circumstances. firstly, the establishment of a genuine community decision-making process on the use of the safety reserves, especially in cases of crisis. secondly, a proper definition of the circumstances which could unlock oil security reserves. the existing national and community regulations are still often based on the idea that safety reserves are an instrument which is only activated when there is a serious shortage of oil. i would like to congratulate the international energy agency on the progress it has made in taking account of the risks of supply disruptions. the third requirement is to have credible and visible quality safety reserves. in many countries, safety reserves are owned by oil companies and are no different from their own operating stocks. so today we do not know exactly how many safety reserves we have. moreover, we have an accounting system which, as you know, differs, for example, from the accounting system for reserves which the international energy agency itself has. the aim of the directive is, in a nutshell, to ensure daily and operational security of supply in a competitive environment. it creates a safety net for long-term supply contracts and strengthens the community's solidarity in cases of very exceptional crisis situations which could no longer be successfully resolved at national level. the second gas internal market directive will complete the creation of a single european market for natural gas, giving all customers, including households and small businesses, the choice of their supplier. competition in gas supply is expected to be encouraged. and large industrial consumers will be able to take the necessary measures to ensure security of supply, but not households or small businesses. for these customers, security of supply is not a market issue and does not influence their choice of supplier. therefore, all gas consumers in the internal market should be reassured that security of supply is guaranteed at the appropriate level, irrespective of the supplier they have chosen. action is considered necessary as increased competition could encourage gas companies to reduce their current levels of security of supply in order to reduce costs and increase their competitiveness. the commission wants to avoid this, and has therefore proposed that the current security of supply rules, which are usually maintained on a voluntary basis, should be made binding. it is therefore clearly a consumer protection measure. i would like the european parliament to take these considerations into account. they clearly demonstrate the contribution of the commission's proposal to the proper functioning of the internal gas market and the importance of security of supply in such a market. other elements of the commission's proposal concern long-term aspects of security of supply, although the commission has no doubt that the market will provide an adequate level of long-term contracts; it is extremely important to convey to both investors and producers that the european union recognises the importance of such contracts and that, in the very unlikely event that a problem arises, it will act accordingly. i was pleased to hear that the european parliament accepts in principle a community solidarity mechanism in the event of an extraordinary crisis in the gas supply of the european union and it goes without saying that in such a case, if national measures do not prove sufficient to deal with the situation, the community must be able to resolve the problem adequately. madam president, with these two proposals, the first, the rapporteur. the commission is not i recommend to the european parliament, on behalf of the committee on economic and monetary affairs, that it confirm mr jean-claude trichet as a suitable been open to the call for greater transparency and democratic accountability of the european central bank. the european central bank has come of age five years after its creation. their political, economic, financial, organisational and personnel independence is guaranteed and is not called into question by the draft constitutional treaty. the high degree of independence, which is greater than that of the american central bank, gives the ecb a high degree of responsibility for overall economic and social development. this requires the greatest possible transparency for democratic and integration policy reasons. the role of the european central bank is therefore to ensure that decisions and the reasons for them are made public. this commitment to transparency is reflected in the quarterly monetary dialogue with the european parliament, in the regular publications and decisions, but also in the reports, conferences and the semiannual inflation forecast. this has led to a kind of cultural revolution in europe. the culture of the national central banks in europe did not know this form of transparency. the transparency of the ecb is also in its interest, because as a young institution it is particularly dependent on the establishment and consolidation of its legitimacy, credibility and trustworthiness as a european authority. after all, a nation's money reflects everything that nation wants, suffers, is. this is what the great european economist, joseph schumpeter, said. i think it is right that, after today's debate, the maastricht treaty has been fully incorporated into the draft european constitutional treaty. the role of central banks has changed over the centuries of their existence, from their private form of organization in history to their changing status in the us and the concept of fighting inflation and enforcing an independent central bank. today it may be too early to respond to new challenges. it is about defining the role of the central bank in a globalised world dominated by trade, transport and international financial markets. this means not only dynamic markets, but also more and higher risks to international financial stability. so what role should and can central banks play in contributing to financial stability, in helping to avoid financial crises? is the ecb equipped to play the role of lender of last resort? is this one wanted? the euro has also given europe an international dimension. the ecb will have to play an increasingly important role in defining and implementing appropriate policies for the world economy. we are concerned about the dramatic imbalance in the us economy and the dangers that this may pose to all other parts of the world in the medium to long term. many questions about the future policy of the ecb are linked to the inauguration of the new president. the question of the definition of price stability is just as much a part of this as the question of monetary policy instruments. the preservation of price stability as a primary objective must not lead the ecb to exclude support for growth and employment from its policy agenda. monetary policy is not neutral, and the ecb, as a macroeconomic actor, must be involved in the coordination of european policies. the willingness to coordinate ex post is not enough. this will have to be decided; the new president must give us the impetus. the european parliament also expects further action to be taken towards greater transparency, from the publication of summary minutes of decisions, with arguments for and against decisions taken, to anonymised voting results in the governing council. the important thing is an open and transparent monetary policy, which takes access to the decision-making process for granted, in the interests of all of us and in the interests of the common good. the future president can build on the successful work of the first president of the ecb, wim duisenberg. meps are confident that the european parliament will face new challenges and be able to find the right answers. substantial demands arising from the historic change. the rationale for the proposed increase is very straightforward: the accession of ten countries on 1 may 2004 will bring a 66% increase in the number of member states, a 20% increase in the population of the union and an 82% increase in working languages. the commission will handle the very diverse and substantive new demands with just 13% more staff: 3900 extra qualified people recruited over a transition period of five years from the beginning of 2004 through to the end of 2008. for 2004 - enlargement year - after 500 deployments of existing personnel within and between existing services, the net addition needed is 780 new posts. to establish this figure, all current tasks performed by commission services were classified on the basis of 'activity-based management'. calculations were strictly based on the additional workload that we know will have to be borne by the commission as a direct result of enlargement. this systematic approach was applied across all services and the information provided was then carefully screened for extra certainty. in short, we based our request for additional human resources on a rigorous and comprehensive analysis of real and proven operational needs. i am very glad that representatives of the council are here. i thank them for their courtesy in attending this debate, but i objectives of eu consumer policy. regional consumer organisations are eligible for grants for specific projects and can also benefit from the capacity-building actions we offer to consumer organisations. for example, the training courses we offer to consumer organisations to help improve their managerial capacity and the contribution of consumer representatives to eu policy development are open to the staff of regional consumer organisations. specific projects that promote the objectives of eu policy at regional level are eligible for cofinancing from the eu budget. i very much hope the integration of consumer interests into all relevant eu policies is enshrined in article 153 of the treaty. it should be pursued by all commission services and by all eu institutions. we have been making progress on this issue. in the important debate about services of general interest, that followed the adoption of the commission green paper, consumer interests are amongst the core issues on the table. we hope that the progress achieved so far - in air transport, for example, with the charter on passenger rights and the denied boarding regulation - will serve as a reference for the improvement of passenger rights in other modes of transport. actions in this proposal for a decision that will contribute to the integration objectives are many; to name but a few: actions to provide consumer organisations with the technical and legal expertise to effectively contribute to policy development in eu policy areas relevant to consumers, and actions to collect data that provide an evidence base for the integration of consumer interests into other eu policies. on the question of comitology raised by mrs thors, i would like to say that since 1999 the consultative committee of the member states has advised the commission, in particular concerning the attribution of grants. it makes a useful contribution to coordinating eu and national policies for project grants. in addition, this committee will become the essential forum for discussion and advice on the implementation of a new type of action - those that are jointly financed by the community budget and the member states. these joint actions will in particular be used for the commission's future activities in the area of administrative and enforcement cooperation and to consolidate the existing networks of european consumer centres and the extra-judicial network. the committee, therefore, has a key role to play in the implementation of the proposed framework. i took full note when mr bushill-matthews said that he will be watching me: that, of course, is his job and that of parliament. we are accountable to parliament and parliament is of course accountable to the elected members. i noted that mr bushill-matthews also said that next time he will fire live rounds. i suppose that means that up until now he has been firing blanks! to conclude, my special gratitude goes to mr whitehead, who has - the next item is the report (a5-0302/2003) by mr jonckheer, on behalf of the committee on economic and monetary affairs and industrial policy, on the draft council directive restructuring the community framework for the taxation of energy products and electricity (com (2003) 0804 - c5-0192/2003 - 1997/0111 (cns))
i would like to thank the commissioner for his reply. i would like to thank the rapporteur on behalf of the pse group for his work and i share his disappointment at the minimal solution. the commissioner has also made it very clear that this minimal solution is a small breakthrough, but that the european union has not really succeeded in adopting a coherent approach to energy taxation. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. it is truly regrettable that the fourth environmental action programme, which already provided that not only environmental legislation but also taxation law could help to promote the sustainability of the economy and development, could not be enforced, and in this respect the history of suffering of this directive actually goes back a little further than 1999. the directive also has, of course, the lack - as has already been said - of low minimum rates, the non-indexation of minimum rates and also the problem of derogations. we have already debated the derogations several times in this parliament. i think there has always been a consensus here that there must be exceptions for energy-intensive companies, but that these exceptions should at least be accompanied by certain conditions to overcome the situation. this was not the case and so this directive will certainly have to be followed by another one soon. the positive aspect is that this directive not only provides a framework for the taxation of all forms of energy, including electricity, but also supports the promotion of renewable energies and can therefore certainly provide an additional impetus for the further development of these renewable energies. this is a positive development, because we know that renewable energy is an opportunity not only for europe but for the whole of world civilization, because everyone benefits from the tax incentives for the use of environmentally friendly forms of energy. firstly, the primary energy itself is - as a rule - free of charge, and secondly, it can be obtained and converted wherever energy is consumed. the steering effect of tax incentives for energy use is therefore an important complement to eu environmental policy and, i think, to emissions trading. i do not see any contradiction here, but i see here also the complementarity of instruments for steering our european economy and life towards sustainable development. it is also welcome that this directive will finally allow the special measures for the preferential tax treatment of biofuels to come into force, on which we have already reached an agreement, but whose regulation was of course linked to the general energy taxation. and i see that the goals we set for ourselves can be achieved here, too. i would just like to emphasize once again that many member states have already benefited in the past from the revenue effect of environmental taxes, especially energy taxes. i welcome the fact that we can now at least have the possibility of a european vote.
commission. mr president, political realism has led the commission to conclude that it is not appropriate at this stage to modify its proposal of 1997. a formal modification of the commission's proposal would significantly postpone the entry into force of the directive, and might even endanger its adoption during this legislature. but as the council will be examining the proposed amendments in early october, the commission will do its best to have the relevant amendments included in the directive. in that context, the commission could agree in principle with amendments 1, 2, 3, 7, 8, 12 and 13. regarding amendment 2, i would like to point out that it is my intention to make a dedicated proposal on this subject early next year. the real issue behind amendment 4 is that of establishing a common definition for reference units in the directive. the commission is pursuing this goal in the council's working group. furthermore, despite some sympathy with amendments 6, 9, 14 and 15, the commission considers that reopening these issues might endanger the whole compromise. therefore, the commission regrets that it cannot support these amendments. the commission furthermore does not support amendments 5, 10, 11, 16, 17 or18. thus far about the amendments. i should also like to make a few general remarks. firstly, members of parliament will understand that this whole business is increasingly made difficult by the existence of the unanimity rule. the commission has proposed very modest changes to the unanimity rule in the form of qualified majority voting in the areas of simplification, modernisation, co-operation against fraud, and the establishment of a harmonised tax basis for company taxation. however i am pessimistic as to the possibility of those very modest proposals being accepted. it is regrettable, but it is the reality. lastly, i would direct a remark towards mrs kauppi. mrs kauppi has said that hydrogen is a source of energy, but i am afraid that is not true. yes, one can use hydrogen in cars and maybe in the future in aeroplanes, but in order to use hydrogen one must first get it. in order to produce hydrogen one needs electricity. therefore, i am afraid that whatever the advantages of the so-called hydrogen economy – and the commission is fully aware of these advantages – let us not forget that in order to get hydrogen one must produce it and that costs electricity, a lot of electricity. i would like to thank the rapporteur for his good work.

i would like to thank the commissioner for his reply. the negotiations on the investment services directive have once again demonstrated the difficulty of reconciling the different european market philosophies and traditions, in particular the continental model of stock exchanges, which have now largely lost their public-law character and have been privatised, and the in-house trading systems of investment banks. the coexistence of these two systems at european level, and the organisation of fair competition while protecting the interests of investors, is a difficult task, and this is particularly evident when we see the large sums of money being traded on a daily basis and the impact of developments in financial markets on the european and global economy. i hope that the compromise reached in the very tough negotiations in this committee will encourage the european council to reach similar compromises so that this important legislative act on the completion of the internal market in financial services can actually be adopted during this parliamentary term. i think that we have tried to take account of the interests of all market participants, including the non-professional investor, and that we have, just as the commission intended, enforced the principle of transparency in key areas. for example, in the interests of price transparency and investor protection, it is necessary that limit orders to internal trading systems, where they cannot be directly executed by the internaliser itself, can be directly routed to the regulated markets, unless explicitly excluded by the client. the best chance of executing the contract in the best possible way in the interests of the clients is to do so quickly, and i therefore believe that we have made the right decision here, as with the disclosure obligations under article 25. i hope that this directive will indeed give all trading systems a chance to compete without neglecting the protection of investors' interests.
commission. mr president, i shall briefly explain some of the points where we have some concerns with the amendments which have been proposed by this parliament. as regards pre-trade transparency obligations for investment firms, article 25, all the amendments related to pre-trade transparency, that is to say amendments nos 33 and 86 to 90, can be accepted at least partially or in principle, but we are not convinced of the necessity to allow for price improvement. we are not convinced that in the way it is presented in the amendments it is necessary or beneficial for the interests of retail investors. we consider that the current exemption for commodity derivatives and the dealers of such instruments should apply on a consolidated basis. as already explained, in the conduct of business obligations we accept - and this is in line with the commission's initial proposal - the limitation of the obligation on investment firms to carry out a full suitability test only for certain services. regretfully, we do not agree with a number of amendments referring to comitology provisions. some of them are against the principles set out in the report of the wise men - the lamfalussy approach in particular. we consider that implementing measures should only contain detailed technical rules, not principles. the purpose of adopting level 2 measures is always to ensure uniform application of eu legislation in all member states, so any vague formulations proposed in that respect cannot be accepted. on the division of responsibilities between competent authorities, in the case of branches we consider that in order to ensure a correct functioning of the single market the principle of the host member state regulation should only apply as an exception for determining the conduct of business rules and record-keeping. in this context the commission is in a position to accept a large number of amendments, some of them in their entirety, but also a large number partially or in principle and with adaptations. to conclude, the commission can accept 36 amendments in their entirety. furthermore, 62 amendments could be at least accepted partially or in principle, with some changes needed in order to ensure the overall coherence of the text. we consider that 60 amendments have to be rejected. the commission's opinion on the individual amendments has been provided in writingcommission's position on amendments by parliament: see annex.. to conclude, i should like to congratulate parliament for its most valuable efforts. the commission considers that many of the amendments adopted constitute a good basis on which to continue discussions. hardly a nanny state position, as i think you will agree. with such a constructive spirit, i am very confident that this parliament, and the council, will be able to adopt a proposal before the 2004 european parliamentary elections. finally, i hope that mrs lulling will gain much profit from investing in various football clubs! i suggest. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i am pleased to present to this house the guidelines which the italian presidency intends to follow in the conduct of the intergovernmental conference. the convention has also written a historic page in the process of european integration, thanks to the vital contribution of the representatives of this parliament. for the first time, the eu institutions, the governments of the member states and the acceding states, national parliaments and civil society have engaged in a structured, comprehensive, public and transparent reflection on the future of europe. the convention has successfully carried out a significant amount of work within the deadlines set by the laeken declaration, achieving substantial consensus on the most important issues which had not been resolved at previous intergovernmental conferences, such as the division of powers, the conferral of legal personality on the union, the overhaul of the pillar structure of the previous treaty, the reinforcement of the principle of subsidiarity, the definition of a clearer hierarchy of union acts, the involvement of national parliaments, and a renewed institutional balance. the convention also showed that it is possible to prepare and negotiate european treaties in an entirely new way. the success of the new method was demonstrated by the fact that, on the most controversial points, solutions were sought up to the last day to reconcile the positions of all the parties. the final result was the drafting of a constitutional treaty which has the merit of drawing on the proposals and suggestions of the various sectors of european political and civil society, on the basis of an ambitious plan to overcome the contradictions which had emerged during previous intergovernmental conferences between countries with a larger and smaller population and between states more or less ready to move towards forms of even greater integration. the final word now belongs to the governments, on the basis of article 48 of the treaty. this formal fact should not, however, make us forget that we are in the midst of a unified constituent process, the first stage of which has been completed by the convention, which is now entering the stage of intergovernmental negotiations and which will hopefully conclude with the ratification of the future constitutional treaty. the negotiations are therefore fundamentally different from those which preceded the treaties of amsterdam and nice. we must also take this into account when defining the organizational and procedural aspects of the intergovernmental conference. in conducting the work of the intergovernmental conference from 4 october onwards, the presidency considers it necessary first of all to respect the timetable defined at the thessaloniki european council: the commission has also proposed that the council should adopt a timetable for the implementation of the programme, which requires that a positive result be achieved in time for the european parliament elections in june next year. this approach has given rise to a central objective of the italian presidency: the european parliament has also called for the adoption of a new constitution, which will be based on the treaty of rome. this will enable the signing of the constitutional treaty - a constitution for europe, as president giscard d'estaing called it - between 1 may 2004, the date on which the ten new member states are due to join, and the elections to renew this parliament. the extension of the constitutional negotiations beyond these dates would raise two serious problems of legitimacy and democratic transparency: on the one hand, the assets of the convention would be gradually dispersed; on the other hand, european citizens would vote for the elections to the european parliament in defiance of the constitutional guidelines of the future union. the presidency therefore intends to safeguard the structure and implementation of the draft drawn up by the convention. the opinion of the european parliament, in the text so far approved by the committee on constitutional affairs, is a valuable support for our efforts, as were the speeches of the rapporteurs who preceded me and who strongly reaffirmed this understanding. we have already expressed our opinion on the inappropriateness of reopening debates which have already been held extensively in the convention and whose reopening would only risk leading to less consensual and less ambitious results. the conference will not therefore have to alter the overall structure and balance of the draft constitutional treaty but will instead be called upon, in the utmost transparency and openness, to improve and complete those parts of the text which require clarification, completion and supplementation. our aim is to achieve a quality result that meets the expectations of european public opinion and ensures the effective and democratic functioning of the enlarged union. giving the european union a constitution is a challenge, not just for some member states or the italian presidency, which is responsible for guiding the council at this stage. it's a challenge for all of us. it is a commitment to our citizens: if we lose this challenge, as minister frattini told his colleagues in riva del garda, it will be a defeat for the union as a whole and a serious setback for our ambition to make europe a major player on the world stage as a factor of peace, democracy, stability and prosperity. we must not hide from ourselves that the final result is far from certain: a stalemate or crisis scenario is indeed possible. i would like to reiterate in this connection that the italian presidency is not prepared to make any compromise to the downside which does not respect the spirit of the most important points in the draft convention. in this context, the presidency believes that closer involvement of the european parliament in the work of the intergovernmental conference is essential to safeguard the convention's constituent heritage and not to fall back on the narrow national logic which produced the opaque nice agreements. at the last intergovernmental conference, the european parliament took part in the group of personal representatives, making a valuable and constructive contribution. the italian presidency considers it logical that, since the formal setting up of technical preparatory groups is not envisaged in this context, the european parliament should be fully associated with the meetings of the intergovernmental conference at the level of foreign ministers. as regards the meetings of the heads of state or government, the italian presidency undertakes to make every effort to ensure that arrangements are agreed for involving and informing the president of the european parliament in a significantly enhanced way compared with previous conferences. the recent discussion in riva del garda did not allow a consensus to be reached on this matter. the heads of state or government will therefore have to decide on this point at the opening of the intergovernmental conference. the italian presidency will then follow the lines i have just outlined. we are today on the eve of a fundamental milestone in the history of the process of european integration. the italian government is aware of the role played by the european parliament over the last 20 years in building a more democratic, cohesive and fairer union. it was the spinelli treaty that launched the process of relaunching european integration, which - through the single act and the treaties of maastricht, amsterdam and nice - led to the completion of the single market, the adoption of the euro and ever-wider shares of sovereignty in the fields of foreign policy, justice and home affairs. at the same time, your parliament, the direct expression of the peoples of the union, has acquired ever more extensive and effective powers of co-legislation and control. your support will therefore be decisive in the months ahead, which will mark the transition of an enlarged europe to a constitutional phase, the culmination of the long journey begun by the founding fathers with the treaties of paris and rome and which will lead us to an ever closer union between our states and our citizens. this traditional shared view reinforces the italian presidency's determination to maintain constant contact with the european parliament: it is in this spirit that the president of the republic, mr ciampi, will speak to you next week to reaffirm that conviction of europeanism which is the common heritage of all the main political, economic, social and cultural forces in italy. (applause) i would like to thank

very quickly. the constitutionalisation of the union's values, principles, institutions and even, at the request of the conventional parliamentarians, of its symbols. the integration of the charter of delimitation of the union's competences. the extension of the scope of the community method and of codecision. election of the president of the commission by the european parliament. real progress in the establishment of an area of freedom, security and justice. i hope that we will be able to preserve real progress in the field of defence. in this connection, i had the honour of chairing the group on the convention on defence, with particular reference to the draft european arms agency and the proposal for a solidarity clause, which will make it possible to pool the response of the union's states in the event of a terrorist attack, which is always possible, such as the one that tragically struck new york and washington on 11 september. the creation of the post of union foreign minister, which will be able to animate what is lacking today in our union, that is to say a place where a common diplomatic culture is patiently built, so that when crises occur - as we saw some time ago in in writing. - (de) i regret that the amendment by the group of the european people's party (christian democrats) and european democrats to introduce a special reference to our judeo-christian roots in the draft constitution did not receive the assent of the majority of the european parliament. however, the draft constitution already contains, in its present form, important elements in terms of europe's christian heritage. thus, the preamble refers to the religious heritage of europe, and the christian conception of man becomes a central foundation of the constitution through the introduction of the charter of fundamental rights. article 51 of the draft treaty also expressly recognises the status of churches and non-confessional organisations. the draft constitution therefore contains important elements concerning europe's religious heritage. with its amendment, the group of the european people's party (christian democrats) and european democrats wanted to add another important dimension to these elements. it is now up to the intergovernmental conference, and therefore the member states, to take up this proposal and add it to the draft constitution.

priority objective of our commitment. we remain convinced that the only way to achieve a just and lasting peace, based on the un resolutions and principles, is through negotiation and the good faith commission. – mr president, this summer we had record temperatures all over europe. we also had very high levels of ozone concentrations all over europe and the two phenomena are unfortunately linked. ground-level ozone, or photochemical smog as it is also called, is the result of three components: vocs – volatile organic compounds – nox – nitrogen oxide – and sunshine. ozone is an aggressive gas which attacks our respiratory systems and damages plants, even at relatively low concentrations. member states have committed themselves to achieving significant reductions in voc emissions in 2010 in order to meet the so-called national emissions ceiling. as requested by member states, this proposal for a directive targets a group of products which contributes significantly to total voc emissions in europe, namely paints and varnishes for buildings and products for vehicle refinishing. limiting the solvent content in these products is considered to be the only practicable way to help reduce voc emissions and, consequently, air pollution from this major source. for the sake of clarity, i also want to emphasise what this proposal does not aim to do. the purpose is not to establish or harmonise measures for the protection of the health of workers or human health in general. although national or community measures for these purposes obviously have to respect the general requirements under the treaty, they clearly fall outside the scope of this proposal and are therefore not restricted or modified by this proposal. this proposal has the simpler and broader aim of improving the quality of the air we all breathe, by reducing emissions of vocs, thereby reducing the formation of ozone. we have to act now if we want summer sunshine and fine weather to be experienced as sources of pleasure, rather than sources of air pollution and threats to human health and the environment.
mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your work. i thank my colleague, mr giorgio lisi, for the report he has presented on the limitation of emissions of volatile organic compounds from paints and varnishes in vehicles. the report is a useful complement to the commission's proposal in many areas, particularly in the sensitive areas of economy, ecology, breathing problems in vulnerable groups. in the environment, effects on photosynthesis should be considered. i support the european commission's initiative to introduce community-wide measures to reduce voc emissions. i think the product-based approach adopted here makes sense in principle. it is also welcome that 70% of decorative paints are now water-based. i also expressly support the extension of the directive, adopted by a large majority in the committee on the environment, public health and consumer protection, from volatile organic compounds in paints, varnishes and car care products to other dangerous substances. this approach concentrates the necessary measures in a single dossier and avoids unnecessary red tape. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the directive is implemented in a uniform manner. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's environmental policy is not distorted by the throughout europe. this is a threat to the entire paint industry, especially smes, and a serious setback for our european economic area. however, in the interests of the health of users and consumers, volatile organic solvents and solvents shall not be replaced by substances which are harmful to health. the health impact of problematic new ingredients on consumers, such as allergens, or long-term exposure of indoor environments to highly volatile components of paint paints must be avoided in all cases. environmental and consumer protection are given top priority. the quality and applicability of the products must not suffer. if the principle of rapid and complete substitution were to be applied, we would have to accept a significant loss of quality, especially in the case of paints and varnishes. i do not want to suggest to myself or to anyone else in the european union that the paint on your front door will soon fade as quickly as the paint on your walls. we need to reduce solvents and hazardous substances in paints and varnishes, but we need a feasible approach. it is technically impossible to reduce the proportion of volatile organic solvents to below 300 g per litre by 2007 and to further reduce it by 2010, but it is technically possible and appropriate to reduce these substances to 400 g per litre by 2007 and to a maximum level of 300 g per litre by 2010. at the same time, reasonable limits must be set to limit the adverse effects caused by the inhalation of paints and varnishes by craftsmen and home-workers. the aim of the directive must be to reduce the proportion of solvents in paints and varnishes in emissions across europe in the medium term by means of practical measures.
