strategy to implement more effectively the eu's 2001 guidelines on torture, in order to strengthen the eu's action in a number of third countries, while analysing information on cases of torture reported by eu heads of mission around the world. significant funding is allocated to non-governmental organisations and international organisations, through the european initiative for democracy and human rights, for the prevention of torture and the rehabilitation of victims. last year, for example, €25 million was allocated to such projects in a call for proposals for 2002 and 2003. your parliament played an important role in 1994 in allocating funds from the budget of the european union for the victims of torture. i am well aware of the serious concerns raised in your assembly by the decision to reduce funds for rehabilitation centres for victims. i would like to briefly describe the origins of the commission's current policy on the financing of measures against torture. in 2001, the commission presented a communication on human rights, which marked a change in the orientations of rehabilitation and prevention, as well as a commitment to 'ensure that its efforts are focused as much as possible on prevention, in particular by providing human rights training to the police and other potential torturers'. the 2002-04 programming document for the european initiative, which emphasises that funding would be redirected towards longer-term prevention actions, therefore fits into this logic. i shall say a few words in a moment about how this policy has been implemented. but first i would like to explain the reasons for this. the emphasis on prevention does not mean that the commission does not attach value to actions to rehabilitate victims, quite the contrary. the legal, social and medical assistance provided by rehabilitation centres is extremely important to us. however, with the funds allocated to the european initiative limited to around €100 million per year to finance four major priorities in the defence of human rights, the commission was forced to make rigorous and therefore difficult choices. the communication it presented in 2001 clearly states that the general principle of the limited budget of the european initiative is to focus on civil and political rights and presents the european union as the architect of change in the field of human rights. as regards the fight against torture, this principle implies tackling the problems at source, in particular through the training of police forces and prison surveillance staff, research into the networks for marketing instruments of torture, awareness-raising and support actions for major developments, such as the optional protocol to the convention against torture. in short, ladies and gentlemen, this means taking the necessary measures to spare the victims of tomorrow. the decision to refocus increasingly union action on prevention was accompanied by specific measures to progressively reduce the dependence of rehabilitation centres on community resources. since 2001, calls for proposals have placed a high priority on the sustainability of projects during the evaluation process. in addition, actions to strengthen the institutional capacity of the centres, in particular through the development of fundraising capacities, were explicitly eligible for funding in 2001 and 2002. i would also like to point out that, irrespective of the community funds available, it has never been guaranteed that individual centres will receive funding in any given year. all funding proposals are evaluated by experts and are awarded a score based on transparent and fair selection criteria. funds are allocated only to the best proposals. this approach must also be seen in the context of the extensive network of rehabilitation centres that exists today. the international council for the rehabilitation of torture victims itself works with about 200 centers around the world. it is clear, ladies and gentlemen, that the commission does not have the resources to meet such needs and can only support a limited number of centres each year. last year, 13 projects in the eu and abroad targeting victims of torture received eu funding. this assistance is in addition to other important sources of funding at international level, such as the funding of the un voluntary fund for victims of torture, to which several member states contribute. the commission is currently finalising the programming of the european initiative for 2004, which will give priority to the prevention of torture and rehabilitation. this document will be presented to your parliament in due course. in conclusion, mr president, i would like to reiterate that the commission does not intend to abolish all the funding decided for rehabilitation centres overnight. the call for proposals for €11.5 million, targeting rehabilitation centres in the european union, which was launched on 9 august 2003, is, i believe, proof and testimony of this. that is what i wanted to say on this question.

freedom, security and justice and relaunching our economy. i want to focus today on these two important chapters. immigration has long ceased to be a purely national issue. it has become a european issue dramatically with the consolidation of ever more massive immigration flows and the establishment of criminal practices that have alarmed all the member states. border management must therefore become a common task that we must tackle together, in the interests of all. with the forthcoming enlargement, the union's external borders will be extended and almost entirely the responsibility of the new member states. the new countries are not able to cope with this burdensome task alone, which involves not only police aspects but also, and i would say above all, political and social planning of the phenomenon: on the one hand, human trafficking and journeys to hope in inhumane conditions are intolerable to our human and civil conscience. on the other hand, we must take a firm stand on the issue of migration flows and manage our common borders in a coordinated way. the thessaloniki european council had shown the way, stressing the need to accelerate the implementation of the tampere programme, especially as regards the common european policy on asylum and immigration. at the next council meeting, in pursuance of the mandate of the european council, the commission will present a series of measures aimed at completing this policy. the establishment of an agency for the operational management and coordination of borders is being considered, and the council will be able to take a decision on it by the end of the year. its task will not be to replace the national border guards but to organise horizontal operational aspects such as risk analysis, training, research and the purchase of equipment to be put into use by the member states. a special study was devoted to maritime borders, to integrate them into the general organisation of external borders. the commission will also propose the introduction of biometric identifiers in visas and residence permits, pending their inclusion in large-scale information systems and in particular in the second generation of the integrated schengen system. finally, we are preparing initiatives to make passports more secure. in dealing with this very sensitive subject, however, we will never forget that security and surveillance must not prejudice the right of citizens to their privacy. the most urgent issue to be tackled is undoubtedly that of migration flows. legal immigrants are in fact an economic, cultural and human resource that we must receive with respect for their dignity and integrate them in the best possible way into our societies. an active policy on economic immigration and integration must therefore take account of the situation in the immigrants' country of origin, our economic and social needs and the actual integration capacities of newcomers. at the same time, it is our duty to combat illegal immigration, and there are two instruments on which we must focus in the coming months: readmission agreements and return policies. as requested by the council, the commission opened negotiations with third countries to define the arrangements for the readmission of illegally entered citizens to the union. despite the great effort, these are difficult negotiations: the commission must obtain from third countries not only readmission of nationals of the country but also readmission of nationals of other countries in transit through that state. in our experience, negotiations will only succeed if they are framed in a broad context and accompanied by the provision of a range of incentives: for example, in the authorized destination status agreement which we concluded last week with china and which includes a readmission clause, economic considerations played a decisive role. some people might think they shouldn't, but that's the way it is. the other is to offer partner council and the commission, which led to the interinstitutional agreement on better law-making. the initiative that led to this result was initiated by the commission's communication on better regulation and its action plan to simplify and improve regulation, but it was the enthusiasm of the european parliament and its president that led the european council, meeting in seville in june 2002, to invite the three institutions to adopt an interinstitutional agreement aimed at improving the quality of community legislation and the conditions for its transposition into national legislation, including the time-limits. our three institutions responded promptly to the request and opened negotiations. the work initially focused on the high-level technical group and in the later stages was carried out at the political level. significant preparatory work was undertaken by the correspondents' group. on behalf of the council, i would like to thank all those who contributed to the successful conclusion of the agreement: i would like to thank mr frassoni, mr medina ortega, mr gargani, mr swoboda and mr clegg, representatives of parliament, and the commissioner, mrs de remind you, mr president, that in this agreement our three institutions undertake, in the exercise of their legislative responsibilities, to ensure better coordination, better communication and cooperation. in it we recognise the importance of greater transparency and accessibility and address the issue of the use of co-regulation and self-regulation. we renew our commitment to improving the quality of legislation and to establishing procedures for pre-legislative consultation and impact assessment. we stress the need to improve the transposition of community law into national legislation. finally, we renew our commitment to simplify and reduce the volume of legislation. mr president, tomorrow the european parliament will vote on the approval of the interinstitutional the commission mr president, i would like to thank all those who have spoken for their important contribution and to express my special thanks to mr della vedova, rapporteur for the committee on economic and monetary affairs and to mr doorn, rapporteur for the committee on legal affairs and the internal market. i am glad to see that the report, in principle, supports the commission's proposal and that we share the same general objectives as regards the need for reform. as for the series of amendments tabled, the commission unfortunately does not think it can accept them. i would like to explain the reasons, albeit briefly for the sake of time, starting with the substantive criterion in the merger regulation. the commission has come to the conclusion that the substantive criterion should be made clearer by adding to the current wording some words which the economic committee of the european parliament would like to see removed. why do we think this change should be introduced? many commentators believe that the current criterion may not be able to deal with concentrations that give rise to competition problems in cases of so-called non-collusive oligopoly. if this is true, the choice to retain the dominant position criterion would mean not taking advantage of the opportunity to clarify that the substantive criterion for assessing concentrations applies unequivocally to all concentrations which are harmful to consumers. i would also point out that the prevailing view in the international economic literature is that oligopolistic situations, created as a result of concentrations, can produce prolonged anticompetitive effects and thus harm consumers. the commission has put forward its proposal because it has recognised the need to ensure maximum legal certainty, which seems to me to be a widely shared objective and one which has been mentioned by several speakers, including mr olle schmidt, mr ilgenfritz, mr santos and others. the greatest legal certainty is to have a truly effective instrument for merger control. we are convinced that the text proposed is the one which maximises legal certainty. as regards jurisdiction - a subject which is dealt with in depth in the reports by della vedova and doorn and on which several speakers have spoken, such as mr berenguer fuster and mr karas - i think we can all agree that there is a need for a reasonable division of labour between the commission and the member states, while minimising the burden on businesses and also on public regulatory authorities. this means having thresholds for allocation that, as far as possible, reflect the optimal allocation, and applying a referral system that can, say, correct as many of the wrong allocations as possible. we therefore propose to simplify and make more flexible the provisions governing the referral of cases from the commission to the member states and vice versa, also providing for the possibility, if deemed useful by the undertakings, that the referral takes place even before notification. why our position on the proposed amendments concerning jurisdiction? the report proposes, mr della vedova, the introduction of a '2+' rule together with new thresholds for turnover. i understand the intention behind this amendment: i believe that it would introduce an additional element of complexity, which companies would have to face before knowing where to notify a transaction. that is why, mr berenguer fuster, we have abandoned the attractive idea of the '3+' because it is contrary to the reality of national laws on non-harmonised mergers, at least for the time being. this may be a longer-term goal, but it's not today. as regards partial referrals to the member states, i agree that we should minimise their incidence, but i also believe that it is not advisable to exclude them altogether because in some cases they may be appropriate. the commission - and i come to the subject that is of great interest and some concern - has also proposed that its implementing powers under the merger regulation should be largely aligned with those under the new regulation no 1/2003. there are two exceptions in particular, namely the powers of house searches and field investigations, which also do not seem to us to be necessary for merger control, and we do not therefore propose to introduce them. as you can be assured, we believe that there is no presumption of infringement in mergers, and that they are therefore different from, for example, cartels. i would like to reassure the rapporteurs della vedova and doorn, and also mr karas, mr mann and others, on this point of view. it is therefore right that the powers of enforcement should not be more extensive than necessary. however, our priority is to ensure that these powers are effective enough to enable the commission to fulfil its mandate and to protect consumers from the risk of harm from anticompetitive mergers, and i believe that the powers we have proposed are necessary for this purpose. it may be argued that merger control, being a different area from other areas of competition, is not sufficiently restrictive in its powers compared with, for example, the fight against cartels. having said that these are two different cases, i would like to disagree with this conclusion about powers. why would you do that? because mergers have a unique, one-off, structural and irreversible impact on the market. for this reason, from a certain point of view, it is all the more essential that the commission's powers to obtain the facts are effective, otherwise the damage to competition caused by our decision would be irreparable. a final word, mr president, on the subject of workers' rights, which was raised by mr berenguer fuster, mr van den burg and mr commission. – mr president, the hot summer weather all over europe saw bathing sites visited by tourists and by local people who enjoy the pleasures of bathing in clean water. unfortunately, there are some risks linked to bathing in natural waters. bathing waters may be contaminated by bacteria which originate from households, hotels or maybe office buildings. agriculture may also be a source of contamination and cattle and livestock can pollute rivers and lakes. as a consequence, where they are placed at risk bathers may contract gastro-enteritis, ear or eye infections, or even more serious illnesses. to reduce the risks related to bathing, a bathing water directive was introduced in 1976. this directive has performed particularly well, and nowadays almost 95% of europe's bathing waters conform to the quality standards it laid down, as opposed to only 60% ten years ago. still, we have to look to the future. the current bathing water directive is based on health and hygiene standards from the 1960s and these have since evolved. social standards have also changed and these days public information and involvement have become cornerstones of good governance. the legislative-style approach at the heart of the 1976 directive is outdated, since it is based only on monitoring and on measuring, not on the proactive and sound management of bathing waters. these are just a few of the reasons why the commission organised the long and thorough public and stakeholder consultation and came up with a new proposal for a bathing water directive which seeks a common and comparable level of protection for all eu waters and all bathers, whether in major tourist resorts or in traditional local bathing sites. this new proposal supports the concept of beach management and public information and participation, but most of all it stands for stricter health standards, thanks to which our children will be able to bathe in safer waters, reducing risks of illness linked to bathing.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the european parliament has been a great help to us. bathing waters are making waves! based on the 1976 survey, the european commission compiles the bathing water inventory at the beginning of each summer. this information is not only being taken up by many citizens across europe, but also has been seen by more than 2 million visitors to the relevant websites. it is clear that bathing waters throughout europe became much cleaner during this period. despite torrential rainfall and flooding in 2002, as much as 98.5% of europe's coastal waters met the requirements of the directive. the revision of a directive after more than a quarter of a century is useful for several reasons. scientific and technical knowledge has evolved rapidly, experience gained from up to 26 years of practical application depending on the length of eu membership should be incorporated into a revision, the water framework directive should be aligned with the bathing water directive, the protection of bathing water users' health should be further improved and, finally, simplification of existing legislation is desirable. my group shares the commission's intention to improve the quality of bathing waters. the bathing as a meaningful leisure activity, but also the tourist benefits of bathing waters, should be promoted in all our member states. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the quality of bathing water is not compromised by the fact that the quality of bathing water is not adequately controlled. the new regulation aims to reduce the parameters to be measured from 19 to 2, with the presence of e. coli and e. coli as the main indicators, and to significantly tighten these two standards. chemical parameters, on the other hand, are not relevant and are regulated by other directives and should therefore no longer be measured. the frequency of sampling should be reduced if good water quality has been consistently measured over a period of three years. the quality of bathing water should be assessed on the basis of the development of the past three years, rather than on the basis of one year. this would make one-off incidents such as bad weather less noticeable. these factors would also reduce the cost of implementing the directive in the member states. it is also important for our group to provide for improved information on water quality, which should also be disseminated more widely through the media and the internet. we support the commission's objective and the amendments tabled to that end. concerns the emissions from construction machinery, excavators, locomotives and inland waterway vessels. i think this is an issue that is obvious to many citizens that we need to do something about. on a construction site on a road in a european city, we have the situation where the excavator, the shovel loader, equipped with the same engine as the truck that removes the rubble, is allowed to emit many times more emissions into the air. there's no way to explain it. the same engine used in the same place in two different machines may emit different amounts. so clearly we have to do something here. i am also very pleased that we have managed to negotiate a compromise with the council before the first reading, which we have brought forward together with the large groups and many colleagues in order to avoid a conciliation procedure in the end. this compromise is in line with what we decided in the committee on the environment. we want to reduce the emissions of these machines that are not on the road in several stages. we are indeed moving in the same direction as the united states. it was only in april of this year that the american epa submitted a proposal which also takes into account our main concern - nitrogen oxides and particulate matter emissions - and which sets out similar directions as those we have discussed. in this respect, i believe that this is the right approach, because these machines are also marketed globally: several stages to reduce nitrogen oxides and particulate matter, so that in the last stage a particulate filter must be installed in all cases, in order to capture the significant health risks posed by particulate matter and ultimately protect citizens, especially in urban areas. we are also including locomotives in this directive. some of you may have seen a diesel-powered railway locomotive passing through a railway station, and you may have seen the amount of particles that are emitted into the air. i think we need to do something about this, but we're doing it a little bit more carefully than with the other machines, by having a review process built in again to make sure that the technological solutions are also feasible. the same applies to the inland vessels. i think that we could have gone a little further, but there was not much movement in the council, not for technical reasons but for political reasons. we agreed that we would also make sure that there can be no electronic manipulation of the engines. we have seen in the united states that, in some truck models, the emissions behaviour in the field was very different from that during the type approval test cycle due to electronic manipulation. that too is ruled out. we have agreed that the behaviour beyond the test cycle must not result in infinitely more emissions into the air, but that here too it must be clearly ensured that this is within a reasonable framework in relation to the test cycle. i think it is an important step in the right direction that we can take here. we also made sure that manufacturers who comply with the standards early on can advertise with them. i think that this is ultimately also a factor for the consumer to buy, so you can say: here are engines that meet emission standards early - this could be a machine for me, and therefore a promotional opportunity for manufacturers who bring them to market early. so overall a very good step in the right direction. we are thus in the tradition of the various regulations we have adopted to protect the air: cars, lorries, motorcycles, chainsaws and lawn mowers. i think it is fair to say that the success story of 'clean air for europe' is being written here again. i thank all those who have contributed to this. the rapporteur. (de) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, it is still early and those of us who work on transport policy are delighted to have the opportunity to discuss this subject in the morning, for once, and not at 9 or 10 p.m. (applause) we hope that some journalists will also be present on this occasion. evenings are always so long that it is sometimes relatively difficult to keep to the schedules originally planned. anyway, enough of the gossip, let's get down to business. what we are discussing today is the improvement of the operating conditions of railways in the european union. we are seeking, through three directives and a regulation, to ensure that the conditions are improved so that european railways can once again carry more freight and passengers. as rapporteur on the directive on the development of community railways, let me first express my great satisfaction at the council's acceptance of parliament's position. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the transport of dangerous goods by rail. since that date, this first step towards the opening up of the rail network in the 15 member states, which in fact covers 90% of the main rail corridors, has given railway companies of all nationalities an equal chance to use the european rail network for international rail freight transport in a way that best meets the needs of customers. secondly, parliament agrees with the council that the remaining lines of the rail network should be opened to international freight transport from 1 january 2006. this is not a major step forward, however, since, as i have just said, the network has been open to international freight traffic at almost 90% since 15 march this year. parliament therefore continues to call for the full opening of rail networks to national and international carriers on 1 january 2006, allowing the entire european rail network to be fully accessible to transport services - both national and international - on that date. in this way we will be able to achieve the objective set out in the commission's white paper - and i am pleased to hear that, commissioner, because we have always followed the same line - of restoring rail transport to its former position on the market by 2010 and of transferring as much freight as possible to the rail network. however, the objective is more comprehensive. the white paper is not just about freight, it is about achieving a balance between the different modes of transport by 2010. parliament therefore considered that passenger transport networks should also be liberalized. if you think about the increase in the number of private cars on our highways and the increase in air traffic, you will understand that our highways and our air corridors are close to the saturation point. that is why we in this house want the railway networks to be open to passenger transport on 1 january 2008. otherwise, the reduction in road and air traffic to rail expected for 2010 will have no effect on passenger transport. it is very worrying to see how low-cost airlines are diverting customers from european railways. i hope, madam commissioner, that in the coming days you will have a statement to make about charleroi airport in belgium. it is unacceptable that the railways are suffering huge losses on their long-distance passenger services because low-cost airlines are taking over their customers and clogging up our skies. in summary, we want to ensure that the objective of rebalancing the transport market by 2010 also applies to passenger transport. some people have pointed out on many occasions that the commission had announced the presentation by the end of the year of a third railway package, a package which will include passenger transport. this is very much appreciated, madam commissioner, but it is of no use to us because, as you know, if the commission is not able to present this package by december this year, we will not be able to adopt it or even consider it at first reading before the end of the current parliamentary term. even if we were to succeed in closing the first reading, the arrival of the european parliament elections, the appointment of a new commission and the need to reactivate the legislative process would mean that we would actually need an extra year or two to pass a passenger transport bill. we could not therefore adopt a third railway package before 2005. however, i believe that railway operators need to know for sure whether they will have a legal right of access to the entire network. we want them to have the time to anticipate the needs of travellers so that we can actually move a significant volume of long-distance road and air traffic to rail by 2010. finally, the commission proposed the abolition of the existing options for member states to allow non-railway undertakings to apply for timetables, in favour of a provision allowing shippers, freight forwarders and others to apply for the use of these timetables alongside railway companies in all member states. we believe that every effort should be made to optimise the use of rail infrastructure. we know that there is still spare capacity today - even on the brenner line - and that there is no reason to continue to struggle against the heavyweights if even this transalpine railway still has spare capacity. in other words, we need to allow more market players to request and use the available time slots if we are to optimise the volume of freight transported by rail. let me, as the spokesman for my group, say a few words about the other two reports, because it would be foolish for me to sit down and then stand up again. i should like to begin by expressing my sincere thanks to the rapporteurs of the other groups on behalf of my group. we have worked very well together, both at first reading and in preparing this second reading. even though mrs ainardi, mr sterckx, mr savary and i have not agreed on certain specific issues, we have always considered the railway package as a whole, hence our close cooperation as rapporteurs. i am very glad to see that we are all striving to follow the same line. you are aware that the council has already tried to find compromises which will enable us to conclude the legislative process quickly. the council, like the rapporteurs, has mainly tried to reduce the number of outstanding questions between the council and parliament, sometimes by accepting the positions of parliament, sometimes by proposing compromises. the conciliation procedure will therefore concentrate on a core of well under 70 points. i hope that the council will make some sensible statements tomorrow about its intention to adhere to the line we started to consider last week. we want to reduce the number of contentious issues so that we can focus fully on the most important issues during conciliation sessions. to this end, my group will look carefully at the latest set of amendments to the railway directives and will vote accordingly on thursday. let me make a couple of comments on the sterckx report. mr sterckx has made considerable efforts - and i thank him for this - to ensure that european rail safety standards guarantee a high level of safety and that there is no possibility of surreptitiously reintroducing national safety rules which would ultimately introduce new arbitrary restrictions on international transport. i think it is very important that we cooperate with the commission in order to find a mechanism to prevent the introduction of so-called essential safety provisions which are actually aimed at discriminating against other railway companies. my group also attaches importance to the proper training of railway staff and all other categories of staff on whom the safety of rail travel depends. we have a problem here, madam commissioner, which is that a directive devoted solely to the training of train drivers might not be enough. we must train all other categories of security personnel to give them the required level of qualification. i support mr sterckx on the last point in his report which i would like to raise, and i think we can all agree on this: staff training certificates must not lose their validity when a staff member leaves one railway company to join another. we also need a single market for train drivers. we need competition in the whole rail transport sector. let us now turn to the savary report. mr savary has very carefully incorporated the new budgetary rules and i believe the council will approve. in this way, all agencies will have uniform budgetary rules and we will avoid a situation where each agency has its own rules, creating an inextricable tangle of budgetary provisions. the main point of the savary report - and we fully support the rapporteur on this - is the imbalance in the council's proposal on the management board. the amended proposal, submitted by the commission, provides for a management board comprising six representatives of the council, four representatives of the commission and six representatives of the non-voting industry, i.e. the railway companies concerned, as well as users. the council now proposes that all member states be represented on the administrative board. this would mean that six representatives of the we have adopted, allows for extrajudicial settlement in one's own country of an accident in another country. the adoption of the fourth directive was followed by the regulation of 22 december 2000 on jurisdiction and the recognition and enforcement of judgments in civil and commercial matters. it provides that, in the case of civil liability insurance, the residence of the injured party is also taken into account for a place of jurisdiction where there is a direct action. we created it with the fourth for cross-border accidents, and we have now created it with the fifth for everyone. this means that not only will it be possible in future to settle out-of-court claims for damage suffered in another country in my own country, but also to bring legal proceedings in my own country. that's all you can do for an accident victim. what else is contained in this fifth directive? the costs of prosecution, which are necessary and proportionate, shall be reimbursed. if legal costs the consultation of a lawyer are necessary and appropriate, then this is a damage that must of course be reimbursed. we need to raise the minimum coverage. in this area we have a patchwork of rules in the european union, and the whole world agrees that after more than 20 years we need a new regulation. now it's about the height. of course there are problems. it is not easy to raise the minimum coverage, and i know this very well, because that will of course also lead to an increase in premiums. the compromise we have found - €5 million for personal injury and €2 million for property damage president of the commission. mr president of the european parliament, mr president-in-office of the council, ladies and gentlemen, in my last speech i said that although the fundamentals are good, the union needs decisive and rapid action to get out of the current stalemate. that is why the commission has presented the european growth initiative, which i briefly described to you at the beginning of the month. today i can confirm that the european council has welcomed our ideas to revive the economy and to give a boost to growth and employment. the growth initiative is a simple and practical strategy. it does not intend to change priorities but to strengthen and accelerate the lisbon strategy. the qualifying points are: first, to remove obstacles to coordination, especially those resulting from complicated administrative rules; secondly, to mobilise the public and private capital needed to finance and launch some infrastructure investments that are already in the advanced design phase. that is why we are preparing a quick-start list, a list of projects of a truly european scale in the field of infrastructure and research. the projects that will be part of the quick-start list are taken from the list of 29 projects submitted previously. these will include the major transeuropean transport arteries and other high-tech projects. the list combines two principles: the desire to produce quick and tangible results and a strong focus on compatibility with the sustainable development goals we have set ourselves. the desire to produce concrete results is expressed in three main aspects: first, to exploit the potential of a higher level of union co-financing. the commission has proposed raising the community contribution to the crossborder parts of projects to 30%. this increases the leverage of our investments to mobilise private capital and other sources of public capital. secondly, to concentrate resources on a limited number of mature projects. the impact of investment is greatly enhanced if, instead of being distributed by the rain, financial commitment is focused on projects that are already taking off. thirdly, to select projects which have the greatest potential to produce rapid results. this means solving the most complex challenges in practice, especially in the run-up to enlargement, creating jobs, stimulating growth and channelling the potential for research and technological innovation, laying the foundations for improving our competitiveness. finally, the quick start list pays great attention to compatibility, as projects are selected on the basis of environmental and economic-financial sustainability criteria. in particular, however, this funding must respect the stability and growth pact and be in line with the commitment to improve the quality of spending contained in the broad economic policy guidelines. in this connection, i would like to express my appreciation for the great define the threats facing the european union today, but it also has the task of identifying the areas on which our security depends for stability. it is a strategy which can guide us in determining the means necessary to become, as we like to say, producers of security, and no longer just consumers of security. that is why the italian presidency is keen to promote synergy between the common foreign policy and the activities of international organisations working in the field of security. i am thinking in particular of nato and the osce, but the role of the united nations remains essential for us. on 24 september, the italian presidency and secretary-general kofi annan signed in new york an eu/un protocol laying down the basis for structured cooperation in crisis management, both in the military and civil dimensions. i think that by now, ladies and gentlemen, everyone must recognize that action is needed to prevent rather than repair the consequences of a crisis that has already erupted. prevention thus becomes a key component of the union's external relationship; it is born and shaped by the coordinated use of both the resources of the member states made available to the common interest and the union's own resources managed by the european commission. we must therefore make the most of the wide range of instruments that the union can put in place in theatres of crisis. we have tools of cultural, economic, political and now even military influence; the union can and must do more than any other international organisation to tackle the root causes of conflict and help to remove them in a preventive manner. we use a policy of influence and incentives to try to promote progress in regional integration and to overcome situations of misunderstanding and instability. this is the winning model on which we built the european union. that's why we're confidently pitching this model to our external partners. i would like to refer in particular to the work together and i think it is particularly important to recognise that france, germany and britain as well as the other member states have to give a lead in working together. i hope that we will see agreed to share. i hope that we will see that sort of effective cooperation. i hope that we will not see too much institutional warfare. i certainly think that the issues that we have to deal with on commission. mr president, you are entirely correct in saying that i have addressed parliament on a number of previous occasions on the death penalty and i have had to observe occasionally in the past that when i first used to make speeches in a parliament on the death penalty, i did not find such unanimity of support for my views. i remember voting for the abolition of capital punishment in various parts of the british isles, not always with great support. the first act that i carried out when i was a colonial oppressor was to abolish capital punishment in hong kong! so i have a certain amount of 'form' on this issue, as football managers would say. can i straightaway apologise for the fact that i will not be able to stay for the whole of this debate. i have to catch an aeroplane for madrid for the iraq donors' conference which is beginning tomorrow morning, and where, of course, the presidency will also be represented. i hope parliament will excuse me of any discourtesy, but my colleague, mr fischler, will be coming to sit here to report anything that i should have heard later in the debate. i hope also that parliament will excuse me if a good deal of what i say treads in the elegant footsteps of the presidency. i want to put many of the same points, but in my own way. parliament knows that we consistently work towards the universal abolition of the death penalty. in the process of attaining this objective, where the death penalty still exists, we call for its use to be progressively restricted, we insist that it should be carried out with the minimum cruelty. the european union also presses, where relevant, for moratoria to be introduced. we have produced internal guidelines for démarches and representations on capital punishment, where relevant, in multilateral fora and towards third countries. at the european summit with china last year, the then prime minister of china, zhu rongii, said: 'you just talk about these issues to poorer countries don't you?' i pointed out to him that the first time i recalled us raising the issue was with the united states. so it is an issue that we raise –i must say that the united states secretary of state was slightly surprised! – with everyone. the european parliament is a long-standing opponent of the death penalty and has been instrumental in promoting this process. parliament has declared in the past that it considers capital punishment, and i quote, 'an inhuman, medieval form of punishment, unworthy of modern societies'. a series of initiatives have been taken to ensure that the abolition of the death penalty should become a key element of european human rights policy. it is on the basis of this strongly held european policy objective that for the last years we have successfully tabled resolutions in the un commission on human rights on the death penalty, as the president-in-office has said. the seventh consecutive resolution was adopted in geneva on 24 april. this resolution contains some significant new features. it calls, in particular, on states not to carry out executions in public or in any other degrading manner and to ensure that any application of particularly cruel or inhuman means of execution, such as stoning, be stopped immediately. while the support for resolutions on the death penalty in the commission on human rights has increased, it has to be said that opposition has increased as well. the resolution adopted in geneva received the support of 24 states, while 18 voted against and 10 abstained. however, the strong disagreement of many states was proved by the fact that 63 countries signed a statement dissociating themselves from the resolution. i thought it would be useful to recall these facts in the context of today's debate on a resolution requesting a moratorium on the death penalty in the general assembly third committee. a first consideration, before presenting any resolution, should be whether such a text would receive sufficient support to be adopted by the general assembly. we all remember the 54th session of the general assembly in 1999. a text notably calling for the establishment of moratoria and the enforcement of certain safeguards was circulated. this draft caused an immediate outcry from states that maintain the death penalty, including egypt, india and singapore. strong attacks were made on the european initiative, and we were perceived as seeking to impose our values on other sovereign states. in the end, the text was withdrawn. that was the situation in 1999. we have no indications that the general assembly would be more positively inclined today towards a death penalty resolution. it would seem that while the hard-line retentionists are resigned to further commission on human rights texts on this issue, they will continue to resist strongly any efforts to secure a general assembly resolution. this would lead to further divisive debate. as a result, the european union has decided to pursue its action against the death penalty in the commission on human rights rather than the general assembly. however, a more fundamental issue is whether a resolution asking for a moratorium would promote the european objective of abolition of the death penalty world-wide. the presidency has suggested that the european proposal should not go as far as requesting abolition of the death penalty but rather a moratorium on the use of this punishment. since the resolution tabled by the european union in the commission on human rights asks states to abolish the death penalty completely and, in the meantime, to establish a moratorium on executions, we may run the risk of being perceived as weakening the european stance by not suggesting the same high standards in the general assembly. i should also let you know that i have been approached by non-governmental organisations on this matter. in july of this year, i had the pleasure of convening a special seminar for human rights ngos in brussels. in the context of that meeting, the world coalition of ngos against the death penalty, and that includes amnesty international and many other prestigious organisations, presented its own view. the message of this group was to ask the european union to refrain from presenting a resolution on the death penalty at the forthcoming general assembly. these ngos in particular pointed out that since there are no signs to the effect that political tensions have eased since 1999, such an initiative could create a highly politicised and counter-productive debate in the general assembly. in their view, another failure in the general assembly could reinforce the position of those states that maintain the death penalty. i attach great importance to the expertise of the many renowned ngos that we work with. they also play an important role as partners in the framework of projects we implement under the european initiative for democracy and human rights programme. on the initiative of this ngo coalition, we also for the first time on 10 october celebrated, if that is the right word, the world day against the death penalty. the european commission will continue to support campaigns designed to achieve a moratorium on the death penalty and on executions and eventually the abolition of capital punishment throughout the world. last year approximately eur 4.9 million were allocated under the european initiative to projects aimed at raising european public awareness in retentionist countries. the methods used include public education, out-reach to influence public opinion, studies on how states' death penalty systems comply with minimum standards, informing and supporting strategies for replacing the death penalty and efforts towards securing the access of death row inmates to appropriate levels of legal support, as well as training for lawyers. during the last months there have also been some positive developments that should be highlighted. in january, governor ryan of illinois decided to commute the death sentences of 156 prisoners on death row. through the entry into force on 1 july of protocol 13 to the european convention on human rights, the use of the death penalty is banned not only in peacetime but also in time of war. lastly, the president of armenia in july commuted all outstanding death sentences to life in prison and, subsequently, in september, ratified protocol 6 to the european convention on human rights, and in that way abolished the death penalty. let me repeat, we take this issue seriously, and i am delighted that we are working with a presidency which has taken it so seriously and has pursued it with considerable skill and very good political judgment. we are making some progress, but it will take time and persistence, as well as the continuing advocacy of this parliament if we are to attain our goal, which is to see the death penalty consigned to the history books as a form of punishment that should have no place in the modern world.

i suggest. in 2002, the commission presented a communication on the integrated management of the external borders of the member states of the union, which provides a broad overview of the future of border management. in 2002, a feasibility study on the establishment of a european border police was presented in rome, coordinated by italy. in june the following year, the justice and home affairs council adopted a plan for the management of the external borders which forms the basis for all further activities in this area. on the basis of these documents, the european council in seville in 2002 identified priority measures and called for the establishment, within the council, of a joint body of experts on external borders, composed of the heads of the member states' border control services and responsible for coordinating the measures provided for in the plan. it also provided for the rapid implementation of joint operations at the external borders and the immediate launch of pilot projects. these operations and projects have been implemented and are being implemented since 2002 and 2003. in june 2003, the thessaloniki european council - as we know - decided to set up a joint body of border experts to make this european strategy more effective. this body has been set up and is currently operational within the council. the thessaloniki conclusions also invited the commission to examine the need to create new institutional mechanisms to strengthen operational cooperation for the management of the external borders, including the creation of a european operational structure. in brussels on 16 and 17 october, the european council welcomed the commission's intention to propose the creation of a european border management agency to improve practical cooperation in time for the council to reach political agreement on the practical elements of this new agency by the end of 2003. this proposal will build on the experience of the joint expert body on the external borders. the european council also took note of the study carried out on behalf of the commission on maritime borders and invited the justice and home affairs council to draw up a work programme on this subject to be adopted by the end of the year. finally, as regards the european police college, it was set up by a council decision in december 2000, started operating in 2001 and is provisionally located in denmark. a decision on its permanent seat will depend on the guidelines provided by the european council.

the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, this proposal for a commission directive fulfils one of the mandates given by the tampere european council and has two main objectives, as the rapporteur has just stressed: to create a minimum standard for the compensation of all citizens and legal residents of the european union who are victims of crime and to facilitate access to compensation in cross-border situations. the added value of these two objectives is, in my view, unquestionable, since two of the current 15 member states and most of the states which will be joining the european union do not yet have any compensation system in place. in addition, there is currently no system of crossborder cooperation that can help the victim to claim compensation. the first objective of the proposal is to ensure that all member states have the possibility of obtaining compensation from the state. the aim is not, however, to harmonise the relevant legislation of the member states. it is simply a matter of setting a minimum standard which each state can exceed if it wishes, thus respecting the principle of subsidiarity. the scope of this directive covers, in particular, victims of terrorism. close relatives and dependants of victims are entitled to compensation when the victim dies as a result of the bodily injury suffered and caused by a crime covered by the definition of the directive. all pecuniary and non-pecuniary losses resulting directly from the personal injury suffered shall be compensated. compensation for non-pecuniary damage, which is currently not available in a large number of member states, is of particular relevance to the commission, in particular in the case of serious crimes such as armed robbery, rape, sexual offences or terrorist attacks. the second objective of the proposal is to facilitate access to compensation for victims of crime in crossborder situations. when a person is the victim of a crime in a country other than the one in which he or she resides, it is unlikely that the victim will have much time to be able to initiate appropriate criminal and civil proceedings beyond reporting the crime. we therefore think that the system should allow the victim to trigger these procedures simply from his own country of residence. the directive therefore proposes a system of cooperation between the authorities of the member states. the commission proposes to draw up a manual which will be made available to the authorities and in which the basic criteria for compensation in each state, the territorial competence of the authorities in each member state, where applicable, and the forms used in each member state for this purpose can be found. the handbook thus produced will be available in all the official languages of the european union.
mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your work. the european union has set itself the priority of ensuring freedom of movement. but this freedom of movement can only be achieved if the union also takes all the necessary measures to protect its citizens, especially when they are victims of crime, regardless of their eu nationality or the member state in which they are victims. the citizens of the european union like to travel and do so a lot. they work in other member states and they also make use of their right to free movement in the eu in a variety of other ways. however, just as in one's own country, any citizen can be the victim of a crime or terrorist attack in another member state. so far, as mrs angelilli has already pointed out, the legal situation is regulated differently in all the member states. this is why two people who are victims of a crime in different eu member states under identical circumstances may receive completely different amounts of compensation and, in extreme cases, one victim may not receive any compensation at all. i therefore expressly welcome the commission's proposal on behalf of the epp/ed group and thank mrs angelilli for her report, which is intended to lead to a system for victims of intentional crime or terrorist attacks within the european union. all eu citizens and all persons legally residing in the eu will receive adequate compensation when the directive enters into force if they have been the victim of a crime. it also means that people who are victims of a crime within the eu will have the right to turn to an authority in their own country where they can seek help. this will ensure that victims have easier access to compensation, even if the crime was committed outside their own member state. this ensures that the victim of a crime finally receives adequate protection and adequate compensation, which paradoxically is still not properly taken into account in many legal and criminal justice systems to this day. i am convinced that the house will vote in favour of this report by a large majority tomorrow, and i am delighted to hear that.

- the agenda calls for the report (a5-0369/2003) by mr liese, on behalf of the committee on industry, foreign trade, research and energy, on the proposal for a council decision amending decision 2002/834/ec establishing a specific research, technological development and demonstration programme: 'integrating and strengthening the european research area' (2002-2006) [com (2003) 390 - c5-0349/2003 - 2003/0151 (cns)) ].
commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i welcome the opportunity to address a subject which has always been of great interest to this parliament. i should like to begin by thanking the rapporteur and all the members of the committee on industry, foreign trade, research and energy for the quality of their work. i would also like to thank the rapporteur and the members of the committee on legal affairs and the internal market. in the knowledge society economy which the union has set itself the objective of developing in europe, scientific research and technological development play, by definition, a key role. more than ever, the competitiveness of businesses and the quality of life of european citizens depend on the progress of scientific knowledge and its exploitation. it has often been said, and rightly so, that the century that is opening up will be the century of the sciences and technologies of life. research on embryonic stem cells seems to be crucial to advancing our understanding of the very early stages of life. it also shows promise for major medical applications such as the treatment of previously unconquered diseases, including degenerative diseases - cancer or alzheimer's disease, for example - which are placing an increasing burden of human suffering and economic burden on european society. in the short term, research on embryonic stem cells will provide a better understanding of the processes of cell differentiation and multiplication, which are key processes in life and the development of certain diseases, and will make possible advances in other areas of research. this research is better conducted at european level, where the added value of cooperation is significant. cooperation between teams from different member states makes better use of the resources required and allows faster results for the benefit of the scientific community and patients across europe. i shall begin by discussing the institutional context of this cooperation. the proposal presented by the commission on 9 july follows on from the council meeting of 30 september 2002, at which the specific programmes for the implementation of the sixth framework programme for research were adopted. it was agreed that the commission would present a legislative proposal amending the specific programme 'integrating and strengthening the european research area' and establishing a framework for research using human embryos and embryonic stem cells. the commission is therefore proposing a set of principles, a framework which sets out very strict, clear and transparent conditions, both scientific and ethical, to govern the funding of research projects using surplus human embryos for the development of new stem cell lines. the commission considers that it has made a responsible proposal in that it strikes the right balance between meeting the needs of research and the expectations of patients and ensuring that research is conducted in accordance with the highest ethical standards. to set conditions even stricter than those proposed by the commission would in fact be tantamount to prohibiting such research, whereas it is possible under the decisions already taken by the parliament and the council concerning the framework programme and its specific programmes. i would like to emphasise that this is not about establishing ethical rules for stem cell research in europe. the proposed conditions apply only to the sixth framework programme and national legislation is not affected. this research will never be funded in a country where it is banned. among the conditions proposed, the commission wished to send a strong signal to those who might have reservations about the type of research in question. it proposes that only surplus embryos created before 27 june 2002 may be used. the purpose of this time limit is to prevent any link between community funding and any incentive to create additional surplus embryos in the context of in vitro fertilisation for use in research. i would also like to point out that funding for research using embryonic stem cells complements funding for research on adult stem cells. research on these two cell types is necessary, in particular because of their different properties and the medical applications envisaged. on the other hand, it is also important to be able to have new embryonic stem cell lines available, since those that exist today are few in number, of poor quality for the most part and - i repeat - essentially non-european, patented and therefore only accessible at high prices, even for research work. in these circumstances, it is in europe's general interest to develop its own capacity. in conclusion, i would remind you that the three institutions have committed themselves to reaching a decision on this matter by the end of the year and i am of course counting heavily on parliament's support in this regard. in writing. i warmly welcome and express my personal thanks to mr linkohr for his own-initiative report on the action plan for research and technological progress in europe. i support the call for a significant increase in research expenditure in europe to meet the lisbon objectives, even though the current budgetary situation in many member states is tense and will make swift implementation difficult. to strengthen research in the eu in a sustainable way, the increase in expenditure must therefore be accompanied by an increase in the efficiency of the use and management of funding and a stronger focus on basic research. i am glad that the committee responsible has accepted my amendments in this respect. the committee, however, rejected the proposal to make the so-called new instruments more meaningful in the current sixth research framework programme. for this reason, my group has tabled amendment no 1 again, in which parliament calls for the concepts of networks of excellence and integrated projects to be more closely aligned with the guiding principle of the european research area in the context of the sixth research framework programme, and in particular for adjustments to be made to the size of projects, both in terms of the number of project partners and the financial volumes. we hope that this will help to bring eu research policy into line with the realities of the day. i therefore ask you to approve this motion.
