president of the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, this is my last opportunity in this parliament to present the state of the union to parliament. it is a solemn occasion in the life of our institutions, when the situation is traditionally taken into account and an overview is given of the activities which the commission intends to carry out in the coming year. unfortunately, this year our spirit is deeply disturbed by the tragic events which you, mr president, have mentioned and which have occupied the news of the last few days. i am referring to the series of violent actions that have sown terror and grief in iraq and turkey. at this moment my thought, like yours, is to share the grief of italy, to which we convey the condolences of the whole european people for the nineteen boys who fell in the peace mission. we also share the grief of turkey and the jewish communities and those suffering around the world from the terrorist offensive. i know that i share the views of the whole commission in expressing my deepest sympathy to all the women, men and children who have been affected by these tragedies. the problems we are facing every day, ladies and gentlemen, show that the union is, despite these difficult times, in good health, with good peace among the eurosceptics and the unprovoked critics. the situation is not easy because we are in a delicate and complex transition phase. however, the prospect of a larger and stronger union is at hand. we have had a difficult two years in the economic field, but judging by the latest indicators, it seems that we are leaving the negative phase behind. there is a widespread expectation that economic activity will pick up in the second half of this year, and then accelerate in 2004. the worst seems to be over: the commission has also launched a new action plan to combat fraud in the eu. in addition to the union, recovery is taking shape in other regions of the world. in the united states, monetary and fiscal stimulus and productivity gains are keeping growth rates high. however, there is great concern that the size of the deficit could increase further next year due to tax breaks and the costs of the iraq conflict. the outlook for japan has finally turned upside down and the trend for the other asian economies remains positive, with growth estimated at 6.7 per cent next year. positive signals are also coming from the acceding countries: in response to the general recovery in europe and the prospect of enlargement, growth in these countries is forecast to be 3.8% next year. this is another sign of the correctness of the political choices made in support of unification. however, as i said, the recovery is still fragile and we must press on with the accelerator of the lisbon agenda and continue on the path of structural reforms. the european growth initiative, which the commission has been working on since the beginning of the year, has now taken shape. it provides for public and private investment to boost growth and employment. the support we received at the october european council has made our initial proposal a genuine road map with specific actions and timetables to remove the financial and, above all, regulatory and administrative obstacles to these investments. the initiative also includes the quick-start list, which includes a number of projects that are or will soon be ready to start work. in close cooperation with the european investment bank, we have identified 56 projects in transport networks, energy, telecommunications and research. in compiling the list we followed some very clear criteria: first, the works are at an advanced stage of design and can be started immediately. secondly, all projects have a strong cross-border impact; finally, we have chosen works that can produce a multiplier effect on investment, especially private investment, and that have a low environmental impact. in addition, in research and development, we have committed ourselves to promoting projects with a strong innovation component. as regards financing, the overall investment package public and private will amount to eur 10 billion per year from now until 2010. private participation will vary from project to project; however, as a general rule, we have planned to finance the projects with 60% public capital and 40% private capital. public investment will thus amount to some eur 6 billion per year from both the union budget and national budgets. this is equivalent to 0.05% of the union's gdp: i think that you will agree that this is a very low price to give a healthy boost to the european economy, a price compatible with the stability and growth pact. what are the steps of this initiative of ours? the first is the european council in december, which will have to decide on its approval. in addition, member states must put into practice the administrative and regulatory reforms which are often the real obstacle to the implementation of these works. this is particularly useful for the involvement of the private sector. i therefore call on the member states to coordinate their national and regional spending plans with the european initiative to maximise the impact of investment. the legislative and work programme for the coming year coincides, ladies and gentlemen, with the major changes for the european union. i 'll just remember the institutional appointments: the official accession of ten new countries on 1 may, the elections in june and the expiry of the commission's mandate on 31 october 2004. the programme i am presenting to you today is intended to complete the achievement of the strategic objectives which this commission has set itself for its mandate. taking account of the special features of the coming year, it comprises 73 new proposals; it seems like a lot, but it's a lot less than in previous years. the proposals respond to the political priorities which were discussed in depth between march and june with parliament and the council in our structured dialogue. the main priority is to shape the future of the enlarged union. it is based on two pillars: ensuring the success of accession and preparing the political ground for the new financial perspective. as regards stability, a neighbourhood policy must be developed to create a ring of friendly countries around europe's borders. the tampere agenda must also be completed by 1 may 2004 in order to complete the project for an area of freedom, security and justice. the third priority - growth - requires an acceleration of the pace towards the lisbon objectives. from an operational point of view, the programme complements the objectives of the new interinstitutional agreement with a view to streamlining legislative work. for example, we have coordinated our proposals with the union's annual and multiannual programming and we are committed to applying the integrated impact assessment procedure to the most important initiatives. in the field of stability and security, we presented a series of proposals to the thessaloniki summit on justice and home affairs and laid the foundations for a new neighbourhood policy. the proposals on economic issues focused on the lisbon strategy, the completion of the internal market, research and transeuropean networks. in this context we must not forget the recent legislative framework for the chemical sector. however, the workload this year has been very heavy and the commission has not been able to achieve all that it had set out to do. for this reason, the 2004 programme takes up some of the initiatives that were left unfinished. i would like to express the appreciation of the whole college for the great cooperation shown by the european parliament in the programming work. structured dialogue has proved to be a good tool, but it can and must be improved. in view of the deadlines that both our institutions will be facing next year, the commission will work closely with parliament to improve our relationship. in particular, we propose that the current dialogue arrangements be replaced by an exchange of views between the conference of committee chairmen and vice-president de palacio in april next year; the commission is proposing to use the written procedure for the mid-term evaluation of the programme and to postpone the presentation of the 2005 programme which will be the responsibility of the next commission until the december 2004 plenary session, in order to coordinate the timetable. finally, we made a first assessment of the internal reform which has modernised financial and personnel management. the serious irregularities in the past management of the union's statistical office, eurostat, have forced us to reflect and investigate further and have led us to propose an action plan, the guidelines of which i now feel it is my duty to explain to you. i apologize for the length of my speech, but this is an important part. i had the opportunity to explain the eurostat question to the conference of presidents on 25 september. i have given my assessment of the facts as they emerged from the investigations carried out by olaf and the numerous work done by the commission services. however, i have acknowledged that certain malfunctions in our communication system, between olaf and the rest of the commission, between the director-general of eurostat and his commissioner of reference, have not enabled the commission to take all the necessary precautionary measures more readily. i have therefore undertaken to present an action plan to remedy the malfunctions. after my intervention, the internal audit service completed its report and presented it to cocobu. it contains no new facts which would call my analysis into question. in short, no one disputes that the most serious events occurred before 1999, that the reorganisation work started in 2000 and that eurostat, the financial control and other sources involved olaf very quickly on the main aspects of this matter. however, the commission was only able to do so from may 2003 onwards, because of certain shortcomings in the communication on the different levels, which i have identified. we moved decisively; we could have moved faster, and that's why we're presenting an action plan. the plan is based on the fundamental principles of the reform, and the key points include the functional independence of olaf, the new financial regulation which entered into force in 2003, the new staff regulations, the provisions on rights and duties and the codes of conduct. all these reforms have been introduced gradually. as i said on 25 september, it would therefore be unfair to judge the reform, its successes and its shortcomings, on the assumption that it was fully operational as from 2000. rather, the years 2000 to 2003 should be considered as a transitional period. however, the eurostat case itself illustrates that the reforms are well founded, especially the mobility for sensitive functions, the separation of those responsible for management and those responsible for control and the establishment of the internal auditor. it is therefore a question of building on what the reforms have achieved and are already bearing fruit. the reforms must be consolidated by strengthening the means available to the political level to assume its political responsibilities. i would like to remind you that, as far as eurostat itself is concerned, we took vigorous measures in the summer of 2003: the replacement of the director-general; the reopening and publication of the positions of operational director internally and externally; the position of director responsible for the resources transferred; the reorganisation of the establishment plan, and so on; finally, the functions of unit heads have been placed in a highly mobile position. in this spirit, i felt it necessary, firstly, to revise the code of conduct between commissioners and their services, which was established in 1999. while maintaining the general principles underlying the 1999 code, in particular the principle of non-interference in management, the commissioner's political responsibility, which includes not only his own activities but also those of the services, should be emphasised more strongly. the revised code of conduct will therefore include a whole series of provisions which reinforce the commissioner's information, allowing him to exercise his responsibilities under optimum conditions, or to supervise the action of his services and give them general guidance, including on financial management. the code will also provide for a specific procedure for the formal involvement of the commissioner by the director-general in any fact or development concerning management which is likely to call into question his or the college's political responsibility. secondly, i would also like to answer another question raised by the eurostat affair. indeed, in various parts of our institution, certain signs, certain elements of information on this matter have emerged before may 2003. these signs, taken one by one, did not allow us to understand the gravity of the situation. if they had been centralised and analysed as a whole, we would not have had to wait for the first detailed information from olaf to take precautionary measures. i have therefore decided to set up a new mechanism to collect and link all information relating to indications of fraud, irregularities or reprehensible acts, to analyse this information and to inform the commission or the commissioner responsible, as appropriate, so as to enable them to take any administrative or financial measures, in particular those to protect the financial interests of the union. i have decided to take political responsibility for this device myself, with the help of neil kinnock and michaele schreyer. our work will be prepared and administered by a group of officials at director-general level, around the secretary-general. this will enable us to ensure better control of information received by olaf, idoc or ias. of course, this is not a matter of carrying out additional investigations or replacing political or administrative officials, who retain responsibility for supervising management and taking appropriate action on information and investigation reports. it is primarily a monitoring and warning device. thirdly, i have decided to strengthen the information circuits between the central and operational services, to strengthen the links, to improve certain practices and to follow up the suggestions mentioned by the auditor in his report. these are essentially technical measures, but i consider them to be very important in order to strengthen the flow of information and the systems of checks and balances, measures which i have already outlined a short while ago at cocobu. at the end of my reflection on the eurostat case, i now come to olaf. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. olaf is a commission service, but it conducts its investigations in complete independence. the office is in control of its own decisions in the exercise of its operational activities, and this is also our wish. however, the legal framework in force remains unclear as to whether or not information is to be communicated to the institutions or to investigations. this proved to be detrimental in the eurostat case. i want to dispel any doubt with this analysis of olaf: i have complete confidence in director brunner. i am analysing the organisation of the institution, not criticising the work of the director, who, in the present context, has acted as he should have done. the commission finds itself in the difficult position of having to assume political and legal responsibility for olaf's work without actually having the means to exercise that responsibility and is legally responsible to olaf in the event of an appeal, especially in the event of any actions for damages that may be brought by private individuals who consider themselves injured parties. i have proposed to parliament that, again in the perspective of a european prosecutor, olaf should be granted autonomy within a clear political framework. that remains my goal. the continuation of the reflection on the complete outsourcing of olaf must remain on our agenda. however, in order to quickly resolve today's operational problems, i would like to propose an immediate step which would provide for an amendment to the olaf regulation, with the aim of its adoption by the current parliament: we must do something to ensure that our successors have a legal framework within which they can work in peace. the olaf monitoring committee and the ongoing work within cocobu in particular the report by mr bösch underline the need to strengthen the regulatory framework; and the commission takes this into account. i now propose the improvements envisaged: first, to strengthen the operational autonomy of olaf by better focusing its activities as necessary, especially in the context of enlargement. to this end, it may be useful to reinstate certain horizontal tasks in the commission services that are not linked to investigations. secondly, the possibility for the office to devote itself to its priorities. to this end, it would be useful to establish a principle of discretion which should be part of the regulation. this would allow olaf to entrust the follow-up of certain cases of minor importance or not falling within the framework of its priority activities to the appropriate bodies, and would also help to increase the speed and effectiveness of investigations. i would point out that any decision to open an investigation or not must remain with olaf. thirdly, the clarification of the flow of information between olaf, the institutions and bodies concerned. this will also require dealing with the issues related to the processing of this information by the institutions concerned. a better balance should be struck between safeguarding the effectiveness of investigations and protecting the financial interests of the union. this will also require clarification of the question of ultimate responsibility for decisions taken. fourthly, the amendments to the regulation also cover the essential aspect of the protection of the rights of the defence. fifthly, in parallel, the governance of olaf will also have to be taken into account, both in terms of strengthening the role and composition of its supervisory committee and in terms of creating an interinstitutional administrative board. in short, i propose that olaf, which will have to cope with a greater workload in an enlarged union, be made more effective by increasing its staffing resources - this is essential in the new union - by focusing on investigative functions and by more appropriate regulation. i also propose that the obligation to report on its activities be strengthened. mr president, these are the basic ideas of the action plan which i propose to launch in response to the questions raised by the eurostat affair. a communication on this will be adopted before the end of the year. as far as the internal measures are concerned, i expect the commission to adopt them as from december. i also hope that our contacts with parliament are sufficiently advanced to bring forward a legislative proposal on olaf which has a reasonable chance of being adopted by this parliament and which will move us towards the idea of a european public prosecutor, which we all continue to support. mr president, i mentioned at the beginning the major events of 2004, to which the intergovernmental conference must of course be added. i shall touch on only one of the known issues on the table today, that of the composition of the commission. there is a lot of talk that a commission with 25 or more members would be impractical, but i would like to say that next year we will test this idea because for six months we will be welcoming colleagues from the new member states and the college will be made up of 30 commissioners. this is of course a transitional situation, in which no new portfolios will be created and which will only last until the end of this mandate: the commission will have 25 commissioners from 1 november 2004. i am convinced that this college of 25 or 30 commissioners can work very well because, firstly, the treaty of nice already guarantees the coherence of an enlarged college and in the next commission the president will have greater powers of organisation, direction and control; secondly, i do not agree that the commission's tasks should be reduced to a dozen portfolios. let us not forget that commissioners are also the face of europe to the public in their home countries, and this will be even more important for the new european citizens. finally, the effectiveness of the commission does not depend on the number of its members but on how resources are used. the reforms we have introduced in recent years have produced good results in this respect. the commission's collegiality and consistency are therefore at the heart of my concerns. an enlarged college certainly presents challenges, but these are not overcome by the proposal for a commission divided into two tiers, giving half the commissioners a role as a compressor. ladies and gentlemen, i have spoken of the near deadlines, but my commission is already looking ahead. at the beginning of this year we launched a broad reflection on the new financial perspective. in 2007, the union could have 28 member states with around half a billion citizens and a new constitutional framework. it is therefore clear that we must start thinking now to get to 2006 with all the instruments ready to work. past experience teaches us that time is running out. in preparing for the future, politics must take precedence because before we do anything, we must decide what we want the overall framework of the union's policies to be. we must keep our eyes on our goals: peace, sustainable development, solidarity and freedom. this means, in particular, working in the following directions: a road map for the lisbon and gothenburg agendas; solidarity between countries and regions to help those who are lagging behind; european citizenship in a space which has become political space; the external dimension of our model and our political choices, starting with the countries that are close to us and with which we must build the circle of friends. it is important that this legislature - the legislature which has concluded enlargement - should help to define the political lines of the project for the enlarged union. in conclusion, mr president, 2004 will be a year of challenges, renewal and commitment. the european elections will be a very important moment to test the degree of participation of citizens in our undertaking. in this context, the commission is aware that it is an important reference point which ensures continuity, stability and dynamism in the system. we are committed to working with the parliament, the council and all the other institutions of the union to win our bet with history. together we can build a union that is bigger, more independent and stronger. mr president, mr president-in-office of the council, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your work. the commissioner said that we were concerned about what we were hearing in part about the deliberations. i can fully confirm that for my group, particularly when it comes to the part which concerns one of the fundamental rights of a parliament in a democracy. the debate is on budgetary law, the royal prerogative of parliaments, which has been the origin and the beginning of all democratic processes, namely the right of parliament - the directly elected representatives of the citizens - to decide on financial resources. this right is being shaken. i admit that not all of us were happy with the outcome of the convention, for we had, of course, expected more. we had hoped for more democratization, to be able to offer citizens more transparency in terms of who is taking what responsibility, where the money comes from and how it is spent. we need more transparency, and the citizens have a right to it! the result of the convention is that we have a financial framework which sets a ceiling and does not allow for an infinite number of expenditure possibilities. in future, this framework will be established by the council with the consent of parliament. that means there's a fixed schedule. the council has the final say on revenue. that hasn't changed. we have criticized that, but it is true. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. this is now being attacked by some member states and also by the finance ministers. what does this mean? it is being said that this parliament is not in a position to decide on expenditure in a fair and informed manner in the interests of the citizens. what image do the representatives of these governments want to give in the next european elections six months from now if they do not trust their own candidates to be able to vote responsibly on expenditure at european level? we have heard the reproach that parliaments cannot handle money. it's happened in all the previous centuries. but we have never heard of a democratically elected government in relation to a democratically elected parliament. this is a novelty, and an intolerable one, if you look at the facts. the budgetary increases, some of which were decided on - by far more than 8% in one area which the council could decide on, namely agricultural expenditure, while the overall budget was to be increased by a maximum of 2.5% - do not speak for the thriftiness of the council, which could decide on its own. look at the council's administrative budget for next year! the council is requesting an increase of 20.8%, more than any other institution, in order to build up and enlarge its administration. we have always respected our limits. we do not need tutorials on how to use the resources which european citizens have put at our disposal in a proper way. we will not give in to any attempt to undermine parliament's basic democratic right to adopt the budget. you will find that no parliamentarian who takes his job seriously can be a part of it. this would be, as mr brok said, a declaration of war on this parliament. i thank the presidency of the council for saying that it intends to uphold the outcome of the convention and to fight for it. i thank all the national governments who are involved. i warn all those who play with the idea of undermining this right that they are exposing themselves to the reproach of not extending, not strengthening, not advancing democracy in europe with the constitution, but undermining and undermining it by wanting to curtail parliament in one of its central rights. i suggest. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the eu-russia summit was one of the most important events of the current six-month period in the field of the union's relations with third countries, because of the strategic importance of the eu-russia relationship. the russian side also attaches similar importance to the summit. initially conceived as a forum for discussion of issues of political dialogue, over the years the summit has become an opportunity for the parties to review and relaunch, at the highest level, the entire sphere of cooperation. the villa madama summit marked the start of the concrete implementation of the st petersburg declaration, which envisages that eu-russia relations will be structured around four common areas to be created in the medium to long term, within the framework of the existing partnership and cooperation agreement. the main objective was to make progress in all common areas, making the best use of existing structures and instruments in order to strengthen the strategic relationship and to make the process of integration of the russian federation into europe prevail. for the european union, the summit was an opportunity to reaffirm in moscow its common commitment to meeting the challenges of the day and to addressing in a coherent way the common responsibilities for protecting the environment on the continent, as well as the exchange of information and cooperation to tackle the problems caused by climate change. the meeting provided an opportunity to discuss with the russian federation current international issues, including crisis situations and the so-called frozen conflicts in the region. the italian presidency nevertheless wanted to maintain its emphasis on the launch of the four spaces and on the positive aspects of eu-russia cooperation, highlighting the important concrete results achieved by the summit: the eu and russia signed a number of agreements, including the joint declaration on the cfsp and cooperation in crisis management, the signing of the europol-russian federation agreement, the start of discussions on visa-free travel, and the renewal of the agreement on scientific and technological cooperation. the russian side shared the approach and the emphasis on the creation of the four spaces. the summit was an opportunity for president putin to consolidate, at a delicate moment in domestic politics - parliamentary elections in december and presidential elections in march 2004 - the path towards a gradual rapprochement between the russian federation and the european union. president putin reiterated the need to establish the permanent partnership council to this end, so that within its framework and its formats those responsible for key areas of cooperation could meet and cooperate. in a tactical sense, president putin raised moscow's concerns about the short and medium-term consequences of enlargement on economic, commercial and political relations between the federation and the countries of the former soviet bloc, with a view to extending the partnership and cooperation agreement to the new member states. we firmly reiterated to president putin that the extension of the partnership and cooperation agreement is an obligation which the russian federation must fulfil within the prescribed time-limits and an indispensable condition for the strengthening of relations with europe at 25. the question of progress in the negotiations for the accession of the russian federation to the wto was raised, for which, despite the presence of important negotiating nodes, both sides agreed to the expectation that it would take place by 2004. the european and russian sides also raised the prospect of exemption from the current visa regime, and welcomed the start of a dialogue on preconditions and the implementation of facilitations in the current visa regime, on a bilateral basis and, of course, on the basis of reciprocity. the summit was marked by the signing of two agreements: the renewal of the agreement on scientific and technological cooperation and the europol-russia agreement on the exchange of strategic analysis and cooperation in the training of police forces is a tangible expression of the russian federation's willingness to cooperate with the european union in the field of justice and home affairs. the italian presidency, in constant contact with the commission and the secretariat, paid particular attention to the preparation of this event: the european union troika met with russian foreign minister ivanov on 28 october and several meetings at senior official level between the italian presidency and the russian federation were held on this subject. in particular, a twofold order of difficulties had to be overcome: on the one hand, russia's high expectations for a qualitative leap forward in its relations with the european union; on the other hand, a more rigid position than that of a majority of member states, which attributes to moscow insufficient commitment to implementing in practice what has been agreed in political declarations. the joint declaration, precisely because it is a joint declaration and therefore the result of a compromise, was finalised in the course of laborious negotiations between the russian federation, on the one hand, and the presidency, commission and secretariat, on the other, and was issued at the end of the summit. it is therefore the result of a conciliation of conflicting needs and constitutes a delicate compromise between the requests of many member states, who wanted explicit references to all the controversial issues, and the russian request for a very succinct statement, which merely highlighted the positive aspects of the cooperation. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, before reviewing the individual elements of the summit, i should like to make it clear that all the issues on the agenda were extensively discussed in our talks with president putin. this also applies to the situation in chechnya, the question of the non-ratification of the kyoto protocol, the problem of moldova and transnistria and the implications of the judicial developments involving the yukos group. in particular, as regards chechnya, i would like to point out that not only was the question raised at the initiative of the president of the council of the european union, but that a great deal of time was devoted to the discussion of this point during the plenary session. if the final declaration of the summit does not contain a reference to this subject, it is because of the considerations i made earlier about the fact that this was a proposal shared and agreed upon, and therefore the result of mediation. the commission, the high representative, ms solana, and the presidency agreed that the reference to the joint declaration was the acceptable product. so these are the reasons. on internal developments in russia, president putin described the internal political and economic situation also in the perspective of the parliamentary elections in december and the presidential elections in march, as well as in the light of the events connected with the yukos affair. he stressed that russia was determined to continue privatisation, the building of an independent judiciary and the strengthening of public institutions. we have indicated that we will be following the yukos affair closely, but without any intention to interfere in russia's internal affairs, because we have confidence that the judicial system will act in accordance with the law and in full transparency, and that it will give full assurance to the international community and to the markets that the reforms under way will not be hindered and that the principles of the market economy will continue to be pursued. at the presidency's explicit request, he outlined moscow's efforts to launch a process of political and institutional reconstruction in chechnya, through the referendum, amnesty and elections, and invited european representatives to visit the region. for our part, we have expressed our solidarity with the fight against chechen terrorism and our support for constitutional reform which will involve ever wider segments of the chechen population, who are not compromised by terrorism. we renewed our call for all possible efforts to be made to hasten the release of the msf representative arjan erkel, who was abducted in the caucasus in august 2002, and for the opening of an echo office in the area. president putin has suggested that it be opened in chechnya itself, for whose security he has himself undertaken to provide guarantees. on the common economic area, i would like to recall that the summit agreed on a strategy which we hope will enable us in the coming years to increase the level of interdependence between our economies, and for which we should now define the appropriate venue for operational follow-up, including by extending the mandate of the high level group. the summit supported russia's aspiration to join the wto by the end of 2004, although it was aware of the considerable difficulties on issues such as energy, aviation and insurance which are still on the eu-russia agenda. the energy dialogue will continue, encouraging progress in reforming the sector in russia, despite russia's difficulties in meeting european demands and wto requirements, in particular with regard to domestic prices and privatisation of the sector. the european side also stressed the need for russia's early ratification of the kyoto protocol and the expectations for a certain russian commitment to develop more advanced cooperation on maritime environmental safety. in the context of the common area of freedom, security and justice, i would like to draw your attention to the signing of the agreement between europol and the russian ministry of the interior: the commission has also adopted a communication on the implementation of the action plan against organised crime. in the same context, we also noted with satisfaction the launch of a technical dialogue on the issue of visa liberalisation; we noted the willingness of both parties to introduce visa facilitation measures for permanent residents and stressed the importance of a swift conclusion of the readmission agreement. the meeting allowed the european union to confirm its conviction that internal security is complementary to justice and respect for human rights and that the strategic partnership between the european union and russia is always based on shared values such as democracy, the rule of law, human rights, freedom of expression. in the context of the common external security area, the joint declaration on cooperation in crisis management is an important signal of the willingness of the european union and the russian federation to work together in an area of vital interest to europe. i believe that this too should be recorded as a positive outcome of the rome summit in the context of the establishment of the common external security area. the russian proposal for enhanced cooperation in the field of civil protection and natural disaster management will be further explored and translated as soon as possible into agreements allowing the union and russia to cooperate to enhance the joint response to future emergencies. a first step could be to establish direct contact between the relevant bodies in brussels and moscow. similar cooperation will be deepened in the context of the relevant multilateral bodies in the field of weapons of mass destruction. in the area of research and education, the summit opened a new chapter of bilateral cooperation, with the russian federation joining the bologna process, the intergovernmental cooperation mechanism that promotes agreements in the field of recognition of qualifications and harmonisation of university curricula, and paving the way for effective forms of intergovernmental cooperation in the field of harmonisation of qualifications, the first step towards the creation of a common space for university teaching. the renewal of the agreement on scientific and technological cooperation will also allow russia to participate in european programmes in this field. finally, the question of the functioning of the permanent partnership council was examined in depth with the aim of finding a solution, inspired by the principles of effectiveness and flexibility, which reconciles the russian side's desire for a more in-depth and articulated dialogue on all issues of common interest with the principle of the autonomy of the union's decision-making processes. i hope that on this basis it will soon be possible to define an understanding which will enable the permanent partnership council to be set up. as regards international issues, in addition to the traditional topical issues - iran, iraq, the middle east - on which there was a substantial homogeneity of views and intentions, we particularly touched on the situation in moldova due to the imminent expiry of certain commitments relating to the transnistrian crisis in which the russian federation has a key role: the european council welcomes the progress made in the negotiations with the five-party talks and the work of the constitutional committee responsible for defining the new form of the moldovan state. we believe that russia must fulfil this commitment in a timely manner and without delay. the russian side confirmed its commitment to withdrawal, but recognised that, as the negotiations had made little progress in resolving the crisis, further efforts would be needed. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, in conclusion i think i can say that the southern neighbours' which sets out the new set of neighbourhood policies that the enlarged european union should pursue towards the countries on its direct land and sea borders. this is the new concept of the 'ring of friends' with which the union is basically offering to share 'everything but the institutions'. the communication also describes possible measures to be offered to neighbouring countries to encourage them to adopt and implement the reforms necessary to benefit from access to the eu's internal market. the new neighbourhood policy will be implemented through national and/or regional implementation plans, adopted by the council on the basis of a commission proposal. they should contain specific objectives and benchmarks, as well as a pre-established implementation timetable for the progressive implementation of the measures for participation in the internal market, which will allow the union to assess on a regular basis the actual implementation of these measures, through a mechanism of constant monitoring and verification of the conditionality and progress made by each country towards the objectives set by the new policy and the effectiveness of the community instruments. in the future, these action plans could become the main policy documents of the union's external relations with these countries, possibly replacing the common strategies launched so far. on the basis of the work done by the commission and the council, which the rapporteur has mentioned, i would remind you that the last part of 2003 will be devoted to the preparation of the action plans. exploratory consultations with the countries concerned will take place in january and february 2004, on the basis of which the commission will finalise, by spring 2004, the draft action plans for ukraine, moldova, morocco, tunisia, jordan and israel, to be submitted to the council. the action plans, which will be the subject of consultations with third countries, will comprise five elements: enhanced political cooperation; the internal market; gha cooperation; communication networks and the environment; measures to facilitate contacts between peoples. finally, i would point on eu-canada relations. as the chairman's statement observed, the eu and canada agreed at last year's ottawa summit, to undertake a comprehensive review of the bilateral relationship during 2003 and to report back to the december summit this year. the commission is working hard, alongside the presidency and with our canadian counterparts, to finalise a joint report to go to the summit. this report will take up many of the themes developed by the commission, council and parliament in their contributions to the review. a driving force behind the review is the changing nature of the eu-canada relationship. given the changing nature of the european union itself, canada was the first industrialised third country to enter into a formal relationship with the european economic community in 1976. as a result, the eu-canada relationship has tended to focus on trade and economic issues. however, canada and the eu's common interests extend far beyond the commercial arena. we share similar social models and global interests. canada, like the european union, is a staunch advocate of the united nations, the multilateral system and the international rule of law. by way of example, canada voted with the european union 96% of the time during the current un general assembly, on those occasions when the european union had a common position. we want to find ways of working together more systematically in the field of security and foreign policy so that we can be more effective in carrying forward those policies where our objectives coincide. we also want to improve our dialogue in other policy areas where we often share common values and face similar challenges. these areas include education and culture, the environment and justice and home affairs. we have also maintained our focus on the very important economic relationship that exists between canada and the european union. the eu is canada's second most important trading partner after the united states. we are the second source of foreign investment in canada. in parallel with our comprehensive review of all aspects of eu-canada relations, we have also been developing the framework for a new type of bilateral trade and investment agreement, with the aim of facilitating trade and investment flows between the eu and canada. commissioner lamy and the canadian trade minister, mr pettigrew, will report to the december summit on the results of their analysis into the potential scope of such an agreement. we expect talks to begin immediately in 2004. the european commission believes that an intensified dialogue between european and canadian parliamentarians is essential to maintain the good health of our relationship. the commission is grateful for the work of parliament's canada delegation and hopes that other members and committees, working on specific policy areas, will also give consideration to increasing contact with their canadian counterparts. the relationship between the eu and canada is very healthy. the european commission is resolved to do all it can to keep it that way. we want the summit to lift this relationship to a new plateau, at a challenging time for the international community and in preparation for major changes taking place in canada and within the european union in the coming month.

president of the commission. mr president, mr antonioni, ladies and gentlemen, the next european council in brussels will be the last of an eventful year. we are faced with developments and decisions of major importance for our future, now on a weekly basis. last week was no exception. before we move on to the debate on the constitution, i would like to touch briefly on another topical issue for the life of the union. the next european council will be preceded, as mr antonione said, by an extraordinary meeting of the tripartite social summit, attended by the heads of state of the troika and the representatives of the social partners and the commission. it is absolutely essential to involve the social partners at this stage of the constitutional process, and it is essential to listen to their voices. the involvement of trade unions and employers is the best guarantee of success for any employment initiative. the meeting will address two themes that are at the heart of the lisbon strategy, namely our growth initiative and the employment strategy. the key moment will be the presentation of the report of the task force on employment by wim kok. the report shows how to deal with the major changes in the economy and the world of work. among its key points is the need to increase the adaptability of enterprises and workers, to increase investment in human capital and, finally, to create new social dynamics to support reforms and accelerate their implementation. the commission will take account of the task force report and the recommendations contained therein in preparing the employment report to be presented to the council in spring next year. mr president, i now come to the central theme of my speech, namely the intergovernmental conference, which is entering its final stages and which mr antonioni has already spoken of with great balance and great convergence. the stakes will be high at the european council in brussels on 12 and 13 december. the decisions to be taken will show the fruits of the new convention method proposed by the european parliament and the commission and approved by the laeken european council in december 2001. a return to the method of negotiation between governments, which we experienced in the night of nice, would be a political failure for the union. public opinion would no longer accept it. the key issue for the intergovernmental conference now is how the union can achieve its objectives and strengthen its decision-making capacity. the european union is faced with three major challenges: firstly, we need strong policies and greater coordination at european level for economic growth and job creation and social protection. secondly, we must respond together to the international challenges of security, freedom and justice. thirdly, we must join forces to meet global responsibilities and to promote our values and interests in the world. article 3 of the draft constitution solemnly states the objectives of the union along these lines. the convention has clearly not produced a perfect constitution to meet these tasks. however, the result corresponds, perhaps even more than expected, to the aims of the laeken declaration. the intergovernmental conference has obviously been more concerned with internal disputes between member states than with creating instruments adapted to the problems and needs of europe. it is certainly disappointing that no progress has been made in adopting a procedure that would make it possible to amend the policy part of the constitution. the commission will support any efforts which the presidency makes to achieve this objective. in view of the new challenges that will emerge, the constitution cannot and must not become a constraint on our future action. the only significant progress so far in relation to the work of the convention has been in the definition of structured cooperation in the field of defence. on all other issues, there is still a risk that the igc will take a step backwards in the direction of the intergovernmental method. this also applies to european cooperation on criminal law, at a time when all the leaders are recognizing the threat of international crime and terrorism. there are also those who want to undermine the credibility of the foreign minister, as mr antonione has rightly said, by always maintaining, in words, that europe must become stronger and play a leading role in the world. some ministers argue that extending the intergovernmental system means strengthening economic policy coordination, while what is needed is to strengthen europe's capacity to put economic governance at the service of the growth strategy. some countries are even proposing the reintroduction of the right of veto where the convention has already abolished it, for example in the area of trade policy. the choice is therefore clearly between these two options: or a divided europe that acts as a spectator on the world political stage, or a united europe that contributes to peace, growth and sustainable development. with these backward choices, europe risks becoming a continent on the fringes of the world map, surrounded by other powerful players. the draft constitution, in its present form, provides the instruments which enable a united europe to operate more effectively. there's nothing less than this and nothing more than this. it does not create a political project for the future. the central issue facing national leaders at the igc summit is not therefore to commit themselves to an ambitious european political project. the real question is whether they will find the collective capacity to adopt the necessary instruments in the future to undertake any european project. the convention has maintained and improved the balance of power between the various institutions of the union. a strong commission is essential to ensure the impartial application of eu rules, and so the commission's powers in crucial areas such as state aid control must not be curtailed at the last minute. our aspiration to become a true union of peoples and states is expressed in the proposed system of double majority voting for council decisions. democratic legitimacy has been increased by strengthening the role of the european parliament on legislative, political and budgetary matters, and the power of the court of justice to uphold the rule of law has been partly strengthened. one thing is clear, ladies and gentlemen: the commission will resist until the last minute of the intergovernmental conference any attempt to reduce the powers of the european parliament, especially on budgetary matters. (applause) i would like to thank how can the european parliament and the commission be expected to explain and defend to the citizens a constitution which parliament itself has rejected? that's not explainable. as far as the commission is concerned, we note with satisfaction that the presidency has recognised that the distinction between commissioners with and without voting rights is too complex and, above all, would not work. there is a simple solution which maintains equality between all the commissioners, namely a commission composed of one commissioner from each member state, with a more decentralised decision-making structure and a system of checks and balances which ensures its absolute collegiality. this is the solution the commission wants to see in the constitution. finally, the double majority voting system proposed by the convention - 50 per cent of the states representing 60 per cent of the population - is simple and fair. if you want to change, you have to go in the direction of making the college's decision-making system easier. the commission obviously still prefers a system based on 50 per cent of the member states representing at least 50 per cent of the population. in no case can the intergovernmental conference decide on a voting system which makes the council's decisionmaking system even more difficult than the one that came out of nice. a constitution worse than nice is simply indefensible. we must also avoid last-minute bargaining at all costs, which would only undermine the credibility of the constitution before it is even in place. we must not forget that the first referendum on the constitution will take place just six months after the conclusion of the intergovernmental conference. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, before usefulness and value of the treaty and the pact depend on the certainty of the rules which all - the commission, parliament, council and member states - must respect. there is a seriousness to this read the council's final declaration as a signal of a stronger and more determined commitment to growth and stability, and will also understand that the rules must be applied in an orderly manner. we will continue to do our duty by applying the treaty and the rules of the covenant. it is our responsibility, especially at this stage, to ensure that all member states are treated equally. i would i suggest. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i thank you for inviting me to discuss the stability and growth pact with you at this part-session. let me begin by recounting the events that led to the eurogroup and ecofin on 24 and 25 november last. in the first half of 2003, on a proposal from the commission, the council addressed two recommendations on excessive deficits to germany on 21 january and to france on 3 june, respectively, aimed at reducing deficits below the 3% reference value by 2004. it should be noted that the recommendations were adopted on the basis of the economic assumption of gradual growth during the year as a result of the exhaustion of the negative effects of the end of the war in iraq. in the months that followed, however, a different, more negative than expected, real trend in the european economy was evident. economic growth, which was about one percentage point below expectations, led to government deficits growing beyond expectations. this has meant that germany and france have been unable to bring their deficits below 3% in 2004, as originally requested. in the second half of 2003, between october and november, the commission fully and formally recognised this new situation and consequently proposed two new recommendations with the aim of postponing the fall in deficits below 3% to 2005. in essence, it is reasonable to assume that if the negative performance of the euro area economy had been known as early as 2003, the recommendations would have explicitly identified 2005 as the year of return from the outset. on this basis, both germany and france have taken steps to implement the substance of the recommendations. in germany, the recommendations were transposed directly into the budget law: a structural correction of 0.6% of gross domestic product is foreseen for 2004 and a correction of 0.5% for 2005, i.e. a total of 1.1% of gross domestic product, which is close to the commission's initial request, with the decline to below 3% in 2005 remaining unchanged. in france, the recommendations were first implemented in the budget law and then in other measures: a correction of 0.8% of gross domestic product is foreseen for 2004 and a correction of 0.6% for 2005, i.e. a total of 1.4% of gross domestic product, which is close to what the commission has requested, with the decline of below 3% in 2005 remaining unchanged. in addition, france and germany have committed themselves to allocating any effects of higher growth to deficit reduction, as requested by the commission. in addition, it should be noted that france and germany embarked on an intensive cycle of welfare reforms in 2003, with a decisive positive impact on the sustainability of public finances. this is a non-marginal element in the political economy of the discussion on the pact that has developed over the course of this year. in substance, first in the work done in october and november, then in the eurogroup and finally in ecofin, a broad consensus was reached on the substance of the commission's recommendations and on the substance of the corrections imposed by france and germany. let's get down to business. the commission proposed its recommendations under article 104 (9) on the assumption that germany and france continued to ignore the council's recommendations. germany and france, while accepting the substance of the recommendations, for political reasons requested a different form, namely the rewording of the second set of ex-article 104 (7) recommendations. the council's legal service, when asked about this matter, stated that the commission could have taken the other way, and i would also stress this second way. the commission has ruled it out. at this point, a deadlock has been reached: for the sake of form, the most important thing was lost, the substance. to overcome the impasse without radicalizing dissent, the eurogroup, on the basis of a broad consensus, transposed the substance of the recommendations into a draft conclusions. the validity of this procedure has been reaffirmed by the council's legal service. subsequently, when the work of ecofin began, the commission made its disagreement explicit, calling for a vote on the second set of recommendations for germany and france. the vote did not produce the necessary majority. it should be noted that the ecofin council's vote on the commission's recommendations is expressly provided for in the rules in force and is therefore perfectly compatible with those rules. following the failure to approve the commission's recommendations, the council voted on the conclusions drawn up earlier in the eurogroup. the council voted in favour of the conclusions and the debate was structured to reach a unanimous vote on a council statement. the content of the declaration can be summarised as follows: stability and growth are the fundamental objectives of european economic policy. the pact is an essential element in the implementation of this policy. it was said: the pact is stupid. we have shown the opposite, we have shown that the covenant can be interpreted in a flexible and intelligent way. the implementation of the pact can be achieved by adjusting budgetary discipline even more rationally to positive or negative economic cycles and by pushing for structural reforms aimed at developing growth potential. in these terms, the letter and spirit of the covenant are not dead; we have worked, we are working and we will work within the framework of the pact and with the support of the commission, in a cooperative and consensual logic. in conclusion, i should like to point out that so far we have talked a great deal about procedure and little about economics. the growth strategy calls for the compact to incorporate economic cycles and structural reforms: this is necessary, but it is not enough. six months ago, at the beginning of this semester, we presented an action plan for growth in this parliament. the support that this parliament has given to the plan has been decisive and now the plan must be implemented. other development initiatives must follow. the commission, governments and markets have a role to play in the growth strategy, but the european parliament must also play a decisive role in driving it forward: in fact, economic policy is either political or it is not.
the commission (es) mr president, in recent months there have been a number of developments in the implementation of the stability and growth pact, which have led to a major institutional crisis. such developments are clear evidence that we need to strengthen economic governance in the union. the origin of the difficulties lies in the fact that germany and france are experiencing serious fiscal problems, which can be summarised as follows: their deficits are excessive, and this is due not only to cyclical circumstances; these high deficits can have perverse effects in the long term because they threaten the sustainability of public finances by causing an increase in debt levels; they also have negative repercussions on potential growth by affecting the expectations of economic agents. in this context, and with a view to reducing the high deficits of both countries, and applying the rules laid down in the treaty, the council sent a first set of recommendations to germany and france at the beginning of the year, calling on them to take measures to correct the excessive deficit by the end of 2004 at the latest. however, in the second half of this year it became clear that the measures taken by both countries would not be sufficient to correct the excessive deficit in the coming year. the commission has therefore applied the procedures provided for in the treaty by presenting new recommendations which include a balanced consideration of the current circumstances. as you know, a minority of member states have refused to accept the commission's proposals in the council and, in an unprecedented step, have reached agreement by majority vote outside the treaty. the implications of the agreement in the form of 'council conclusions' are far-reaching and go far beyond the mere application of the pact to france and germany. the commission deeply regrets that the council has not followed the spirit and the letter of the treaty and the stability and growth pact, which were agreed unanimously. we believe that only a rules-based system can guarantee the fulfilment of commitments and equal treatment for all member states. we must be aware that the council's decisions will make it difficult to apply the treaty rigorously. procedures relating to other countries will be affected. it will be very difficult for the council to take formal decisions under the excessive deficit procedure, including the possibility of issuing precautionary warnings. opinions on stability and convergence programmes may be weakened if the council does not accept a rigorous multilateral surveillance procedure. as regards the new member states, strict application of the convergence criteria could be made more difficult, since the euro countries are allowed, without applying the treaty and the pact procedures, to maintain deficits above 3% for several consecutive years. the political agreement reached in the council implies the implementation of intergovernmental agreements for the management of our currency and sets a dangerous precedent for the future. the court of justice will probably have to clarify whether governments have the power to create new procedures, de facto replacing an existing community framework in the treaty, for certain aspects of economic policies. however, we must bear in mind that the council statement at the end of the ecofin council shows that the member states understand the need for a commitment to growth and stability and the need to apply the rules systematically. in any event, the commission will continue to apply the treaty and the provisions of the pact. this will allow all member states to be treated on an equal footing and ensure sound public finances in the union. the commission shall ensure that the procedures are applied in an appropriate and non-partisan manner. at the same time, we need to strengthen economic governance in the union in order to ensure the proper functioning of our single market with a single currency. we believe that the decisions taken at ecofin show that the real problem to be solved is the weakness of the current system of economic governance at european level. in order to tackle this problem, and after careful reflection, the commission will prepare an initiative on better economic governance in the union. but this reflection will not start from scratch, but will follow the path already taken by the commission in the past. in line with the november 2002 communication on strengthening the coordination of budgetary policies, it seems necessary to examine how to combine better discipline and flexibility while ensuring better compliance with the rules. we believe that, among other things, greater emphasis should be placed on sustainability and debt, differentiation between country-specific situations should be allowed, and symmetry should be increased throughout the cycle, with particular rigor in the boom years. the commission will also carry out multilateral surveillance more effectively, using all the possibilities to make public its views on economic and budgetary policies. the budget debate needs to be framed in the general context of the currently low growth potential of the european economy. in this respect, we must pay more attention to the quality of public finances without compromising long-term stability or sustainability. this means placing the debate on budgetary policy more prominently in the context of economic policy coordination, giving a greater role to economic policy guidelines and their implementation in ensuring the smooth functioning of economic and monetary union and the achievement of the lisbon objectives. in this process, the active contribution of parliament will be essential. had. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council and parliament, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. i had the opportunity to give a detailed account of the observations and conclusions contained in our report. i would like to draw your attention today to the conclusions concerning three areas: the declaration of assurance, budgetary management, and the commission's reform process. the first chapter of the court's report contains the statement of assurance (saa) which will be published in the official journal together with the consolidated accounts of the community. it is a good practice that will bring more transparency. the court is adapting its das methodology to suit the commission's financial control reform process. we intend, as the council and parliament have been asking, to provide more precise information on the location and origin of the deficiencies found. to this end, our observations and conclusions are supported by four main elements. firstly, the quality of the control systems of the community institutions and the member states. we have made our assessment based on several indicators. we have also examined the extent to which the commission has followed up our previous comments. the second support element has been the examination of a sample of commitments and payments in each area of expenditure. thirdly, the annual declarations of the directors-general of the commission have been examined. and fourthly, the work done by other auditors has been examined. as a result of this audit work, the court considers that the 2002 annual accounts presented by the commission have been drawn up in accordance with the financial regulation. the accounts shall give a true and fair view of the revenue and expenditure for the financial year and of the financial situation of the community. however, as in previous years, the court has made a number of reservations concerning the commission's accounting system. it should be noted that the commission adopted an action plan for the modernisation of accounting in december last year, which is expected to be operational in 2005. i think we should be a little cautious about the timing, because too much haste should not jeopardise the scope and quality of the necessary reforms. the court considered that the transactions were legal and regular, although checks should be strengthened in the latter case. in the case of the eaggf guarantee section, we consider that the number of erroneous operations is still too high. the most frequent errors are made at the level of the final beneficiary of the aid. we have identified a higher risk in those measures not managed by the ims, such as production aid, rural development and export refunds. the court noted an improvement in the controls on structural operations, particularly at commission level. however, the errors are similar to those of previous years and are mainly due to management by the member states. as you can see, the court's report presents a mixed picture. to improve it, it will be necessary to further strengthen the management systems of the commission and the member states; this is the basic requirement for achieving a fully satisfactory declaration of reliability in the future. let us now turn to the remarks on budgetary management contained in chapter 2 of the report. firstly, there is a rapid change in the income structure. compared with the previous year, traditional own resources (duties, agricultural levies, etc.) fell by 23%, while revenue from gnp increased by 32%. secondly, we note that the budget surplus has been reduced significantly, from eur 15 000 million to eur 7 000 million. the figure remains high and indicates the existence of systematic problems which need to be corrected. one of the main causes of the surplus is the difference between planned and actual expenditure. in 2002 member states overestimated expenditure on the structural funds by almost eur 5 billion. as a result, this item ended the year with over eur 66 billion in commitments pending settlement (the 'rals'), almost eur 10 billion more than in the previous year. the commission should adopt a more active policy and make budgetary adjustments to keep the revenue and expenditure forecasts in balance. the overall improvement in the rate of payments is a positive aspect. a notable exception is the rural development programme in the candidate countries - sapard - which after three years of operation has transferred only 2% of the available funds to final beneficiaries. finally, i would like to point out that, following the court's recommendations, the commission has improved its report on budgetary and financial management. this report will be of great use throughout the budgetary cycle. in connection with the budgetary management of the european development funds, the commission has accelerated the decision-making process for financing programmes. however, the pace of implementation remains slow: at the end of 2002, the available balance was almost eur 3 billion and commitments still to be settled amounted to more than eur 8 billion. the court considers that the integration of the edf into the general budget could contribute to improving management. let us now turn to the state of administrative reform. the court has paid particular attention to the extent to which internal control standards have been introduced. the balance is balanced. despite progress in all directorates-general, standards were still not fully up to par at the end of 2002. achieving these levels rapidly must be a matter of priority. one of the main difficulties facing the commission is the control of operations carried out under shared management with the member states (mainly the eaggf guarantee section and the structural funds). although article 274 of the treaty confers on the commission full responsibility for management, in practice the commission is bound by the action of the national administrations. improving the management of european funds requires more rigorous control by the member states. the activity management plans of the directorates-general have been improved. however, it would be advisable to specify the objectives and to introduce indicators to measure and compare results. the activity reports and the statements by the directors-general have also shown progress. most of the measures announced by the commission following the synthesis of the 2001 reports have been implemented. in accordance with the recommendations made by the court, the commission has improved the reporting procedure. however, directors-general should define more precisely the content of their reservations about the functioning of the controls and describe better the deficiencies found. finally, in the interests of greater transparency and to facilitate the monitoring of the reform, the court recommends updating the 2000 white paper and revising the planned timetable. in conclusion, the reform has made progress during 2002. the commission has been able to apply the new provisions of the financial regulation diligently and progress has been made in all areas. but as the commission itself acknowledges, much remains to be done. i think the commission's reform plan is sufficiently comprehensive and coherent. the plan will undoubtedly require adaptations and adjustments, but at this point it would be a mistake to scrap it or launch a risky "reform of the reform". the plan already contains the appropriate measures to improve management and control, now it is a matter of making a sustained effort to ensure that these measures are applied with determination in all the commission services. this is the main responsibility of the commission - and of all the institutions - to launch plans is not enough, we must ensure that they are put into practice. in my view, this is one of the lessons of the eurostat case. before i conclude my speech, i would like to take a few words off the agenda. i would like to refer to the intergovernmental conference and the draft european constitution. the court expressed
