position at the end of the year. the commission's budgetary authority is the european parliament, and the council is the european parliament. the court's observations on the 2002 financial statement also show that the european union's claims and liabilities are not fixed but change with the tasks. i mention the example of participation in galileo, which is not only a technological challenge but also a challenge for auditing and financial statements. the court of auditors also issues a positive statement of assurance on revenue, examining both the collection of customs duties and the calculation of european union vat revenue and national contributions on the basis of gross national income. this is the figure given by the member states, not by eurostat, as has been misrepresented in various ways in connection with the eurostat affair. while the court confirms the reliability of commitment appropriations and administrative expenditure, it does not do so for other expenditure. this clearly shows where further emphasis needs to be placed on improving financial management both at the commission level and in the member states. i note that the court acknowledges the increased controls by the commission and stresses the difficulties of shared management, which affects 80% of expenditure. for example, in the case of the agricultural budget, the court found that, in its examination of 64 paying agencies, three could not be certified as reliable because of the absolute high error rate. this was a payment institution in portugal and the other two payment institutions are in germany, namely in baden-württemberg and bavaria. in the case of the structural funds, the court again criticised the fact that, in the event of foreseeable under-utilisation of payment appropriations, the surplus should not be returned to the member states until the following year but should be included in a supplementary budget for the current year. this year we have taken up this criticism and presented a supplementary budget of 5 billion euros, which will probably be adopted in this house on 18 december. the annual discussions on the financial management of the union may give the impression that nothing is progressing. it is the court of auditors which is emphasising the fundamental and comprehensive nature of the commission's financial reform, as the court had called for. the key point is that financial management is finally adjusting to the reality of a budget that will be close to €100 billion next year, with over one million payments per year, managed by 35 dgs, 15 member states - soon 25 member states - international organisations and ngos. the responsibility for ex ante control of financial transactions has been shifted to the operational services and any attempt to reverse this - whether by requiring ex ante controls by the accounting officer - bypasses the requirements of modern public financial management. the abolition of central budgetary control, which could only make limited samples, did not reduce the intensity of control. the new financial circuits in the directorates-general, with the mandatory inclusion of trained financial experts in each service, the ex-post controls by the auditors in each directorate-general - all of which are reinforced by increased human resources in this area and by an unprecedented effort in training and continuing training in the field of control - create the conditions for each director-general to report regularly to the commission on financial management. if we take account of the internal audit service's audits, the regular evaluation of the analysis of the control systems by the central financial service, the investigations by olaf and, of course, the ever more extensive audits by the commission's external auditor, the court of auditors, this gives a comprehensive control architecture for the european budget, to which the controls in the member states are added for 80% of the budget. according to the member states, 16 000 persons are responsible for monitoring the agricultural funds and 6 700 for the structural funds. i agree with the court of auditors that we need to achieve a stronger coordination here in order to make these checks efficient. controls require clear rules. the entry into force of a new, completely renewed financial regulation on 1 january has created the conditions for this. the way in which this has been done can be seen in the example of financial grants to institutions. until the commission's first vademecum of 1999, there was no framework for this central instrument of community spending. the new financial regulation and secondary legislation now provide for this in detail and in a binding manner, and the necessary new legislation for these subsidies will soon be adopted in this house. the commission has also been asked to provide a report on the implementation of the budget, which is a very important one. the procedure for drawing up the annual reports of the directors-general has been improved considerably, in particular to improve comparability. the implementation of the internal control standards just mentioned by the president of the court of auditors, which he rightly described as the main and cornerstones of the reform, is now being pushed forward once again, particularly with regard to the rotation of officials in sensitive positions and, where this has not yet been done, precise deadlines are being set. we are learning from the experience of eurostat. first of all, of course, in eurostat itself, but also in relation to the relationship between the directorates-general and the political level and in relation to olaf. the incidents at eurostat in the years up to 1999 are not proof that the reform has failed - no, they are proof that the reform was necessary and that we took the right measures. where there were gaps and gaps became apparent, we close them. let me emphasize again the scope of the reform. it means that this international authority will finally introduce uniform rules and standards for all areas of management. this is a cultural revolution, because before that, different cultures had very different, mostly unwritten rules. in the future, to quote mr fabra vallés, there will be no more "principals" but an administration which must and will meet high and verifiable standards in all areas. the presentation of the court of auditors' annual report is the beginning of the discharge procedure. the commission hopes to have a good working relationship with the rapporteur, mr bayona de perogordo, and with the committee on budgetary control as a whole. ladies and gentlemen, a public budget which is predominantly subsidized and which is in 15 member states today, and in 25 tomorrow, will always have to fight to protect its financial interests. the commission is committed to this objective and we will not be discouraged by the setbacks but on the contrary will intensify our efforts and we see ourselves encouraged by the european court of auditors in this direction. commission. mr president, in 1977, the council adopted the sixth vat directive. it was a tremendous step towards the effective removal of restrictions on the movement of persons, goods, services and capital and the integration of national economies. for the first time, the community had a harmonised base of taxation and a harmonised list of exempted goods and services. among them, the community legislator, in 1977, included those supplied by the public postal services. this exemption dates from a time where in most member states, the post office was a branch of the government with a monopoly on postal services. at the time, the post office undoubtedly was a public postal service and the exemption of its services caused no distortion of competition because no competition was possible. these facts no longer hold true. in most member states, the post office is no longer a branch of the government, but a commercial enterprise operating under commercial law. in some cases its shares are sold on the stock markets. some member states already apply vat to post, or to some or all services provided by the universal service provider, recognising the problems caused by an outdated exemption. some of these companies are now expanding their operations to other member states in order to reap the benefits of the internal market just like other third-country postal operators are doing. consumers now demand services that only companies with a presence in several european markets can provide. but, under current rules, a company which supplies exempt postal services in member state a is obliged to charge vat in member state b, because that country does not recognise it as a public postal service. the postal market is now largely liberalised. although, as is often the case, post liberalisation advances at a different pace in each member state, in all of them - in great measure due to the approval of directive 97/67/ec, operators other than the former monopolies can and do operate. since several operators provide postal services and vat legislation does not treat them equally, distortion of competition inevitably occurs. a vat exemption is not an unmixed blessing. notably, it results in an inability to deduct input vat, which in turn discourages investment. at a time where competition exists in the postal market and the communications revolution has created new channels that to some extent compete with post, lower rates of investment put public operators at risk. as is often the case with european tax legislation, the vat directive has lagged behind all these changes and now requires urgent changes since it no longer reflects the needs or the factual situation in the community. under article 93 of the treaty, provisions concerning vat must be adopted to the extent that harmonisation is necessary to ensure the establishment and the functioning of the internal market. the commission, in presenting its proposal, is fulfilling its obligations under the treaty. it has done so after extensive consultation with universal postal services and other postal operators, as well as representatives of postal consumers. it has taken into account their opinions, in particular, those of private customers and charities by proposing that a reduced rate be applied to those services such as letterpost, small packages and direct mail which such customers need most. the combined effect of the savings to postal operators resulting from the right of deduction which the proposal would open to them and the application of a reduced rate to a wide scope of postal services is intended to limit or even neutralise any increase in postal prices. the commission was the proponent of the universal service concept at the heart of directive 97/67/ec and considers that every citizen in the union has the right to a wide range of affordable and high-quality postal services. universal postal service providers will not be in a position to provide such a service if they are discouraged from investing and modernising and as a result can no longer compete with other operators in the parts of the market which are already open to competition. in order to compete in such markets they need a europe-wide presence and tools such as package tracing, which private and third-country operators already offer to european customers. the current vat exemption makes the required investment more expensive. universal postal operators in europe recognise such challenges and accordingly most of them support the objectives of this proposal. to conclude, i would invite members to support the commission's proposal.
draft opinion of the consultative committee on regional policy, transport and tourism. the commission has already made a number of proposals. the regional policy committee has been working very hard on this dossier because we have had the honour and hope to continue to have the honour of accompanying the development of postal services. we have therefore been looking at the possibility of introducing vat in a liberalized environment, which is what we are all striving for - and i hope that we will have achieved this important task by the end of this decade. first of all, i would like to say that the proposal the commission has put forward is a serious approach to solving this problem. but the fact remains that anything that is good can be improved. that was our approach in the committee on regional policy. there are three main things i want to address. firstly, we wanted the minimum rate of vat, 5%, to be applied as a general rule to postal services. we are aware of the legal problems that this may lead to the introduction of a fourth vat rate in certain member states. we also believe that special sensitivity should be shown here. secondly, we should consider what weight limits should apply to a reduced vat rate. the commissioner was right to comment on the universal service obligation. but there is also the universal postal convention, which also sets out consumer rights. that is why we are proposing to follow the example of the universal postal convention and to introduce reduced vat rates for postal items up to 10 kg. thirdly, our proposal for entry into force is to bring this into line with the further liberalisation of postal services announced for 2006. the commission should, after a study, draw up and submit appropriate proposals, which would then be considered by the european parliament and the council of ministers. i would be glad if these proposals from the committee on regional policy could be taken into account.
commission. mr president, it is with the greatest of pleasure that i shall reply to the question put by mrs lulling. i could have done so earlier but she did not ask for it and therefore i did not think it was necessary to reply. in answer to her question, the commission considers that any study of the postal sector and particularly those which must be done according to directive 97/67/eec should take into account the impact of vat in the sector and that it undertakes to take into account the spirit of amendment no 6. as regards amendments nos 7 and 13 proposing to delay the entry into force of the directive until each member state has achieved a certain degree of liberalisation, the commission's position is that it cannot accept linking two issues which are quite separate, but the commission could accept a date of entry into force of the directive no later than january 2006, by which date the community postal market as a whole should have surpassed that degree of liberalisation. the commission does not support amendments linking the scope of the proposed place of supply rule and reduced rates to article 2(1) of directive 97/67/ec. postal services as defined in that article are those supplied by the universal service provider. the linkage proposed by that amendment would not eliminate current distortions of competition in the postal market and therefore the commission cannot support amendments nos 1, 8, 11 and 12. for reasons of subsidiarity the commission cannot support amendments nos 2, 4 and 9 which seek to oblige member states to apply a reduced rate and to prescribe how a certain part of national vat revenue should be spent. nor can it accept widening the scope of applicable rates as suggested by amendments nos 3 and 10. such amendments would not be acceptable to a majority of the council either. as regards amendment no 5, the commission considers that the issues posed by philatelic stamps are no different to those existing today. under current legislation, stamps are only exempt when sold at face value. they are taxable in all other cases. since this different tax liability is not causing problems today, it should not cause problems once the proposal is approved.
commission. mr president, i wish to begin by thanking the rapporteur, mr manders, for his work on environmental liability. the process of getting the proposal this far has not been an easy one, as mr manders has already said. it took a long time to develop the proposal and the subsequent discussions have demonstrated a great diversity of opinion in the council and parliament. with the overall goals of the proposal in mind, the commission has shown flexibility in helping a balanced compromise to be achieved within the council. this compromise enabled the overall goal of the proposal to be preserved. the common position aims to establish a community framework whereby environmental damage would be prevented or remedied through a system of environmental liability. the main features of the liability regime itself have not been significantly altered except on one point, which is the very broad discretion that is now available to member states when deciding to remedy or otherwise environmental damage for which no solvent polluter can be held liable. the amendments under consideration by the parliament concern several key issues, on which i should like to comment. firstly, it is proposed in amendment no 6 that remedial measures in case of damage to habitats and species are only taken within designated natura 2000 areas. this means in effect that the scope of the future directive would be restricted to the natura 2000 network. the commission cannot support an approach which would narrow the scope of the future directive even further than was agreed in the common position, which in itself was less comprehensive than the original commission proposal. conversely, the commission does not believe it either justifiable or workable to expand strict liability to all occupational activities in the eu. it cannot therefore support amendment no 45. the scope of the directive is also touched upon in amendments nos 41, 42, 50 and 51 seeking to ensure that the directive should apply in future when environmental damage caused by an incident involving nuclear activities is not remedied on the basis of the relevant international conventions. the directive would in a way 'complement' the international conventions. regarding the proposed 'complementarity' approach, the commission does not believe it can work since it would oblige member states having ratified those conventions to denounce them. we believe, on the contrary, that the international liability regime for damage caused by nuclear activities should be preserved. it is true that environmental damage will only be covered by this international regime once the new protocol to the paris and brussels conventions, recently negotiated under the auspices of the oecd nuclear energy agency, enters into force. this protocol does not allow the eu to become a party to it. it thus falls to member states to ratify this protocol so that it becomes applicable. i should also like to mention that the application of the relevant international conventions will be part of the review to be conducted by the commission, as required by article 18 of the draft directive. with regard to state subsidiary action, amendments nos 11, 13, 47, 59 and 60 require member states to take remedial action in certain cases. the commission’s view, after 13 months of difficult negotiations with the member states, was that the time and conditions were not ripe for such an approach. it agreed consequently to amend its proposal. the common position leaves a wide measure of discretion to the member states in deciding whether or not remedial action ought to be taken. this was a key point in achieving agreement among the member states. the commission will therefore not support those amendments. concerning the so-called regulatory compliance and state-of-the-art or development risk issue, some amendments – amendments nos 9 and 16 – have been tabled that both seek to exclude from the scope of the directive damage caused by lawful events or which were scientifically unpredictable and to ensure that, under the same conditions, the operator will be entirely exonerated from any financial responsibility. the commission stated on the occasion of the first reading that it considered that better specification of the scope of the so-called 'permit defence' would be useful, to avoid any suggestion that this might be tantamount to a 'blank cheque' to pollute. the commission does not see that the alternative wording proposed by these two amendments would constitute a further improvement. amendments nos 48 and 61, for their part, seek to ensure that the liable operator will be entitled to invoke regulatory compliance and the unpredictable character of damage as mitigating factors. these amendments are acceptable in part and in principle insofar as their thrust goes closer to the current thinking on these issues, as it emerged from the debates that led to the adoption of the common position. amendments nos 52, 53, 57 and 58 seek to exclude from the scope of the directive good agricultural and forestry practice, as defined in some agro-environmental regulation. a total exclusion would be only warranted if the agro-environmental regulation ensured the same level of environmental protection as the liability directive. this does not seem to be the case. the commission would rather see good agricultural and forestry practices as part of the circumstances which would lead to an attenuation of liability. amendment no 17 seeks to impose proportional liability in case of damage caused by several parties. the commission considers that member states should retain the right to opt either for joint and several or proportional liability – or a mix of both – according to their national legal traditions. with respect to biotechnology, amendments nos 43, 44, 54 and 55 require the commission to present a proposal to supplement the regulatory framework on liability for economic damage caused by genetically modified organisms. the issue of economic damage to conventional and organic farmers has been discussed and is still being discussed in the context of the so-called 'co-existence' debate. insofar as this type of damage represents damage which has traditionally been dealt with by national civil liability laws, it is by no means clear whether community action is necessary and would show such an added value as being justified under the subsidiarity principle. i believe that the outcome of that debate should not be prejudged here. on the question of financial security, amendments nos 22 and 49 require the commission to submit proposals for a harmonised compulsory financial guarantee, should no appropriate instruments or markets for insurance or other forms of financial security have developed on their own. everybody is convinced of the important role that financial security, including but not limited to insurance, can play in the implementation of the directive. member states and market operators, as well as the commission, will have an important role to play in encouraging a timely emergence of financial assurance systems, products and markets to that effect. having said this, it is clear to me that member states should have the possibility to develop financial assurance solutions at their own pace which are well adapted to their own needs and institutional conditions. it would be particularly difficult to adopt rules mandating financial security when the economic operators most knowledgeable and economically interested in developing such products have been unable to do so. the commission is therefore not in a position to support the amendment on financial security. it is certainly willing, however, to encourage initiatives whereby further impetus should be given to the market and all financial security providers to develop financial security products that would meet the new demand resulting from the adoption of the directive and the fact that operators will now be exposed to liability. finally, on the issue of the extent to which damage should be remedied, there is general agreement that the polluter-pays principle should imply for the liable operator, as for the polluter, payment of all damage caused to the environment. in addition, there is a clear need to have a common understanding, within the community, of the costs of environmental damage to be borne by the polluter. furthermore, the rules set out in the proposal specify the full range of remediation actions to be carried out by the operator liable. amendments nos 31 to 36 narrow down the scope of damage remediation by suppressing the remediation of interim losses, together with suppressing the concept of compensatory remedial measures. deleting elements from this range of actions would inevitably result in the polluter not having to carry the full cost of the damage he has caused. having said all that, the commission can support either fully, in part or in principle several of the amendments proposed. those amendments are: 4, 9, 10, 12, 14, 15, 23, 27, 40, 48, 61 and 63. we all agree that we want ambitious and workable legislation. the commission sees the common position as a minimum in this respect. finding a balanced compromise will be difficult, but the commission will do all it can to help achieve this. finally, i wish to thank the rapporteur, mr manders, once more.
thank you very much, mr president. i would like to thank our rapporteur, mr toine manders, in advance. he has been very active in the committee on legal affairs and the internal market in supporting this directive and has tried to consolidate the different opinions on the scope of the directive into compromises acceptable to all political groups. i would like to thank mr toine manders once again. there are over 300 000 contaminated sites in the european union. in this context, it is important and right to adopt this directive and thus make a good deal of progress in environmental protection. i would like to make it clear on behalf of my group that we support this directive. but our group has already made a strong case in the first reading for the directive to be approached with caution, because sometimes the best is the enemy of the good. we are pleased with the consensus reached in the committee on legal affairs and internal market. it is clear that anyone who causes environmental damage in the course of his professional activities must be held accountable. the polluter pays principle is not affected. the person who causes damage is liable. the adoption of the directive marks a new step in the way of effective environmental protection in europe. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's environmental policy is properly implemented. this is the new thing that is changing with the directive. for the first time, damage to protected species and habitats will also be compensated. this is what we're about. but i repeat: let us approach this new step with moderation. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the environmental impact of the project is not underestimated. i would now like to address a few points which have been the subject of controversy in the legal affairs committee. firstly, what are the consequences of a company operating within the limits of its authorization? the polluter pays principle applies. companies that pollute the environment must be held accountable. however, i think it is a matter of fairness that anyone who remains within the limits of a licence granted to him can be confident that this will be taken into account by the authorities in the event of any damage that still occurs. secondly, compulsory insurance for damage covered by the directive. i do not think it is right to introduce compulsory insurance for environmental damage as long as reliable reference data are not available. we must work to identify these data. the directive, which for the first time also makes environmental damage subject to an obligation to compensate, is designed to do just that. but companies, and therefore the insurance industry, need time to develop affordable and predictable insurance models. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full. in concrete terms, this means that our group opposes the introduction of compulsory insurance as soon as the directive is adopted. the last point i would like to raise is the issue of farmers and forestry. without such clarification in the directive, farmers and forestry workers would be particularly affected by the provisions of the directive. farmers live by nature and with nature. it is therefore only logical that they should be excluded from the scope of the directive if they comply with good agricultural practice in their activities. this formulation is not a free letter either. good professional practice is a concept recognised in national and european law, but only recently specified by the commission. it is the expression of a recognized standard. let me conclude with this conclusion for our group: we want to adopt the directive and thus strengthen environmental protection in the european union in a sustainable way. but let us not make the mistake of taking the second step before the first one out of good intentions!
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your report. we owe it to ourselves and to future generations to take care of the environment. the environment is one of the most precious assets we have been entrusted with. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's environmental policy is not distorted. to achieve this, we must apply the polluter pays principle consistently. this means that whoever caused or was responsible for environmental damage must pay for its removal and bear the burden of proof. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full. two ship names, erika and prestige, stand for disasters that have cost the public purse and the livelihood of many people. small environmental disasters can bring a community to the brink of ruin. we will never be able to rule it out completely, but a ruthless liability for environmental damage is a deterrent to potential polluters. my group believes that no exceptions should be made. we therefore want to include areas of great uncertainty, such as the nuclear industry or genetically modified organisms, in this directive. the house of lords has received corresponding motions. finally, let me say something about compulsory insurance, which the epp group in particular is so opposed to. in germany, anyone who buys a house or owns an apartment must take out compulsory insurance against fire and natural disasters, even though in case of doubt, he is only himself in the rain. it'll be similar elsewhere. it is therefore absolutely unacceptable that operators of environmentally hazardous installations or users of dangerous substances should not take out insurance in the event of liability. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full. and do we really need to introduce less protection, less precautionary principle in this area here in the european parliament than the council is prepared to admit?
the commission is aware of the difficulties facing the community in the field of the internal market. this proposal for an amendment to the council directive of 22 july 1974 on seats and head restraints in motor vehicles is one of the two proposals associated with the 1977 directive on the fitting of safety belts. the latter directive is also amended to make the fitting of safety belts in all vehicles compulsory. these provisions follow the imposition of the wearing of seat belts in vehicles provided for by the directive of 8 april 2003. at present, only car seats have to meet the technical criteria and the stress tests laid down in the 1974 directive. all seats, and in particular those in passenger coaches, fitted to vehicles put into service in the community from july 2004 onwards will have to be tested in accordance with the directive. they shall be compatible with the installation of safety belts. the commission proposal also includes a ban on the installation of side seats in all vehicles for the transport of passengers, with the exception of urban buses with more than 22 seats. the commission cannot support the rapporteur's proposal to allow the installation of side seats on tourist coaches. it should be recalled that this issue was already discussed when the directive of 20 november 2001 on the safety of buses and coaches was drawn up. the commission was then asked to carry out a study on the safety of passengers transported in side seats. this study demonstrated the absence of technical solutions adapted to this arrangement of seats and recommended the prohibition of side seats in all vehicles intended for the transport of passengers. another study, carried out by the commission in 1996, had already shown all the dangers faced by passengers wearing a seat belt, which was unsuitable for this seat configuration. the commission cannot therefore accept amendments nos 1 and 2.
i have to say that i am not in favour of this. the commission has already made a number of proposals. in the white paper on european transport policy we set ourselves ambitious targets, particularly in terms of increasing road safety. these commit us not to blind activism but, on the contrary, to effective action in a wide range of fields. the measures in question are far from always associated with high investment costs. a good example is the introduction of the requirement to wear safety belts on all seats fitted with belts in a motor vehicle. i think that is sensible, effective and welcome. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the safety belts are not worn by motorists. i thank the commission for that. even in buses, which are already among the safest modes of transport in the european union, seat belts will help to reduce injuries and save lives in the event of an accident. the commission is now proposing that side-facing seats, for which there are no effective restraint systems, should be allowed only in buses used in urban and intercity transport. the commission does not see any particular risk to persons using these seats. this includes seats on thousands of buses that transport millions of adults and schoolchildren every day. there are no relevant accident analyses yet. i think it is quite illogical that the commission should have to do so in its proposal for a directive. the commission is therefore proposing to ban side-facing seats in comfortable coaches - and only in those coaches. these are a few individual seats, integrated into comfortable groups of seats that hardly any of us will know. the commission sees a potential danger here for the user. it does not even try to encourage or oblige industry to develop appropriate restraint systems for such seats. in all fairness, i first wondered if this was just an oversight, an accident. no, the answer was given by the discussion in committee, which led me to ask two questions, both of which i admittedly have a populist connotation: firstly, does the commission accept that people sitting in the 'cheap' side-facing seats on buses in urban and intercity traffic, which it intends to allow, pose a greater risk to safety than people using such side-facing seats in luxury buses, or, secondly, is the demand for a ban on comfortable seats in luxury buses based on envy and resentment towards those who can afford to travel in such so-called luxury buses? i think that both questions cannot be answered with a clear conscience. i therefore propose that the tourist industry should retain the comfortable seats in its luxury buses, for which we have only laid the foundations a few years ago with the directive on the use of 15 m buses. but we should encourage industry to develop such restraint systems for side-facing seats. the aim must be to protect people equally in all seats in motor vehicles, i.e. in side-facing seats and in forward-facing seats. european policy should be less about forbidding than about demanding and promoting. this strengthens our economic position in the sense of the lisbon objectives, and does not impede development.
president of the council. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i am writing to you to explain the work of the italian government, which has presided over both the council of the union and the intergovernmental conference in this half-year which is about to end. as regards the conference, italy's commitment from the outset was to agree on a high-profile document, without any downward compromise, and thus a document which would enable the union of the future to function and to take its place as a leading actor on the international scene. this commitment was accompanied by the hope that the enlarged union would be able to have a genuine constitution on the basis of the draft drawn up by the convention within the time limits agreed at thessaloniki and thus in time for the elections to renew this parliament next june. as we know, the common wish to conclude the constitutional negotiations within the 60 days we had available from the opening of the conference in rome could not be fulfilled. we must face this reality with calmness, without dramatization and mutual recriminations, but at the same time with a clear vision of the steps that must be taken from now on. the commitment not to fall back on the logic of compromises and agreements, which are hardly understandable to our citizens, has been fully respected. this is a duty which the presidency has been inspired by since the beginning of these complex negotiations, believing that the contribution of the national parliaments and the institutions of the union - and first of all, as you recalled, mr president, your own - the synthesis action of president giscard d'estaing and vice-presidents giuliano amato and jean-luc dehaene, should represent a basis on which to build a unanimous agreement without falling back on the key points of the draft which was approved last july. at the formal opening of the intergovernmental conference, the presidency intended to reaffirm these concepts in the rome declaration, adopted by the heads of state or government of the member states, the acceding and candidate countries, and by presidents cox and prodi. we have remained faithful to this line throughout the negotiations, reconciling our desire to maintain the draft convention as far as possible with our obligation to pay attention to the legitimate needs of all the member states in relation to matters which they consider to be priorities. our working method has been visible and transparent. we have fully involved the representatives of the european parliament in the work of the igc, going beyond what had been done in previous intergovernmental conferences, and we have ensured the utmost publicity and accessibility of all documents presented during the negotiations. thanks to this impressive, patient and painstaking work - for which i would like to publicly thank all those who have contributed, in particular the foreign minister franco frattini, who is sitting here beside me - we have managed to resolve almost all the issues raised by the igc participants, without substantially reducing the overall level of ambition of the draft convention. during the first few days of the conference we reviewed over 80 controversial issues on which there was disagreement between the various states. for each of these issues, with the exception of one strictly institutional point, appropriate mediation solutions have been identified. i would add that in certain respects, particularly the absolutely crucial aspect of defence, the igc has completed and improved the draft convention, by coming to the definition of permanent structured cooperation, which is fully compatible with the atlantic framework and respects the political needs of certain member states. this major step forward will be achieved in accordance with the union's own decision-making procedures, in an inclusive logic that will allow some countries to proceed more quickly, on the basis of a specific protocol laying down the military capabilities necessary to participate in this permanent structured cooperation. in practice, this point seemed very difficult to us at first. we have managed to reach an agreement, in full harmony with the nato summits, and as you know, the three pillars on which the spring council will be able to act and decide have been accepted by all. the first pillar, the structured cooperation training and operational regulation, will have to be approved by the european council. the second pillar will allow any member state to enter into cooperation at any time; the third pillar states that european defence necessary to give europe an autonomous strength and dignity to be able to sit at all tables with the other world military powers should not be understood as being in opposition to nato itself, but should rather operate jointly with it, as a way has also been found to include a european defence headquarters cell in nato's operational base in europe. the final session of the conference therefore had to concentrate its work on the major institutional nodes which, because of their particularly sensitive political character, could not be dissolved in the earlier stages of the negotiations. the composition of the european parliament and that of the commission had therefore to be decided at the last part-session; there were still some points to be clarified on the extension of qualified majority voting in the council; but above all, the way in which this vote was calculated had to be defined. the last bilateral contacts which the presidency held at close paces during the days and nights of thursday, friday and saturday, showed that it was possible to find a solution to some of these problems, although all the heads of state or government who met wanted to stress that the institutional framework of the future union should ultimately be assessed as a whole through an agreement which was general and all-embracing. the agreement on the composition of the commission and on the issue of qualified majority voting was close at hand. there was virtually no discussion about the number of members, mr president. the countries with smaller populations asked for an increase in one mp from four to five, and all the other countries agreed. on the other hand, on the question of qualified majority voting, it was not possible, despite all efforts, to find a convergence of positions. and so, after consulting all the delegations, we decided to end, with the agreement of all, a debate which was in danger of becoming antagonistic and which, at best, could have led us to those downward compromises which we had ruled out from the start. the real failure would have been a cheap deal, inadequate to ensure the future functioning of the union, its ability to present itself as a decisive political actor on the international scene. at the end of the debate, all my colleagues expressed their great appreciation for the italian presidency. these words, of course, made me and my colleagues very happy. in fact, we have counted 82 points on which agreement has been recorded: the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. the negotiating achievements of the conference, which were considered by all to be important and, i would say, not to be reopened, remain. for this reason, all the speeches that have been made at the council table have indicated that the next work of the conference will have to concentrate on the points, or rather on expectations of european businesses and economic operators. i have to clarify this point: i had the opportunity to attend a conference organised by the european business association last month in of the individual states and of europe that the european economy is a giant imprisoned by too many ropes and bows, which industrialists identify in the excesses of regulations, directives and laws that prevent them from fully competing with foreign economies. (applause) i would like to thank we must take this very seriously, because the european economy is going through a difficult period, which i fear will become even more difficult, caught as it were in a screw represented, on the one hand, by the united states economy, which is growing rapidly, being supported by an injection of 350 billion dollars decided by the bush administration, an economy supported also by tax rates which are the lowest in the western world and, on the other hand, by the economies of the countries of the far east which are in a situation of almost total anarchy, with no rules being respected either with regard to workers or the environment, nor even a minimum of fiscal control. european entrepreneurs therefore welcomed the creation of the competitiveness council, which will henceforth have to examine the measures to be taken by the european authorities and institutions from the point of view of their impact on the competitiveness of our companies. it is a sensitivity which we should all acquire if we do not want our economy to become uncompetitive with other economies. i would also like to recall the agreement recently reached on the proposal for a directive on public procurement. it is a major political agreement, which puts an end to a negotiating affair that has lasted for almost 15 years. the agreement now allows us to say that we have helped to define an important element in the completion of the internal market. i should like to thank the italian minister, mr rocco buttiglione, who drew up this agreement. however, much remains to be done to ensure that businesses operating in europe have the overall conditions of the regulatory framework and the labour market situation to ensure their effective competitiveness on world markets. this is an important commitment to be pursued in the coming months and to be put into practice at the spring european council. now we come to the important subject of safety. in its efforts to bring the community institutions ever closer to the real needs and interests of citizens, the italian presidency has worked to strengthen the security of the citizens of the union, in the awareness that, even more than on other issues, it is on this ground, which is particularly close to the daily lives of all of us, that public opinion will assess the effectiveness of the union's action. one of the central themes of our work has been the development of common strategies for managing migration flows. first, the concept of 'common external borders' has been further strengthened. in this context, the european council took note of the agreement reached on the main elements of a dedicated community border management agency. the establishment of this agency has been decided and the commission has committed itself to making it operational as from 1 january 2005. the european council also took note of the adoption, on a proposal from the presidency, of a specific programme of measures on immigration by sea, a concrete sign of the union's special attention to the often tragic phenomenon of attempts by illegal immigrants to get to our shores. we must also inform parliament of the meeting between the five mediterranean countries and the five north african countries, which took place in the presence of the presidency and the commission. these countries are being crossed by increasing migratory flows, which they call 'epic', from citizens of that continent towards europe, seen by all as the paradise on earth. these countries, urged by our individual countries on a bilateral basis, have agreed to cooperate in order to control departures from their coasts. but they have asked us, at this five plus five meeting, to be more involved in this action and, of course, to take on the significant economic costs they face in the european interest. the council therefore invited the commission to study the problem and propose solutions. the presidency paid due attention to the issue of the reception and integration of legal immigrants and to the protection of persons in need of international protection. we expect the commission to carry out a study on the relationship between legal and illegal immigration, which should also include the issue of the establishment of european-level quotas. we have taken note of the progress made on asylum, although unfortunately it was not possible, as we had hoped, to reach an agreement on the two directives under discussion, concerning minimum procedural rules and the definition of refugee status and subsidiary protection status respectively. moreover, effective management of migration flows cannot be achieved without fruitful cooperation with third countries of origin and transit. with this in mind, we have continued the process of fully integrating migration issues into the union's external relations. we have recorded the way in which the third country evaluation mechanism has been working in the fight against illegal immigration. this is a mechanism requested at the thessaloniki summit, on which we have very quickly reached an interinstitutional agreement with the european parliament by means of a regulation establishing a new programme of technical and financial assistance to third countries in the field of asylum and immigration. this programme will bring new financial resources to a sensitive area; the amount of eur 250 million is to be spent over the next five years: the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the future of the european union. on the subject of immigration, but with obvious aspects linked to the security of citizens and also to the fight against terrorism, we, as the european council, have recorded the agreement reached on the introduction of biometric data in visas and residence permits. the prospect is that this innovation will soon be extended to passports for community citizens. significant progress has also been made in the fight against drug abuse. i would particularly like to mention the political agreement on the framework decision on the fight against drug trafficking, which was achieved thanks to the patient mediation of the presidency. the european council highlighted the importance of interreligious dialogue, to which we devoted a special conference in rome in october, as a tool for the integration of immigrant communities in europe and, more generally, as a tool for understanding and cooperation in international relations. the issue of the west's relations with islam, of the christian religions with the muslim religion, is a theme that emerges in every meeting we have with the countries of the arab league. we must be very active on this issue, because there is means to deal with them. on this basis we should be able to improve our capacity to intervene, both in the field of conflict prevention and in the field of crisis management. finally, the european council noted the progress made in the development of the cfsp. acquiring more capabilities remains our first commitment and, in this sense, the decision to create a european agency specifically ability to succeed in the undertaking, and the agreement reached on the agencies is important for two reasons: first, because it develops a more flexible and efficient model of community structures, a model which will bring the union ever closer to the citizens of europe; secondly, because it is the result of a global vision capable of reconciling the interests of each country, which, if not harmonized, can delay or impede progress towards the common interest. i now turn to the other major issue of the brussels summit, namely the failure to adopt the constitution of the european union, which is a source of sadness and disappointment to me. let us go back two years to the laeken european council: what were the motives for those historic conclusions in laeken? it was a response to the need, shared by all, to give the union a more coherent and structured institutional framework. the member states agreed on three basic points: firstly, to improve the functioning of our institutions, as a result of the famous night in nice; secondly, to rationalise the legislative and institutional stratification which, after many decades, had made the union's policies and procedures less coherent; thirdly, to bring citizens closer to the construction of europe. the great novelty of laeken was the creation of the convention, which is the most ambitious and democratic institutional project in our history. we have invested years of work in the company, we have brought under one roof 105 representatives of the democratic realities of europe: the european parliament is the only institution in the world which has the power to legislate on matters of common interest. the convention has worked well and in 18 months has presented us with a draft constitution which we have described as a good starting point for the intergovernmental conference. we have also repeatedly said that the text needed only a few minor amendments, because we were convinced - and still are - that it had struck a difficult balance for the whole system of the european union, allowing it to function. the work of the convention was excellent on the following points: i am thinking of the charter of fundamental rights, the majority voting system and the distribution of political responsibilities. i am also thinking of the evolving role of the european parliament, to which the draft constitution finally gives greater powers of decision-making on the union's budget. the time has run out on other issues, in particular the way the constitution should be reformed. finally, as regards the composition of the constitution, the principle of one commissioner for each member state was already present in its essence. its practical translation was unsatisfactory but the work done subsequently by the intergovernmental conference had remedied this. as with any starting point, the draft convention was intended to serve as a stepping stone. instead, some member states have used it as a way of backing down. that is why i am here today, ladies and gentlemen, to express my sadness and disappointment. the project of european integration, last week, came to a halt and we all lost, all of us, a great opportunity. the consequences will not be dramatic, however, if we persist in the direction indicated by the convention. the problems to be solved are always those of the laeken declaration; the basic text is always that of the convention. although it is pointless to blame this or that national delegation, i must stress that our institutions cannot be shaped by the sole criterion of being able to block decisions. that is not our role, that is not the role of parliament, that is not the role of the commission. the brussels stop sign means that the council as a whole has not reached agreement on a united proposal. however, collective responsibility is not enough. now we must explain to the citizens how to protect their future: is it better to protect it alone or is it better to protect it together? is it better protected divided or better protected united? the answer is obligatory, just open your eyes. i still believe, in line with the laeken declaration, that the solution cannot be found in a sum of vetoes but in a combination of interests and aims. the right of veto is not an expression of democratic will: the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. i understand that we are currently looking for a common solution and i realise how difficult this is when there are still so many important problems on which there is no agreement. however, given these conditions, i am convinced that with more time and patience the right solution will be found. i hope, therefore, that the next european councils will return to our constitution with a realistic timetable but also with a vision of the whole which we may have lost in the course of these months. we must all show courage and imagination, which are the qualities needed for big political decisions. it is only a few days since the brussels summit and it would be premature, and perhaps even presumptuous, to propose a ready-made response. but we certainly have an obligation to reflect on what has happened and what needs to be done in the future. some people think of a vanguard of pioneering states, which opens the way to closer cooperation and can serve as a starting point for a stronger, more integrated and open union. such solutions are part of the tradition of european integration and, if we look at our history, they emerge especially in the most complex and difficult moments. we are facing one of these dramatic moments today and we must therefore start thinking about it with courage, with a sense of responsibility and with an open mind towards the future. i would like to conclude my brief remarks with a heartfelt appeal: i ask you to put your political intelligence, your foresight and your experience at the service of the first constitution of a united europe. i know that many of us in this chamber see in the european union the only winning answer to the challenges of history and politics. you are here to speak directly to our fellow citizens, you know their thoughts, and you know that people are well aware that europe is not an abstract ideal or a whim, but an elementary necessity of history. just get out of our geographic enclosure: china, india and the americas no longer represent individual countries, but europe as a whole. just get out of our time enclosure: in historical terms, the integration of the whole continent is the only chance for the survival of the nation states themselves. only europe gives us the strength to maintain and develop our regional and local cultures and traditions, of which we are so proud. if we do not all come together around our union, which we have been building for the past half century, we will lose our autonomy and influence in the world. the union will lose it, but above all the member states and our citizens will lose it too, and we will all end up inexorably on the margins of history. i suggest. the right to the enjoyment of the highest attainable standard of physical and mental health is a fundamental right, in line with the provisions of article 25 of the universal declaration of human rights. more than one fifth of the world's population is currently denied this right. the lack of care and services, supplies and information and the spread of hiv and aids undermine all efforts to eradicate poverty, which the treaty states is the main objective of community development policy, as reaffirmed in the joint declaration of the council and the commission of 10 november 2000 and in line with the united nations millennium development goals. article 35 of the charter of fundamental rights of the european union requires that a high level of human health protection be ensured in the definition and implementation of all union policies and activities. the european community's development policy on sexual and reproductive health is based on the programme of action of the united nations international conference on population and development, held in cairo in 1994, and on the key actions known as 'cairo + 5', adopted in 1999 by the 22nd united nations general assembly. these key programmes and actions specify that reproductive health should cover: counselling, information, education, communication and services in family planning; education and services in pre-natal care, safe delivery and post-natal care, with particular regard to breastfeeding and health care for newborns and women; prevention and appropriate care of sterility; prevention of unsafe abortions and appropriate care of complications arising from such abortions; care of infections of the reproductive system, sexually transmitted diseases and other reproductive health conditions; information, education and counselling, where appropriate, on human sexuality, reproductive health and responsible parenting. on 15 july 2003, the european parliament and the council adopted the regulation on support for policies and actions on sexual and reproductive health and rights in developing countries. this regulation aims to provide financial assistance and specific advice to improve reproductive and sexual health in developing countries and to ensure respect for their rights. recital 16 clearly states that the regulation prohibits the promotion of incentives for sterilisation or abortion and that abortion should never be presented as a method of family planning. it should be noted that article 3 of the regulation includes among the specific measures eligible for community financial support the reduction in the number of abortions carried out in unsafe conditions. within the framework of the european union's policy on the promotion of human rights, fundamental freedoms, democratisation and the rule of law in third countries, council regulation no 975/1999 on development cooperation policy and council regulation no 976/1999 on community actions other than development cooperation aim, inter alia, to provide technical and financial support for actions aimed in particular at the promotion and protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms as proclaimed in the universal declaration of human rights and other international instruments concerning the development and consolidation of democracy and the rule of law. finally, as regards the last question, recital 5 in the preamble to regulation no 1567/2003 states: the community and its member states maintain that every individual has the right to decide freely how many children to have and how often. they condemn all human rights violations committed to curb population growth, whether it be forced abortion, compulsory sterilisation, infanticide, rejection, abandonment or maltreatment of unwanted children.

the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your work. we are debating tonight the revision of the medicines legislation in the european union and its implications for patients and the pharmaceutical industry. in this context, it should be noted that knowledge of the manufacture of medicinal products and the mode of action of a medicinal product is not general knowledge. the complexity of the scientific context and manufacturing processes means that there will be few patients in europe who can assess the risks and benefits of a drug. this means that we need an institution that is able to evaluate the safety, efficacy and quality of a medicine for the patients. the high scientific quality of this evaluation is necessary not only for the benefit of patients but also for the benefit of the pharmaceutical industry. because if problems arise because of the side effects of a drug, the manufacturers risk a significant loss of image with financial consequences, and the patients suffer the consequences as well. in other words, the reform of the authorization of medicinal products now under consideration must guarantee the safety of a medicinal product, but at the same time provide a framework to allow and support research in pharmaceutical companies and thus strengthen the competitiveness of these companies. this not only benefits companies, it also safeguards jobs, and last but not least, patients benefit from the knowledge gained from research and from new effective medicines. with this legislation we have, in my view, managed to strike a balance between the high demands on health and the demands of industry to strengthen research and competitiveness. in a global economy with different regulatory frameworks in europe, asia and the us and with the forthcoming enlargement of the european union, this was no easy task. the joint compromise now reached between the council and parliament offers the opportunity to complete the package of reform of the legislation on medicinal products at second reading. it is a good compromise, since the key issues of legislation, pharmacovigilance, the scope of central authorisation, data protection and the tasks of the composition of the european medicines agency are essentially the ideas of parliament. it is, i believe, a tailor-made adaptation of legislation to scientific progress and economic developments for the benefit of the patient. let me briefly comment on the main issues: a particularly important aspect of the pharmaceutical reform is the improvement of pharmacovigilance. the parliament has thus succeeded in establishing a high level of safety in the licensing process and effective official supervision and control. the emea will play a key role in an efficient pharmacovigilance system by establishing a database with the emea, the european agency for the evaluation of medicinal products. this is particularly important because a well-functioning pharmacovigilance system is the life insurance of patients. although not all new active substances will be subject to central authorization, as decided by parliament at first reading, the extension of the indication to include orphan drugs and a further extension after four years to include the indications autoimmune and viral diseases will make a wide range of new active substances subject to central authorization in future. the european medicines agency in london, with its structure and its way of working, as we now provide for in the legislation, ensures that scientific resources are optimally coordinated and thus a high scientific quality of the opinions is ensured. the central authorisation through the emea ensures that all patients in europe have an equal chance of rapid access to innovative, effective medicines. another controversial issue was the regulation on the protection of data. the 8+2+1 period of protection for the central and decentralised authorisation procedures now agreed in the compromise ensures that on the one hand an incentive is created for research and on the other hand the further development of proven active substances is rewarded. this uniform european-wide system of protection of proprietary data will serve the economic interests of research-based drug manufacturers and generic manufacturers and will relieve the burden on national health systems compared to the period originally proposed by the commission. the joint compromise of parliament and council puts the needs of patients at the centre, promotes research and innovation and also takes account of the competitiveness of european industry. i therefore ask you, ladies and gentlemen, to support the compromise reached in the council. as always with a compromise, not all wishes are fulfilled. but even for the controversial issues, such as homeopathic medicines, i think we have found a solution. the mutual recognition of these medicines will make it possible for all patients in europe to have access to them. and i think we have also found an acceptable solution to the wto issues, especially since this issue is not to be regulated in this legislation. the commission has promised to submit a proposal on this issue in the new year. that is why i think that the overall result is correct and that it is worth supporting the compromise. i think that a conciliation procedure with the council will not improve the result and will not solve the two questions i have raised. with tomorrow's approval - and i ask my colleagues to do the same - we will be able to put forward a future-proof legislation on medicines. i should like to thank mrs grossetête for her excellent cooperation, which is also true of cooperation with the secretariat, the council and the commission.

i suggest. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the arms embargo against the people's republic of china was adopted by the european union in 1989 following the tiananmen events. the embargo allows, on a case-by-case basis, only exports that are not linked to repressive activities and human rights violations. beijing considers that the embargo is now outdated and that the level of cooperation in all areas between china and europe and the speed of changes taking place in the people's republic of china justify its lifting. this fact is being emphasised more and more often and forcefully by our chinese partners on all useful occasions, multilateral or bilateral, and they have recently come to refer to the abolition of the embargo as a short- and medium-term priority in their relations with the european union. in terms of results, however, the abolition of the embargo against china would still allow the european code of conduct to apply, with the result that the substance of the results regarding arms exports would not change. the issue of the possible abolition of the embargo has been discussed within the european union in recent months, but there is no consensus on the need for a review. the european union recognises that the political situation in china has evolved significantly since 1989 and that important changes have taken place in the relations between the european union and china, including the quality of the political dialogue. the eu-china human rights dialogue has been established as an important vehicle for exchanging views on both sides and developing projects to promote concrete improvements. on the other hand, and this is something the chinese are particularly insisting on, the party congress last year saw a complete change of leadership in china and the current leaders declare themselves to be unconnected with the events of tiananmen. however, from the point of view of the union, in whose public opinion the memory of the tiananmen events is still alive, the issue is considered highly sensitive because serious human rights problems continue to exist in china. economic liberalisation and the country's progressive integration into the international community do not correspond to political liberalisation and there is still a long way to go to reach the standards of respect for human rights that are considered normal in our societies. the eu's policy on this subject is under intense scrutiny and non-governmental organisations, as well as the general public, expect tangible results. it should also be noted that beijing has rejected the hypothesis that the lifting of the embargo is linked to concrete progress in human rights. however, the conditions within the union are not yet in place for the lifting of the embargo to be implemented, as was clearly demonstrated to the chinese counterpart at the recent eu-china summit. it is also clear that there are different positions within the union on this issue and in particular on the attitude to be taken in the face of china's repeated demands. this will therefore require further and more in-depth reflection in the future. a decisive impulse to this end was given by the european council of 12 december last, which invited the general affairs and external relations council to review the matter.

chairman of the committee on economic and monetary affairs. – mr president, on 18 november this parliament rejected by a very large majority the commission's proposal on excise duties on petrol and diesel. pursuant to rule 68(3) of the rules of procedure, and after the commission's refusal to withdraw its proposal, i am reporting back to you to say that on 2 december the committee on economic and monetary affairs considered the matter again and reconfirmed its previous decision to reject the proposal. representing the rapporteur, mrs kauppi, who is unable to be here today, i reiterate our belief that this harmonisation effort is not justified either from an environmental or from a competition point of view. we call upon the commission to submit a new proposal and withdraw the current one in order to have a text more in sympathy with the recently adopted energy tax directive. an approach that eschews absolute harmonisation, for example with a rate band with an upper and lower limit, would be a more realistic option both in terms of chances of progress in the council, and also in terms of allowing a degree of tax competition between member states. there is also a need to coordinate taxation of fuels with infrastructure charges in order to guarantee a level playing field. for all these reasons, the committee on economic and monetary affairs calls upon the plenary of the european parliament to reconfirm its rejection of the commission's proposal on excise duties on petrol and diesel.

the rapporteur. first of all, i would like to thank my colleagues in this house, and in particular the shadow rapporteurs, for their very constructive cooperation. thank you very much. the commission had put forward a very ambitious proposal. a promising new technology, groundbreaking, based on satellite navigation and mobile communications. this technique should be made mandatory for member states for the collection of tolls from 2012 at the latest. this would have meant the abolition of all other technical systems currently in existence based on microwave short-range communications. the main objective of the draft law, technical interoperability, should be achieved in this way. that is the right objective. in a common internal market, technical barriers must not impede the flow of traffic and hence the transport of goods. the commission has not yet received any information on the extent of the damage caused by the accident. they create problems for international road traffic and hinder the smooth functioning of the internal market. the draft law also aims to ensure interoperability of contracts. one contract per user, valid throughout europe, is a good thing! this is also an ambitious objective, given that there are still many harmonisation measures to be implemented within the eu, both in the tax, administrative and legal fields. as rapporteur for this house, however, i could not follow the commission's proposal on technical interoperability. why is that? the problem we are facing is that the new tolling technology which the commission is favouring and which is currently being developed only in germany, does not work yet. but a technique that doesn't work doesn't actually exist. can the legislator make a binding prescription for something that does not exist? is it the legislator's job to prescribe a particular technique? i mean, no, it's not that. the market should decide on the use of certain techniques. this is the view of the majority of my colleagues. we have therefore agreed not to follow the commission on this point. we want to be more technically neutral. we say that the real objective to be achieved is the technical interoperability of the different systems. the users, the operators from the different member states where electronic toll systems are in use, tell us that this is feasible. we are also insisting on this in the amended proposal before us. technical interoperability must be achieved. this means that, in the final analysis, it is only when an existing technology cannot be made to communicate with other technical systems that it must be replaced. it is important to us that subsidiarity be maintained. the decision on whether to levy tolls, on which vehicles and on which routes or types of roads, must in principle remain the responsibility of the member states. it is equally important for me to emphasise once again that data protection must be given the highest priority. we don't want to get to the glass driver. and another thing: i have emphasized again and again in all the discussions that i think satellite technology is extremely important. i am convinced that we are doing the right thing by building the european satellite system galileo. i would like to stress this point in a lasting way by tabled a stronger amendment for the first reading. i would like to emphasize that this amendment was originally tabled in the committee on regional policy, transport and tourism by my esteemed colleague brigitte langenhagen, but i did not think it could be supported by a majority in the committee on regional policy, transport and tourism because of its rigidity. but for the vote tomorrow in the plenary, i expect that this parliament will support this clear vote in favour of a european satellite navigation system of its own, which will make us europeans independent of others. i would like to ask you once again for your support. in conclusion, i would like to say this: i am not saying that the commission should not be involved in this. the commission's original proposal would have been a huge opportunity for german industry. the new innovative tolling technology could have proposed here. like the satellite system, which is not fully tested - is premature, and that i think we could perhaps have gone further, the final result of the debate is positive. i also believe that a strong recommendation for the future of the galileo system sends the right signal to the whole sector which is going to invest, is investing or is thinking of starting up the galileo system and therefore we combine support for the galileo system - which is a european system - with the necessary flexibility so that each country can, however, take the appropriate measures, provided they are compatible and interoperable systems, although there may be other solutions in the event of problems arising, for example, with investments, the amortisation of investments, etc. in reply to mr swoboda's question very briefly about the negotiations with the united states, i would like to say that they have made very positive progress. in recent times, with regard to the problem of overlapping frequencies, we have already fully solved -
