and we have found formulae which do not harm the quality of the galileo system in any way and which at the same time give the security guarantees demanded by the united states. we have to solve the overlap that exists - as the americans say - between our open signal and one of their signals. we have made it very clear that we cannot accept the initial proposal from the united states - to go from 1 5 1 5 (what we would like) to 11 (the americans' demand) - because we believe that we would lose a great deal of quality in the service. we also understand that in the 15th we did not create any security difficulties for the american security system. we are in any case finishing these discussions, but i hope, ladies and gentlemen, that there will be no further difficulties and that we will have a total solution, since almost all the issues are practically resolved, which i am very glad about. in addition, countries such as china, india, brazil and other third countries have shown interest in participating in this project. the next point i want to make very briefly is the case of london, although other cities can be considered. ladies and gentlemen, the area in which we are calling for interoperability and compatibility does not apply to the london toll, for a number of reasons, firstly because it is a local area, which does not fall within our competence, and, above all, because there is no equipment in london. in addition, it is noted that in cases where it would entail an exorbitant and unbalanced cost for the objective pursued, it would not apply. mr president, i conclude by saying that for reasons of brevity and to ensure accuracy in a field which has a very strong technical component, we believe that the wording - not the substance - of amendments nos 2, 14, 18 and 32 should be partially revised. i would also like to thank mrs sommer for her excellent work and the honourable members for their cooperation, and i would like to conclude that this is the technological system which will later enable us to apply the euro-vignette directive properly. today we are not talking about tolls themselves, but about the methods of collecting tolls in a simpler way, which creates fewer problems for users and facilitates the functioning of the internal market.

i have to say that i am not in favour of this. the commissioner! have a good night. i found my place in time for the start. i think the debate we are having tonight in the small circle of insiders is about a technology, about the chp technology, which is recognised as an environmental policy instrument. the application of chp is more diverse than district heating in northern europe or in industrial plants, e.g. ceramics or paper industry, in other countries. chp is the simultaneous generation of electricity and heat in a process, which usually leads to energy savings. this directive focuses on highly efficient cogeneration, i.e. cogeneration processes which achieve energy savings of at least 10%. this is one of the reasons why chp is an instrument for increasing energy efficiency and thus contributes to increasing security of supply. the blackouts of the past few months have shown that we need to do something about it. let me say a few words first about the council's dealings with parliament. we have been negotiating this directive since september 2002, almost a year and a half. the first reading was controversial during the parliamentary year, the second reading was much more consensual. the council's common position unfortunately accepted only a few of the european parliament's amendments. the council was also unable to show much flexibility and openness to our demands at second reading. i think that from the very beginning a blockade was adopted and it was repeated that there was no room for negotiation beyond the common position. the way in which the negotiations were conducted, in my view, was somewhat more akin to a consultation procedure than a codecision procedure. the compromise was ultimately accepted not because i, as rapporteur, was fully satisfied with the result but because the council had put pressure on parliament to allow it no longer sufficient time for a conciliation procedure when the council had exhausted its time-limits. pressure was also exerted by the statement that a number of delegations in the council considered a directive on the promotion of chp not necessary and that the directive would be blocked in the event of parliament's demands going beyond this promotion. let me come to this and say what i think is positive about this directive. the purpose of the directive is to promote cogeneration technology which can contribute to increasing energy efficiency and improving security of supply. combined heat and power is being placed on the european union's energy policy agenda. the directive will give us a policy on cogeneration in the union. the definition of cogeneration is being standardized in europe, thus creating a uniform understanding of cogeneration. the determination of high efficiency cogeneration shall be carried out using a two-step approach using annexes ii and iii to this directive. first, the calculation of the cogeneration electricity is based on the prothermo method, as set out in annex ii. on this basis, and taking into account the results of a cen workshop currently under way, the commission is to adopt a harmonised calculation for cogeneration electricity and the necessary guidelines for its application. secondly, to qualify as a highly efficient cogeneration plant, energy savings of at least 10% must be achieved, as specified in annex iii. the commission will present harmonised reference values for the calculation of energy savings. this was an important success and an important demand of the european parliament. the order of application of annexes ii and iii shall not be harmonised. the alternative calculation methods currently in force should therefore be harmonised in a new commission proposal for a directive. a uniform approach to the issue of a proof of origin is already ensured. this is important for crossborder trade and for the internal market. member states are required to compile statistics on their national production of electricity and heat from cogeneration. member states must continue to analyse their potential for the use of chp and report to the commission. the commission shall evaluate these reports and, where appropriate, present an action plan for the development of cogeneration in the union. national support and instruments should be geared to primary energy saving. legal and other obstacles should be removed. a definition and a specific position for micro-chp is created. micro-chp plants are defined in this directive as those with a maximum capacity of 50 kilowatt hours. micro-chp operators may use certified values for the necessary calculation. it reduces their administrative burden. member states may facilitate access to the grid for small and micro-chp plants. we certainly would have liked more in that situation. what is not in the directive, what would we have wanted in addition? no specific targets are mentioned for the eu or individual member states, no specific support and no sufficient facilitation for micro chp plants, so that market penetration is unfortunately not encouraged in the coming years. there are no concrete measures to increase the share of cogeneration in total electricity generation in europe and the network access for cogeneration is not sufficiently regulated in terms of promotion. there is no harmonisation of the calculation method at present. rather, alternative methods are allowed until 2010. the commission has not excluded from the scope of the directive the use of cogeneration technology based on nuclear energy. the european parliament would certainly have liked a more ambitious directive. but at least it creates a uniform understanding of cogeneration and lays the foundations for the promotion of cogeneration in europe. the commission is proposing to harmonize the calculation methods for cogeneration electricity and primary energy savings. the member states must deal with the technology by evaluating the capacity of national production and its potential and reporting to the commission. the commission is encouraged to present an action plan for the development of chp if it does not observe an increase in chp applications. the european community has thus adopted a policy on cogeneration. this is a great success for the european union. i would like to conclude by calling on the member states to identify and exploit their potential for the expansion of cogeneration as quickly as possible and to remove all obstacles to the increase in the share of cogeneration, and by calling on the commission to adopt as soon as possible a new directive on a european support framework and complete harmonization in the energy market. i would like to thank the co-rapporteurs, the shadow rapporteurs and all the other colleagues who have contributed, as well as the commission. i think we worked well together. i have repeatedly stressed in the discussions that a compromise is, in my opinion, one which hurts all sides a little. i hope that everyone is equally hurt, and i hope that tomorrow, when we adopt the compromise proposals, we will have a sensible directive. i would like to thank the commissioner for his reply. in view of the dramatic developments in georgia in recent weeks and the imminent presidential elections on 4 january, six groups in the european parliament have requested this urgent debate. with a peaceful and, thank god, bloodless revolution, the georgian people have earned our respect. this is a convincing proof of the desire of the georgian people for democracy, despite the oppressive economic hardship. now is the chance for a fresh start. the right elections are a prerequisite for a stable development in georgia. a lot of time has been wasted since the revolution 12 years ago, the state coffers are surprisingly empty. not only the european union, but many parts of the world have given financial aid to georgia, but the population has left empty handed. the georgian people have high expectations of their new president: the establishment of a democratic order and the satisfaction of the existential needs of the population. i thank the european parliament for making it possible for us to go to the elections with a special delegation; the european parliament has already expressed its concern about the situation in georgia. the european union's heads of state or government have just reaffirmed their commitment to building a balanced and reciprocal strategic partnership with russia, based on the values of the rule of law, democracy, human rights and fundamental freedoms and the free market economy, at the brussels summit. the governments of the member states and the european parliament must, however, face the fact that such a strategic partnership is only possible with states that keep their promises. russia has not respected its international commitments to georgia, which it made in istanbul in 1999, and this attitude has made democratic development in an already weakened region very difficult in the past. i can only hope that in future russia will support constructive negotiations in all parts of georgia, as the osce has been treating since 1999, and will not further impede democratic development. russia has a key role to play in georgia and the whole of the south caucasus. we must address this in the european parliament in our discussions on relations with russia. but now we must help georgia to overcome its crisis.
i would like to thank the commissioner for his reply. an ancient christian kingdom that had long resisted all conquerors became a russian colony. then, after world war i, there was the caucasian spring of nations, which is often forgotten. it was ended by lenin, who did not adhere to his own principles of nationality. then, with the end of the soviet union, there was a strong freedom movement. we must not forget that the freedom movement in the soviet union started very strongly and very early on from georgia. we also owe a great deal to georgia in terms of the breaking of the iron curtain. then came the assassination of president gamsachurdia. the internal turmoil, the so-called separatism, the era of the shevardnadze, which has now ended, thank god, without bloodshed, came. and now the country is at the point where it finally has a chance to move towards a truly free system. we must be aware that this country, after a long period of foreign domination, is finally getting a chance to become what it has been throughout history, a truly independent peace-making factor in a very important and very dangerous region. and that is why we must insist that russia fulfils the commitments it made to the osce in 1999. if we are often very arrogant in demanding that small countries fulfil obligations which have often been forced upon them, then we must also demand that a great power which has voluntarily assumed these obligations fulfils them to the letter. i agree with ursula schleicher when she says that russia cannot be a partner for us if it does not fulfil its obligations on this crucial point. we see that there are other powers that are trying to establish a certain dominance in the region for geostrategic and energy reasons. that is why it is our european obligation as partners to stabilise georgia, even if i do not go as far as olivier dupuis, who is calling for full membership. this is a country with a great european tradition, which is a valuable partner for us and can be a beacon of freedom in a very dangerous region.
i would like to thank the commissioner for his reply. i agree with mr meijer on many points. i am afraid that it is a bit simplistic to call the death penalty a relic of the middle ages. i am afraid that the death penalty is also a modern phenomenon in a special way: the guillotine or the electric chair are symbols of the modern age. the european union is not only a political force, but also a political force, and it is a political force, and it is a political force. we have great sympathy and understanding for the philippines; the philippines is threatened by organized crime, by separatism, by terrorism, as few countries on earth are. but on the other hand, we must make it clear that the only way to fight terrorism and violence and crime is through the rule of law and the rule of law, that the thousands of prisoners and those sentenced to death in the philippines have the same right to life as any other human being. we reject the death penalty in all cases, whether his name is saddam hussein or whether he is a great criminal. the same, of course, applies to the prisoners in the philippines. we must be clear about one thing: no state has the right - except in cases of emergency - to question a person's right to life. for this reason, and for reasons of principle, the eu is against the death penalty and is making it a membership criterion. but we must also make it a yardstick by which we measure our partners. we therefore call on the philippines, very clearly, to: a) respect the moratorium; b) review the thousand trials, many of which are questionable with judicial errors and political arbitrariness ; and c) abolish the death penalty in general, because it is not a means to help the rule of law to break through.

i would like to thank the commissioner for his reply. if we look at the demands and expectations we have expressed in our resolution, we can see the archaic state of the country in terms of democratic and civil society standards. among other things, we expect the government to respect democratic principles, to respect human and minority rights, to allow civil society and the parliamentary opposition to exercise their constitutional rights, and to prevent trafficking in human beings in general and trafficking in women and girls in particular. these are demands we made to other countries years ago and which have now been met in many areas of central and eastern europe. in moldova, these foundations of democracy and market economy have apparently not yet been laid. firstly, the situation is further complicated by the situation of the de facto regime in transnistria, which can only hold on there with russian support. we are seeing here, as in georgia - it was mentioned in the previous debate - that russia is unfortunately using its influence not to stabilise but to destabilise. i would really like our governments to make this clear in their frequent contacts with the russian side, also in relation to moldova. it is clear that economic and political stabilisation of moldova can only be achieved if this conflict is resolved. we can't do this without russia. it is to be condemned that russia does not withdraw its troops from that country by the end of 2003, as it had already promised. it is not a contribution to a solution if russia unilaterally presents a plan that prolongs the status quo. that is why a peace plan must not only be announced but also presented in moldova itself. i would like the government and the opposition to come together. we must do our part as the eu to ensure that, for example, the osce mandate discussed here can be implemented. i think we should stress again in this context the importance of multilateral approaches to the problem and we should urge russia, ukraine and romania not to take unilateral steps.
